title: Retirement Housing Options in Texas Hill Country (2026)
excerpt: Retirement housing options in Texas Hill Country in 2026 range from low-maintenance patio homes to 55+ communities. Here’s how to pick the right fit for your next move.

faqItems.q: 1) Is New Braunfels a good place to retire in the Hill Country?
faqItems.a: It can be, especially if you want strong access to shopping, services, and the San Antonio–New Braunfels corridor. The best fit depends on your drive-time needs, your monthly budget, and whether you want a low-maintenance home or a more rural setup.

faqItems.q: 2) Are there 55+ communities in the Texas Hill Country?
faqItems.a: Yes. The Hill Country has multiple 55+ and active-adult style options, plus non-age-restricted neighborhoods that still offer single-story, low-maintenance living. The key is to compare HOA costs, what the dues include, and how the rules affect daily life and resale.

faqItems.q: 3) What should I look for in a retirement-friendly home layout?
faqItems.a: Prioritize single-story living (or a true primary suite on the main level), minimal steps, and a functional bathroom layout. Pay attention to shower entry, hallway width, and how many “little steps” exist throughout the home.

faqItems.q: 4) How do Texas property taxes affect retirement housing costs?
faqItems.a: Property taxes can be a meaningful part of the monthly budget in Texas, even if you’re downsizing. Before you decide, estimate the all-in monthly cost including taxes, insurance, and HOA. For tax strategy or exemption eligibility, confirm details with the appropriate professionals.

faqItems.q: 5) How far in advance should I plan a Hill Country retirement move?
faqItems.a: Ideally 60–180 days out. That gives you time to run the numbers, tour neighborhoods at different times of day, and line up the sale and purchase timeline without feeling rushed.

opening_question: What are the best retirement housing options in the Texas Hill Country in 2026?
quick_answer: If you’re planning a Hill Country retirement move in the next 30–180 days, start by choosing the housing style that matches your daily life: a low-maintenance patio home, a 55+ active-adult community, a townhome/condo, or a single-story resale in a neighborhood with the right access to healthcare and errands. In Comal County, about 19% of residents are age 65+ (a good reminder that homes designed for “right-sizing” are a real part of the local market). The best option is the one that keeps your costs predictable, your drive times reasonable, and your future flexibility intact. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Which retirement housing style actually fits your next 3–5 years?
content_sections.p: Most retirees I talk to aren’t looking for “a smaller house.” They’re looking for fewer hassles and more predictability. In the Texas Hill Country, the right answer usually falls into one of four buckets, and the differences matter more than the zip code. Option 1: Low-maintenance patio homes and single-story resales. This is the most flexible path because it’s not tied to age restrictions. You can find one-story layouts, smaller lots, and HOA-managed exteriors in many New Braunfels-area neighborhoods. The tradeoff is that “low maintenance” is not the same as “no maintenance.” You still want a clear plan for roof age, HVAC, and foundation history before you commit. Option 2: 55+ active-adult communities. These can be a great fit if you want community amenities and a social calendar built in. The big thing to check is how the community is structured: HOA costs, what’s included, and how rules affect future resale. If you’re used to a big workshop or you want a third garage bay, some 55+ products will feel tight. Option 3: Townhomes and condos. Condos can reduce yard work fast, but you’re trading it for shared-wall living and stricter HOA budgets. I always tell clients to look at the HOA’s reserve situation and recent special assessments early. It’s boring until it’s expensive. Option 4: “Lock-and-leave” homes plus a plan for future care. Some people want a smaller home now, but they also want to be realistic about mobility later. That can mean prioritizing a wider hallway layout, fewer steps, and proximity to medical services. A “forever home” in the Hill Country is usually less about square footage and more about layout and location. If you’re still mapping your move timeline, start by clarifying your must-haves and your monthly target first, then we can line up the right neighborhoods and price points before you’re under pressure.

content_sections.h: How do you compare New Braunfels versus other Hill Country towns without guessing?
content_sections.p: The Hill Country is beautiful, but it’s not one uniform lifestyle. For retirement housing, the practical differences are what make a move feel easy or frustrating. Drive-time reality beats the map. The part out-of-area buyers miss is that two places can be “20 miles apart” and feel totally different because of IH-35 congestion, FM roads, and peak-hour patterns. If you want to be in New Braunfels for shopping, medical offices, and restaurants, you’ll want to test your real drive times at the hours you’ll actually be on the road. Healthcare access and weekly errands. I’m not ranking any provider or facility here, but I will say this: if you need frequent appointments, you’ll be happier choosing a home where the routine stuff is straightforward. Your day-to-day quality of life can swing based on whether you’re 8 minutes or 28 minutes from what you use weekly. Property taxes and “all-in” monthly cost. Texas has no state income tax, but property taxes can surprise people relocating from out of state. Before you fall in love with a house, run a realistic monthly budget that includes taxes, insurance, HOA, utilities, and maintenance. If you want a quick reality check, start with a simple list of your weekly stops (groceries, pharmacy, favorite restaurants, any medical routines), and I can help you compare neighborhoods based on what you value most. Only Cody would say this: if you tell me you want “quiet,” I’m going to ask, “Quiet at 2 PM on a Tuesday, or quiet at 9 PM on a Saturday?” In some pockets, weekend traffic, short-term rental activity, or event seasons can change how a street feels. That doesn’t make an area “good” or “bad.” It just means the right fit depends on your routine.

content_sections.h: What numbers should you run before you downsize or relocate in Texas?
content_sections.p: A retirement move usually has two math problems: what you’ll net from the sale (if you’re selling) and what your next home will cost you month-to-month. Getting those numbers clear early keeps you from making emotional decisions with financial consequences. Start with net proceeds, not just list price. People often anchor on an online value estimate, then get frustrated when the actual net doesn’t match the dream number. Closing costs, title fees, and concessions can change the outcome. That’s why I like to run a seller net sheet up front, even if you’re months away. Use my seller net sheet calculator to get a first-pass estimate, then we’ll dial it in based on your home’s condition and the buyer pool at your price point. Plan for Texas property tax rules. Homestead exemptions and your specific tax situation matter, and you’ll want to confirm details with the right professionals. But practically, the goal is simple: make sure your “all-in” monthly payment stays comfortable, especially if you’re moving from a paid-off home to something with HOA dues or higher insurance. If you’re buying, model the payment range with today’s rates. Rates and insurance can change quickly. A quick run through the mortgage calculator helps you see what the same home price looks like at different down payments, terms, and rate scenarios. One more number most people forget: budget time, not just money. If you’re moving from out of state, the cost of extra trips, temporary housing, storage, and overlapping utilities can add up quickly. A clean timeline can save you more stress than a slightly lower purchase price. My experience here: in New Braunfels and the Hill Country, the “right size” is usually less about getting smaller and more about getting simpler. The best retirement moves I’ve helped with start with clear monthly targets and a realistic timeline, not a perfect Pinterest floorplan.

content_sections.h: How do you pick a home that works now and still works later?
content_sections.p: Retirement housing decisions get easier when you treat them like a two-stage plan: what you need now, and what you might need later, without overbuilding for a future that may not happen. Layout matters more than age of the home. Single-story living, fewer steps, and a functional primary suite can show up in both new builds and resales. If you’re touring, I recommend you pay attention to door widths, shower entry, and how many times you have to go up or down a step just to do normal daily tasks. HOA rules are part of the house. Especially in lock-and-leave products, the HOA can be a feature or a frustration. Make sure the rules match how you actually live: parking, visitor policies, exterior changes, and what the dues cover. Do not ignore flood maps and drainage. In parts of the Hill Country, water patterns matter. Even if a home isn’t in a high-risk zone, you want to understand the lot drainage and the neighborhood’s history. This is one of those “cheap to check, expensive to learn later” items. If you want a simple way to narrow the field, I’ll build you a short list of homes and neighborhoods that match your budget, your must-haves, and your drive-time priorities. You can also read my New Braunfels move plan for life changes and my practical Hill Country living guide to get a feel for the tradeoffs before you tour anything.

title: Comal County property tax rate changes 2026
excerpt: Comal County property tax rate changes 2026 can shift your monthly housing cost. Here’s how to verify adopted rates and estimate your real payment before you buy or sell.

faqItems.q: 1) What is Comal County’s tax rate per $100 valuation?
faqItems.a: Comal County posts adopted rates in its annual ‘Tax Rates for all Taxing Units’ packet. In the 2025 packet, the COMAL COUNTY adopted rate is listed as 0.305015 per $100 valuation. Your total bill is higher because school, city, and special districts add additional rates.

faqItems.q: 2) Why do two New Braunfels homes have different property tax bills?
faqItems.a: They may be in different school districts, different city limits, or different special districts like MUDs or emergency service districts. Even when two homes are close to each other, the taxing-unit map can change across boundary lines. Always verify the taxing units tied to the specific address.

faqItems.q: 3) Does the tax rate going down mean my property taxes will go down?
faqItems.a: Not necessarily. Your taxable value can increase, and your combined rate includes multiple taxing units, not just the county. A lower rate can still result in a higher bill if the appraised value rises or if other taxing unit rates increase.

faqItems.q: 4) Will I keep the seller’s homestead exemption after I buy a home?
faqItems.a: No. Homestead exemptions do not automatically transfer from the prior owner to the new owner. After closing, you typically need to apply for your own homestead exemption with the appraisal district when you qualify.

faqItems.q: 5) What’s the safest way to estimate my monthly payment with taxes included?
faqItems.a: Use a tax estimator based on the correct taxing units and a realistic taxable value scenario, then have your lender quote your payment using that estimate. Avoid generic placeholders, because New Braunfels costs can vary by district and special districts. If you’re comparing multiple homes, run the estimate for each address.

opening_question: What changed with Comal County property tax rates in 2026, and what does it mean for your payment?
quick_answer: Comal County property tax bills are driven by two moving parts: your appraised value and the combined rates adopted by overlapping taxing units (county, city, school district, and special districts). For tax year 2025, Comal County’s adopted county rate is listed as $0.305015 per $100 of valuation in the county’s published consolidated tax-rate packet, and that county rate is only one slice of the total you actually pay. The practical takeaway for 2026 planning is this: don’t react to a headline about “the tax rate.” Instead, verify the adopted rates for your exact taxing entities and run a payment estimate that includes exemptions, then decide whether your budget or pricing strategy needs to adjust. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: How do Comal County property taxes actually get calculated?
content_sections.p:
If you’ve ever looked at a property tax bill in New Braunfels and thought, “Why is this so complicated?”, you’re not wrong. Texas property taxes are not one single rate. They are a stack of rates from multiple taxing units that overlap your address, and then that stack is applied to your taxable value (market value minus exemptions).

Here’s the simplest way to think about it. Your annual property tax estimate is roughly: (taxable value ÷ 100) × (combined tax rate per $100). The combined rate includes the county, your city (if you’re inside city limits), your school district, and sometimes emergency service districts, MUDs, water districts, or other special districts. That’s why two homes with the same price tag can have very different tax totals.

The other piece people miss is that the “county rate” is not the same thing as the “school rate,” and the school portion is usually the biggest line item. In Comal County, the county publishes a consolidated list of rates for all taxing units each year so you can see the pieces. The county’s tax-rate page links to PDFs for recent years (including 2025), and those documents list the adopted rates by unit. When you hear talk about “rate changes in 2026,” what you really want to know is: (1) what rates were adopted for the current tax year for your specific units, and (2) what your taxable value will be after exemptions.

content_sections.h: Where should you check the 2026 rate changes (and what numbers matter)?
content_sections.p: For Comal County, I send clients to three places first, because they’re the least interpretive. One is Comal County’s official Tax Rates page, which posts PDFs like “2025 Tax Rates for all Taxing Units.” Another is the county’s official tax estimator tool, which helps you model scenarios without guessing. The third is the Texas Comptroller’s truth-in-taxation resources, which explain what “no-new-revenue” and “voter-approval” language means in plain terms. In the Comal County “Tax Rates for all Taxing Units” packet for 2025, the adopted county rate for COMAL COUNTY is listed as 0.305015 per $100 of valuation. That number is useful, but it’s not the whole story. What matters more for your real payment is your combined rate. For example, school district rates differ by district. The same packet lists 1.074800 for COMAL ISD and 1.037700 for NEW BRAUNFELS ISD (both per $100). If you only look at the county number, you will under-estimate your annual taxes. A quick caution from the field. The worst surprises I see are when someone relocates into New Braunfels and compares two homes that feel similar, but one is in a MUD or has a special district layered on top. They budget based on a friend’s tax bill and then their own is meaningfully higher. It is not because anybody did anything wrong. It’s because the map of taxing entities is different. Before you set your max purchase price or set your listing price expectations, verify the taxing units tied to the address and run the math. If you want a shortcut, start by reading my earlier breakdown on estimating property taxes as part of your monthly payment in New Braunfels, then come back and apply the steps below to your specific street and neighborhood.

content_sections.h: What does a rate change mean for buyers and sellers in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: Buyers: the biggest impact is your debt-to-income comfort level and what you feel safe committing to each month. (I’m deliberately not giving financial advice here. Talk to your lender for underwriting specifics.) Even a small difference in the combined tax rate changes the monthly escrow portion. And the escrow portion is the part that often gets forgotten when buyers focus on interest rates. Here’s the practical pattern. If you’re shopping in a price band where you’re right up against your monthly budget, taxes can be the difference between “this works” and “we’re stressed every month.” This is why I’d rather you compare total monthly cost between neighborhoods than compare list prices. If you’re bouncing between areas like Veramendi and a neighborhood without special district layers, it’s smart to look at the tax structure early. If that’s your situation, you may also want to read the specific deep-dive I wrote on Veramendi MUD taxes and monthly cost. Sellers: taxes influence buyer psychology more than many homeowners expect. When taxes are high, buyers get pickier on condition and concessions because they’re watching their full payment. In 2026, if a buyer sees multiple similar homes, they will often choose the one that feels like it has the lowest ongoing cost or the clearest value story. That means your pricing strategy and your negotiation posture should be built around the full monthly payment reality. This is the part I say in listing appointments that some sellers don’t love at first: your home is competing against new construction incentives and against resale homes with different tax structures. You cannot control the county’s adopted rates, but you can control how you position the home and whether the buyer’s math works at your price point. When taxes push payments up, the market tends to reward homes that are clean, well-maintained, and priced inside the buyer’s comfort band instead of just above it. If you’re also thinking about exemptions, homestead filing, and what’s transferable and what isn’t, my guide to the Texas homestead exemption for 2026 is a good companion read. It helps you understand what could change after closing versus what you can plan for up front.

content_sections.h: How do you estimate your 2026 taxes without guessing?
content_sections.p:
When someone asks me, “Cody, what are taxes going to be on this house?”, I treat it like a small checklist, not a gut-feel answer. Here’s the process I use so we don’t build a plan on a bad assumption.

First, identify the exact taxing units for the address. County and school are obvious, but city limits and special districts are the ones that trip people up. Second, confirm the most recent adopted rates for those units. Comal County posts the consolidated rate packet, and it’s the fastest way to see the exact line items. Third, estimate the taxable value. If you are buying, remember that your taxable value can reset toward market value after a sale, and exemptions will not automatically carry over from the prior owner.

Then, run a scenario in the Comal County tax estimator tool. I like the estimator because it forces the right structure: value, exemptions, and rates. It also helps you compare “what if” cases, like: What if you qualify for a homestead exemption next year? What if you’re comparing New Braunfels ISD territory versus Comal ISD territory? What if the house is inside city limits versus outside? Those are all normal New Braunfels decisions, and they all change the math.

Finally, translate that annual estimate into a monthly number you can actually live with. Divide by 12, then layer in insurance and HOA if applicable. If your numbers feel tight, don’t panic. There are strategic options, like adjusting your target neighborhood, adjusting purchase price, negotiating seller contributions (when market conditions allow), or changing the must-have list. That’s exactly the kind of tradeoff conversation I walk buyers through before they write an offer, because surprises happen fastest when people rush.

If you want me to sanity-check your estimate against what I’m seeing in your pocket of New Braunfels right now, use the mid-post link below. I’ll help you spot the hidden line items before they become a monthly problem.

title: Canyon Lake Water Levels 2026: Real Estate Impact
excerpt: Canyon Lake water levels in 2026 are hovering around 59% full. Here’s what that changes for dock access, views, insurance questions, and pricing near the lake.

faqItems.q: 1) What is Canyon Lake’s water level right now in 2026?
faqItems.a: As of 2026-05-04, Water Data for Texas shows Canyon Lake at about 59.0% full with a mean water level around 886.78 ft. Because readings change, always check the most recent daily and instantaneous values when you’re shopping a specific property.

faqItems.q: 2) Do lower Canyon Lake levels reduce home values?
faqItems.a: Sometimes, but it’s usually property-specific. True waterfront and certain lakeview homes can be more sensitive because the experience changes, while many nearby homes are valued more by lot, condition, and access than by the day’s lake reading.

faqItems.q: 3) Is “lakefront” the same as guaranteed water access?
faqItems.a: Not always. “Lakefront” can describe proximity, but usability depends on the shoreline slope, cove behavior, and any restrictions or shared access rules. Verify what access looks like from the lot and what’s actually included with the property.

faqItems.q: 4) Should buyers avoid Canyon Lake when the lake is lower?
faqItems.a: Not necessarily. A lower-water year can highlight which pockets hold their experience better, and some buyers find better value by choosing “near-lake” lifestyle homes over premium waterfront pricing. The key is buying based on the experience you’ll have today, not assumptions.

faqItems.q: 5) How can a seller market a Canyon Lake home when water levels are down?
faqItems.a: Price and market the home for today’s experience and buyer questions. Clear photos, honest expectations about shoreline conditions, and a comp set that matches the property type help reduce renegotiation and keep the listing competitive.

opening_question: How do Canyon Lake water levels affect real estate in 2026?
quick_answer: As of 2026-05-04, Canyon Lake is about 59.0% full with a mean water level around 886.78 ft, per Water Data for Texas. For real estate, that usually shows up in three places: how usable the shoreline feels from a specific lot, what buyers believe they’re buying when they hear “lakeview,” and how lenders and insurers treat flood-related questions (which often depends more on mapping and access than the day’s reading). If you’re buying or selling near Canyon Lake in 2026, the smartest move is to verify access and shoreline conditions for that exact property, not just go off the headline percent full. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does “59% full” actually mean for Canyon Lake homes?
content_sections.p: A lot of people hear a single number like “59% full” and assume it’s a straight-line price impact. It’s not. It’s a useful signal, but it doesn’t tell you what you really want to know as a buyer or seller: what does the lake look and feel like from this property today, and what will a typical buyer think when they stand on the back patio? At 59.0% full on 2026-05-04, Water Data for Texas reports storage around 223,597 acre-feet versus a conservation capacity of 378,781 acre-feet. That can translate to a noticeably pulled-back shoreline in some coves, while other areas still feel “normal” because of slope, rock shelves, and how the shoreline was built out. Two houses can be priced similarly and sit a few minutes apart, but one feels like it has water right there and the other feels like it has “a view of where the water usually is.” Here’s the practical real-estate takeaway I share with relocating buyers: don’t shop “Canyon Lake” as one bucket. Shop it as a set of pockets with different shoreline profiles and access patterns. If you’re still deciding where to focus your search, start with the broader Canyon Lake area overview, then narrow down based on whether you care most about water proximity, privacy, HOA rules, or commuting back toward New Braunfels and IH-35. One more nuance: “lakefront” and “walk-to-lake” get used loosely in casual conversation. When water levels are lower, that difference becomes obvious fast. It’s not a deal-breaker either way, but it changes expectations, and expectations drive negotiations.

content_sections.h: Which types of properties are most sensitive to water levels?
content_sections.p: In 2026, I see water level sensitivity show up most clearly in three property types: true waterfront lots with shoreline rights and dock-related expectations, “lakeview” homes where the view corridor is the selling point, and short-term-rental style homes where the buyer is underwriting demand based on the lake experience. Waterfront and dock expectations. Buyers often assume “there’s a dock” means “there’s always usable water at the dock.” In practice, usability depends on the specific cove and slope. If the waterline is farther out, the experience can change even if the address is the same. When that mismatch shows up during due diligence, it can create price pressure or repair requests because the buyer feels like the marketing didn’t match reality. Lakeview homes. For many Canyon Lake buyers, the view is the emotional trigger. Water levels can change the look of the view, especially in coves. The mistake I want you to avoid is valuing a “lakeview” home the same way you would in a year when the shoreline is tight to the bank. A good pricing strategy anchors on what a buyer can see from the main living area and outdoor spaces today, not what it looked like in a listing photo from another season. “Close to the lake” without the premium. This is where deals can actually exist. A home that is not truly waterfront can still be the right fit for someone who wants Hill Country living, a bit more space, and access to the lake lifestyle without paying top-of-market waterfront pricing. If you’re comparing lifestyle options, my post on living near the river vs. the lake in the Hill Country is a good companion read, because it helps you decide what “water access” really means for how you live.

content_sections.h: How should buyers verify access, risk, and true value before making an offer?
content_sections.p: If you’re buying near Canyon Lake in 2026, your goal is simple: make sure the home you’re offering on matches the experience you think you’re buying. Water levels are part of that, but they’re not the only part. 1) Validate the experience from the lot, not just the map. Stand where you’ll actually live: back patio, primary bedroom, main living area. Ask yourself, “If I came out here every weekend for the next year, would I feel like I got what I paid for?” In lower-water conditions, you’ll notice whether the shoreline feels like a short walk or a hike, and whether the cove stays attractive. 2) Treat “waterfront” as a facts checklist. When a listing says waterfront, lake access, or dock, confirm what’s included, what’s permitted, and what’s shared. HOA rules and deed restrictions can matter just as much as the lake level. This is also where I see relocating buyers get tripped up. They’re used to different shoreline rules in other states, and they assume “lakefront equals private beach.” That’s not how most properties around Canyon Lake function in real life. 3) Separate today’s water level from long-term decision-making. Water levels can move. What stays consistent is the property’s location, slope, access route, restrictions, and how buyers shop that pocket. So instead of asking, “Will the lake go back up?” the better question is, “If the lake stays roughly in this range for a while, is this still the right purchase for my plan and budget?” If you’re early in the process and still figuring out which part of the region fits, use my Hill Country area comparison guide to narrow to 2 or 3 target pockets first. That keeps you from overpaying emotionally for a “dream view” that doesn’t match the day-to-day experience.

content_sections.h: How can sellers price and market a Canyon Lake home when the lake is lower?
content_sections.p: Sellers can absolutely win in a lower-water year, but you have to price and position the home for how buyers are shopping right now. The fastest way to create problems is to price the home as if the lake looks like it did in the best photo from three summers ago. Start with a comp set that matches the experience. If your home is lakeview, your comps need to be other homes where the view is a primary driver, not just “near the lake.” If your home is “close to the lake” but not waterfront, you’ll often compete against newer construction or larger lots farther back that still deliver Hill Country lifestyle. That’s why the marketing and pricing story has to be precise. Show the truth, but show it well. Buyers don’t want surprises. They’ll forgive lower water. They won’t forgive feeling like a listing hid it. When I’m advising sellers, I’d rather we show the actual shoreline condition with clean photos and set expectations than invite a renegotiation later. The goal is to attract the buyer who says, “This is exactly what I expected,” not the one who arrives hoping for a different lake. Have the answers ready. In 2026, I get the same three buyer questions on repeat: “How far is it to the water from the yard?” “Is there reliable access?” and “What’s the real tradeoff versus a neighborhood in New Braunfels?” If your listing can answer those clearly, it builds trust and keeps the negotiation focused on value instead of doubt. If you want a broader lifestyle fit check, my post Is Hill Country living right for you? helps buyers self-select, which is great for sellers because it reduces showings from people who were never going to commit.

title: VA Funding Fee Rates 2026 in Texas (New Braunfels)
excerpt: VA funding fee rates 2026 in Texas range from 1.25% to 3.30% of the loan amount. Here’s how to estimate your cost in New Braunfels and plan your offer.

faqItems.q: 1) What is the VA funding fee in 2026?
faqItems.a: The VA funding fee is a one-time percentage of your VA loan amount that many buyers pay at closing. For many purchase loans in 2026, common rates range from 1.25% to 3.30% depending on down payment and whether it’s first use or subsequent use. Your lender confirms your exact scenario using your COE and VA guidelines.

faqItems.q: 2) What are the VA funding fee rates for first-time use vs after first use?
faqItems.a: On the VA’s current chart, a common purchase-loan scenario is 2.15% for first use with less than 5% down and 3.30% for subsequent use with less than 5% down. If you put 5% or more down, the fee is typically lower. Always verify the rate that matches your specific loan type.

faqItems.q: 3) Do I pay the VA funding fee on the purchase price or the loan amount?
faqItems.a: The funding fee applies to the loan amount, not the purchase price. If you make a down payment, your loan amount is lower, and the funding fee is calculated on that lower number. This is why the fee can change even when the home price stays the same.

faqItems.q: 4) Who is exempt from the VA funding fee?
faqItems.a: Some buyers are exempt, including Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability and certain surviving spouses receiving DIC, among other specific scenarios listed by the VA. Your lender will verify exemption status based on your COE and documentation available by closing. If you think you qualify, confirm early so your cash-to-close plan is accurate.

faqItems.q: 5) Can I roll the VA funding fee into my loan?
faqItems.a: In many cases, yes, buyers can finance the VA funding fee into the loan amount rather than paying it in cash at closing. Whether that’s the right move depends on your payment comfort level and your overall cash plan for closing, repairs, and moving. Talk with your lender to compare the monthly payment difference.

opening_question: What are VA funding fee rates in 2026 for Texas home buyers?
quick_answer: In 2026, the VA funding fee for most Texas purchase loans ranges from 1.25% to 3.30% of the loan amount, depending on down payment and whether it’s your first time using a VA loan. On a typical first-use purchase with less than 5% down, the rate is 2.15%. If you’ve used the benefit before and you’re putting less than 5% down, it’s typically 3.30%. Many buyers are exempt (for example, certain service-connected disability situations), so it’s worth confirming your status early with your lender and your COE before you start writing offers in New Braunfels. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: How is the VA funding fee calculated (and what does it apply to)?
content_sections.p: The VA funding fee is a one-time charge on many VA-backed loans. It’s calculated as a percentage of your loan amount, not the home’s purchase price. That distinction matters in real life because your down payment changes the loan amount, and the funding fee changes with it. Here’s the fast way to think about it in New Braunfels: if you’re buying at $400,000 and you put 0% down, your loan amount is $400,000 and the funding fee percentage applies to that number. If you put 5% down, your loan amount is $380,000, and the percentage applies to $380,000. The fee can often be financed into the loan, which can help preserve cash for inspections, appraisal gap strategy, or moving costs. One more detail I see trip people up during PCS season: the funding fee is not the same thing as lender fees, title fees, or prepaid items. It’s separate from your rate and your closing-cost negotiation. When I’m coaching a VA buyer through numbers, I like to separate the conversation into three buckets: the VA funding fee, lender and title closing costs, and prepaid items (taxes and insurance). That keeps you from making the classic mistake of thinking one percentage explains the whole cash-to-close. It also helps you decide what to negotiate and what is simply part of the math. And since Texas is a title-company-led closing state, your exact fee line items and timing will come from your lender’s Loan Estimate and your title company’s Closing Disclosure. Those two documents are where the guesswork ends.

content_sections.h: What are the 2026 VA funding fee rates for purchase loans?
content_sections.p: The most common question I get is, “What’s the rate if I’m doing a normal VA purchase with little or no down?” On the VA’s current chart (effective April 7, 2023, last updated January 15, 2026), the purchase and construction rates for Veterans, active-duty service members, and National Guard/Reserve members are: 2.15% for first use with less than 5% down, and 3.30% for subsequent use with less than 5% down. If you’re able to put 5% or more down, the fee is typically 1.50%, and at 10% or more down it’s typically 1.25%. Market reality in New Braunfels. A lot of VA buyers assume they have to do 0% down because they can. You don’t. Sometimes putting 5% down is a strategic move if it meaningfully lowers the funding fee and strengthens your offer. Other times, keeping your cash is smarter because the home needs a roof tweak, foundation check, or a realistic post-closing repair budget. The “right” move depends on the house and your timeline, not the internet’s idea of a perfect VA loan. If you’re also negotiating seller concessions, keep the rules straight. VA allows seller concessions, but they’re not unlimited. I wrote a separate breakdown on VA loan seller credits and the 4% rule in New Braunfels because this is one of those details that can make an offer look stronger or weaker without changing the price.

content_sections.h: Who is exempt from the VA funding fee (and what about refunds)?
content_sections.p: Some buyers don’t owe the VA funding fee at all. The VA lists several exemption scenarios, including Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability (and some cases where a buyer is eligible for compensation but is receiving retirement or active-duty pay instead). Certain surviving spouses receiving DIC can also be exempt, and there are specific situations for active-duty Purple Heart recipients when documentation is provided by closing. This is where I see avoidable stress during a move. A buyer assumes they’re exempt, but their paperwork does not match what the lender can use at closing. Or they pay the fee, then later learn they might qualify for a refund if they’re awarded compensation retroactive to before the closing date. The VA has specific rules here, and your lender will follow what’s on your COE and your verified status. If your status is in progress, don’t wait until you’re under contract to sort it out. The cleanest plan is to ask your lender what documentation they can actually use by closing, then build your cash-to-close range around the conservative assumption. If the exemption comes through in time, great. If not, you still close without scrambling. If you’re anywhere close to the line, get your lender involved early and keep your file clean. It’s also a good reason to build a real homebuying plan instead of winging it. If you want a structured checklist built for how VA purchases actually work in Texas, my Texas Veteran Home Buying Plan post is a good starting point, and I also keep a PCS-focused version here: Texas VA Loan + PCS guide.

content_sections.h: How does the funding fee change your offer strategy in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: In New Braunfels, your winning offer is usually a mix of price, timelines, and certainty. The funding fee affects certainty because it changes your monthly payment and sometimes your total loan amount if you finance it. That can change your debt-to-income picture, which can change what a lender is willing to approve. I’m not your lender, but I am the person who makes sure your offer terms match what your lender can actually deliver. Only-Cody moment. The pattern I see with relocating buyers is they focus on the “VA label” and forget the house. In a builder-heavy pocket, you might be competing with incentives that make the numbers look very different. In an older neighborhood, the inspection and repair reality can matter more than whether the fee is 2.15% or 3.30%. I’d rather you understand your true cash plan, your concession ask, and your repair buffer than obsess over a percentage without context. If you’re trying to decide whether to bring extra cash, ask for concessions, or simply keep your offer clean and move faster, that’s exactly what I help my VA and PCS clients map out before we write the first offer. Here’s the practical move: before you fall in love with a house, decide what you want your payment comfort zone to be and how much cash you want left after closing for moving, repairs, and life. Then we match neighborhoods, age of home, and offer strategy to that plan. That’s how you avoid the whiplash of changing your budget every time a listing surprises you. title: Selling in Comal County: Beating Builder Incentives
excerpt: Selling in Comal County against new construction means matching the builder’s total deal, not just price. Here’s how to price, package, and negotiate so buyers choose your resale.

faqItems.q: 1) Should I match the builder’s incentives dollar-for-dollar?
faqItems.a: Usually, no. Builders package incentives to change payment and cash-to-close, and the best resale strategy is to solve the buyer’s specific obstacle with one clean, verifiable concession. The right structure often beats the biggest headline number.

faqItems.q: 2) Is it better to lower my price or offer a seller credit?
faqItems.a: It depends on what buyers in your price band are struggling with. If buyers are cash-tight at closing, a credit can be more persuasive than a small price cut. If appraisal risk is high or your home is competing with many similar resales, a price adjustment may be cleaner.

faqItems.q: 3) Do builder incentives affect my home’s appraisal value?
faqItems.a: Not directly. Appraisals focus on closed comparable sales and property features. Incentives can influence what buyers are willing to pay, but they are not the same thing as a recorded sale price. That’s why we price from comps first, then adjust for the buyer’s real comparison set.

faqItems.q: 4) What’s the fastest way to make my resale feel “as easy” as new construction?
faqItems.a: Reduce uncertainty. A pre-listing inspection or documented repairs, clean disclosures, and simple contract terms create confidence. Pair that with a comp-backed price and one clear concession option, and you remove the reasons buyers default to the builder.

faqItems.q: 5) How do I know which builder communities I’m competing with?
faqItems.a: We look at buyer showing behavior, the most similar price points, commute patterns, and what’s actively being marketed nearby. In New Braunfels and north Comal, the comparison set can shift quickly as new phases open and incentives change month to month.

opening_question: How do you sell your Comal County home when builders are offering big incentives?
quick_answer: Yes, you can absolutely win against new construction, but you have to compete on the buyer’s full math: monthly payment, cash-to-close, and perceived risk. National builder data shows incentives are common right now. NAHB reported 64% of builders offering sales incentives and 37% cutting prices (April 2026). The resale homes that still move are the ones with a comp-backed price, a clean inspection story, and a concession plan that feels simple to a buyer. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What are builders really competing with in New Braunfels and Comal County?
content_sections.p: Most sellers think the competition is the builder’s list price. In real life, buyers compare your home to a bundle: the builder’s price, their advertised rate (usually tied to a preferred lender), closing cost help, and upgrades that make the house feel move-in ready on day one. If your home is in New Braunfels or north Comal, you feel this most in neighborhoods with active new phases nearby and a steady flow of relocating buyers who want something turnkey. Here’s the tricky part. Builders often protect their recorded sale prices because that helps their future appraisals and marketing. Instead of a huge public price cut, they use incentives that change the buyer’s monthly payment and cash-to-close without moving the headline number as much. That means a resale home can look “more expensive” even when it is actually the better value. My local reality check. In Comal County, I see buyers talk themselves into new construction because it feels simpler. They think new means fewer surprises, and they assume the builder’s incentives make the payment unbeatable. Sometimes that’s true. Often it is not. The sellers who win are the ones who make the resale feel just as easy to say yes to: clear condition, clear terms, and a price that makes the comparison obvious.

content_sections.h: How should you price a resale home when builders are using incentives?
content_sections.p: You cannot out-market a math problem. When a builder is advertising a rate buydown or large credits, buyers are translating that into a monthly payment story. Your pricing strategy has to start with comps, but the finish line is the buyer’s payment and cash-to-close comparison. Insight: treat incentives like a competing “discount,” not free money. A builder’s incentives are real value, but they are rarely free. They often require the buyer to use a preferred lender, close on the builder’s timeline, and accept the builder’s contract terms. Your advantage as a resale seller is flexibility. You can negotiate structure. You can solve a buyer’s specific problem. That is why I like building a plan that includes a price position plus one clean concession option, rather than trying to match every promotion line-by-line. Insight: the best pricing isn’t “lowest,” it’s “easiest to choose.” If the builder’s offer makes their home feel like the safer choice, your price has to create a clear why. That might mean pricing a touch sharper than the obvious comp range, or it might mean staying in range but pairing it with a simple credit that reduces a buyer’s cash-to-close. If you want a deeper walkthrough of how I build comp-backed ranges, see my New Braunfels home pricing strategy (2026). When sellers ask me “Should I just match the builder’s credit?” my answer is usually no. Match the buyer’s problem. If the buyer is payment-sensitive, a credit that supports a rate buydown can matter more than paying for cosmetic upgrades. If the buyer is cash-tight after a move, closing costs are usually the lever. If they are worried about condition, your lever is inspections and repairs. The winning strategy depends on which buyer pool your neighborhood is attracting right now.

content_sections.h: What concession strategies actually work without giving away your equity?
content_sections.p: Concessions work when they are simple and tied to a buyer’s decision point. They backfire when they look like desperation or when they create extra uncertainty. The goal is not to “pay buyers.” The goal is to remove the last obstacle that keeps a buyer from choosing your resale over the builder model. Insight: one clean credit beats a complicated menu. A single, clearly stated seller credit (with the right price positioning) is easier for a buyer and their lender to process than a long list of promises. In Texas, everything still has to be written into the contract correctly and supported by the lender’s rules. If you want the buyer-facing version of this, my post on New Braunfels seller concessions breaks down what buyers actually care about when they compare offers. Insight: pre-inspection can be your “incentive.” Builders sell certainty. You can too. A pre-listing inspection (or at least a strong repair and disclosure plan) reduces the fear of “what will we find?” That is a real value add when a buyer is comparing your 2012 home to a brand-new build with warranties. It also protects you from re-trading late in the deal. Insight: make the resale advantage obvious. Resale homes often bring things builders cannot: mature landscaping, larger lots in established sections, better yard usability, and a location that is already fully lived-in. The part buyers relocating from Austin often miss is that some “brand-new” communities feel great on a Saturday tour, but weekday traffic patterns and school-route congestion can change the experience. You do not need to sell fear. You just need to help buyers compare reality. One more note that matters: builders can sometimes offer incentives that look huge, but the terms can be very specific. Encourage buyers to compare the full loan estimate and the total cash-to-close. I regularly see situations where the headline credit is real, but the fees and rate structure change the net benefit. That is why a resale seller’s plan should be built around what buyers can verify, not what marketing signs promise.

content_sections.h: What should your negotiation plan look like when you’re up against a builder?
content_sections.p: Your negotiation plan should assume the buyer has options. That is not bad news, it is clarity. If builders are widely using incentives, it means they are actively managing affordability and inventory. NAHB’s April 2026 Housing Market Index update shows incentives have stayed elevated, with the share of builders offering incentives reaching 60%+ for more than a year. That is the environment resale sellers are negotiating in. Step one: decide your “walk-away” number before showings start. When you have builder competition, the worst time to decide how far you will go is after a buyer asks for concessions. We set a firm bottom line based on your net proceeds goal and your timeline. If you want to see your numbers clearly, start with the seller net sheet so you know what each concession actually costs you. Step two: negotiate structure, not just price. Price is only one lever. If the buyer needs help with closing costs more than they need a lower price, a structured credit can be cleaner than dropping the price and hoping it “feels” better. If the buyer is worried about condition, a repair credit or pre-agreed repairs can be more persuasive than a discount. The point is to solve the decision. Step three: control the story with documentation. Builders sell on certainty and speed. Your counteroffer should feel just as professional. Provide a clean disclosure package, receipts for key work, and a clear list of what stays. If the buyer is using a lender, keep the contract terms simple so underwriting does not create delays. If you want a macro view of what is shaping demand in the corridor right now, reference my San Antonio–New Braunfels market update (April 2026). Then bring it back down to your street. Neighborhood-level comps and buyer behavior are what matter for your sale.

title: Builder incentives in New Braunfels: Spring 2026 guide
excerpt: Builder incentives in New Braunfels are shifting fast in spring 2026. Here’s how to compare rate offers, credits, and upgrades so you don’t overpay or misread the market.

faqItems.q: 1) Do builder incentives usually require using the builder’s lender?
faqItems.a: Often, yes. Many builders tie their best rate, buydown, or closing-cost credit to using a preferred lender and sometimes a preferred title company. You can still shop lenders, but you need to compare the full worksheet side-by-side to see the true difference.

faqItems.q: 2) Is a lower advertised interest rate always a better deal?
faqItems.a: Not automatically. You need to look at APR, points or credits, and total cash to close. A “low rate” can be supported by fees, points, or time-limited structures that may or may not fit your plans.

faqItems.q: 3) Can builder credits be used for the down payment?
faqItems.a: Usually no. Builder incentives are commonly applied to closing costs, prepaid items, or rate buydowns, not to your down payment itself. Your lender can tell you exactly what is allowed for your loan type and how it will show on the Loan Estimate.

faqItems.q: 4) What’s the biggest mistake buyers make with incentives in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Comparing only the monthly payment without verifying property taxes, HOA, and the exact incentive terms for that home. In this area, the tax picture can move the payment more than people expect, so you want the real numbers early.

faqItems.q: 5) If builders are offering incentives, should resale sellers automatically drop price?
faqItems.a: Not automatically. The right move depends on your condition, location, and what builders are offering at your price point that week. Sometimes pricing is the lever, and sometimes it’s presentation and a targeted concession strategy that protects more equity.

opening_question: What builder incentives are common in New Braunfels in spring 2026, and how do you compare them?
quick_answer: In spring 2026, many Hill Country and I-35 corridor builders are using a mix of financing promos (like rate buydowns), closing-cost credits, and upgrade allowances, usually tied to specific homes and a preferred lender. The key is to compare offers using the same loan assumptions and look at total cash-to-close plus the long-term payment, not just the headline rate. Also separate incentives that reduce price (permanent) from incentives that only change payment for a limited time (temporary). For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What incentives are builders actually offering right now?
content_sections.p: In New Braunfels and the surrounding Hill Country, the builder incentive menu is usually some version of the same three buckets: payment help, cash-to-close help, and upgrade help. What changes week to week is which bucket a builder is pushing the hardest, and whether it is available on every home or only certain inventory homes (quick move-ins). Payment help. This is where you’ll see advertised interest rates that are lower than what you’re hearing from friends who are buying resale. Sometimes it is a fixed promotional rate through a preferred lender. Other times it is a structured temporary buydown, where the payment is reduced for a set period and then returns to the note rate. It can be a real win, but only if the fine print matches your timeline. Cash-to-close help. Builders may offer credits that can be applied to certain closing costs when you finance through their preferred partner. If you want a quick way to estimate how much cash you will need, use the closing costs guide as your baseline, then treat the builder credit as a line item you must verify in writing for your exact home and closing date. Upgrade help. This might be “design center” money, a package of included features, or credits for options. For example, The Highlands publishes rotating builder incentives that include design credits and limited-time promotions (often with end dates), and some programs are only available when using a preferred lender and title partner. Use upgrade incentives as a tiebreaker after the numbers make sense, not as the reason to stretch your budget.

content_sections.h: How do you compare incentives without getting fooled by the headline rate?
content_sections.p: The fastest way to get clarity is to force every offer into the same format: price, rate, APR, points or credits, total cash to close, and estimated monthly payment with taxes and HOA. If you cannot get a clean side-by-side, you do not have an “amazing deal” yet. You have marketing. Start with the tradeoff between points and credits. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains the basic exchange: paying points generally means paying more up front to get a lower rate, while lender credits generally lower upfront closing costs in exchange for a higher rate. Builders often package incentives through their preferred lender, so a “low rate” may be supported by a credit structure you need to understand before you sign. (CFPB overview: points and lender credits.) Ask one simple question: does this incentive change my loan balance, or only my payment? A price reduction changes your loan balance and usually your taxes tied to purchase price. A credit or temporary buydown changes your cash-to-close or early payments, but the loan balance may stay the same. That difference matters if you plan to keep the home long term. Then reality-check the monthly payment with local taxes. In New Braunfels, monthly payment surprises usually come from the full tax picture (city, county, ISD, and sometimes special districts), plus HOA. This is why I’m big on running a clean estimate early. The mortgage calculator is a good starting point, but your real answer comes from your exact property’s tax rate and HOA dues. If you want a seller-side perspective on how these incentives ripple through the resale market, I covered that in Selling in Comal County: beating builder incentives. Even if you are buying, it helps you understand what builders are competing against, and what that means for negotiations on both sides.

content_sections.h: What should New Braunfels buyers watch for before they commit?
content_sections.p: If you are shopping new construction in or near New Braunfels, your job is to protect yourself from “payment shock” and timeline pressure. Incentives can be real, but they are also designed to move inventory on the builder’s schedule. Make sure the incentive is tied to your exact home. Many promotions apply only to select homesites, specific floorplans, or homes that can close by a deadline. If you are building from the ground up, incentives can change during construction. I like to confirm what is locked in at contract, what can be replaced by a new promotion later, and what happens if the closing date slides. Know what you are giving up if you do not use the preferred lender. It is completely normal for a builder to structure their best incentive through a preferred lending and title setup. You are still free to shop lenders. The practical move is to get one quote from the builder’s preferred lender and one from an outside lender on the same day, using the same down payment and credit assumptions. Then you can see whether the incentive is truly saving you money, or simply rearranging fees. Don’t let upgrades hide the total cost. I see buyers fall in love with the model home finish level and then get surprised by what it actually costs to replicate. Upgrade incentives are helpful, but your “real deal” is still the full payment and the total cash required to close. If you want me to sanity-check a new construction offer, I will. I’ll tell you which numbers matter, which ones are fluff, and what you should negotiate next based on what is happening in New Braunfels right now.

content_sections.h: What does all of this mean for New Braunfels sellers and the local market?
content_sections.p: Builder incentives do not just affect new construction buyers. They change the competition for resale homes, especially in neighborhoods where a buyer can choose between a brand-new home with a payment promo versus a resale home with a yard, mature trees, or a more established location. Here’s the market reality I keep repeating to sellers. You are not competing against “new construction” in general. You are competing against the best deal a buyer can get this week on the homes that are most similar to yours. If the builder’s deal is a payment play, resale sellers often need a strategy that makes the buyer’s payment and cash-to-close feel competitive, not just a price drop. That is why timing and positioning matter more than ever. When incentives get aggressive, the best resale listings win by being extremely clear on condition, repairs, and what the buyer is getting for the money. The stale listings are the ones that look like “average plus wishful pricing.” In New Braunfels, that gap is what creates longer days on market and bigger concessions. If you’re thinking about selling in the next 30 to 180 days, a good next step is a comp-backed value range for your neighborhood, plus a plain-English plan for how to counter whatever builders are offering at your price point. You can start with a pricing baseline at what your home may be worth, and then I’ll help you translate that into an actual list price and negotiation plan.

title: Home-Sale Contingency Offers in Texas: New Braunfels
excerpt: Home-sale contingency offers can work in New Braunfels, but only when the dates, backup-offer terms, and proof of sale are tight. Here’s how to negotiate it in 2026.

faqItems.q: 1) Are home-sale contingency offers common in Texas?
faqItems.a: They can happen, but they are not always common in competitive segments. In Texas, they are often structured using TREC’s Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer (10-6), which sets deadlines and what happens if the seller receives another offer.

faqItems.q: 2) What’s the biggest risk with a contingent offer?
faqItems.a: Timing and uncertainty. If your current home does not close and you do not receive proceeds by the deadline in the addendum, the contract can terminate or you may have to waive the contingency to keep the deal alive.

faqItems.q: 3) Can a seller accept a backup offer in Texas if I’m contingent?
faqItems.a: Yes. The contingency addendum can allow the seller to notify you after accepting another offer and require you to waive the contingency within a set number of days, or the contract terminates. The details depend on the terms negotiated in the addendum.

faqItems.q: 4) Can I waive the home-sale contingency later?
faqItems.a: Often, yes, but only if you can still close without your sale proceeds. Before you write the offer, decide whether you can bring additional funds, change loan terms, or walk away if the seller forces that decision.

faqItems.q: 5) Is a home-sale contingency the same as the Texas option period?
faqItems.a: No. The option period is a negotiated time window that gives a buyer the unrestricted right to terminate for any reason, typically used for inspections and due diligence. A home-sale contingency is tied to the sale of the buyer’s other property and is usually handled with a specific addendum.

opening_question: Can you win a New Braunfels home with a home-sale contingency in 2026?
quick_answer: Yes, but in Texas you have to treat a home-sale contingency as a negotiation package, not a single line in the contract. Most buyers do this using TREC’s Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer (Form 10-6), which sets the deadline for receiving proceeds from the sale of your current home and what happens if the seller gets a better offer. The way you structure dates, proof of your sale, and your plan B matters as much as price. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does a home-sale contingency mean in a Texas offer?
content_sections.p: In plain English, a home-sale contingency means: you will buy the new home only if you receive the proceeds from selling your current home by a specific deadline. In Texas, that is commonly handled with the TREC Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer (10-6). It ties your purchase to your sale and spells out the key dates and consequences. Here’s the part most buyers miss. It is not enough that your current home is under contract. The addendum is built around receipt of proceeds. If your sale is delayed, doesn’t fund on time, or the net proceeds come in later than expected, your contingency can fail. That is why the deadline you propose is a negotiation point, not a formality. The other big feature is how Texas handles pressure from other offers. The addendum gives the seller a path to say, “We accepted another offer, waive your contingency by X days or the contract terminates.” That “fish or cut bait” moment is why contingency offers feel risky to sellers. Your job as the buyer is to shrink that risk with a clean timeline and credible evidence that your home will sell. If you are already learning the Texas contract timelines, you’ll also want to understand how the Texas option period protects earnest money in New Braunfels. The option period and a home-sale contingency solve different problems, but sellers often react to both as “uncertainty,” so you have to be intentional about how the whole package reads.

content_sections.h: When does a contingency offer work in New Braunfels, and when does it fail?
content_sections.p: A contingency offer is most workable when your current home is already under contract, has cleared major inspection issues, and is close to funding. If you are not under contract yet, you are asking the seller to take the home off the market while you try to create a buyer for your home. That is a much tougher ask in many New Braunfels price points. Market reality (what I see in New Braunfels). A lot of buyers relocating from Austin assume they can “just write contingent” like it’s normal everywhere. In our market, the seller’s fear is not that you are a bad person. It is that your home won’t sell on your timeline, and they will lose leverage, showings, and maybe their own next purchase. The fastest way to calm that fear is showing you are already executing: professional photos scheduled, a realistic list price backed by comps, and a marketing plan that is already in motion. A contingency offer tends to fail when the seller has multiple clean options and your offer does not compensate them for the extra uncertainty. Compensation does not always mean paying more. Sometimes it means tighter dates, fewer moving pieces, clearer documentation, and fewer opportunities for surprises. If you want a bigger-picture view of the steps and decision points buyers face in this region, start with my Hill Country home buying checklist. It helps you see where a contingency fits, and where you should get ahead of lender and title timing so you are not negotiating blind.

content_sections.h: How do you negotiate a strong contingency offer without overpaying?
content_sections.p: Think of your contingency offer as four levers. You do not have to max out all four, but you should be deliberate. 1) Tight, realistic dates. Your contingency deadline should match the reality of your sale, not your hope. If you are already under contract, use the scheduled closing date plus a small buffer for Texas funding timing. If you are not under contract yet, it is usually smarter to delay house hunting until your home is listed and showing, or to set expectations that your offer will be less competitive than a clean one. 2) Proof that your home will sell. This is where I see buyers win. Provide documentation that you are listed (or about to list), your pricing is grounded in comps, and you have a plan to handle appraisal or repairs if your buyer requests them. In New Braunfels, this is especially important when builders are offering incentives and resale homes have to compete on value and certainty. 3) Your “backup offer” response plan. The addendum gives the seller a way to force a decision if they accept another offer. Before you write, decide what you will do if that notice hits. Can you waive the contingency and still close? Do you have access to bridge financing or savings? Would you walk away and move to the next home? If you do not decide in advance, you will make a rushed choice under pressure. 4) Terms that reduce friction at closing. Clean up the rest of your contract so the seller is not stacking risks. Solid lender pre-approval, responsive timelines, and clear communication matter. And if you are trying to line up all the “money” pieces, don’t skip the cost side of the equation. My plain-English closing cost breakdown is a good starting point, and we can tailor it to your price range and loan type. I’ll say this as directly as I can: a contingency offer is not automatically “bad.” It is just unfinished until we build the rest of the strategy around it. That is exactly the kind of thing I walk buyers through before we ever hit submit on an offer.

content_sections.h: What should you do before you write a contingent offer?
content_sections.p: Before you write, you want a decision tree, not a pep talk. First, get clear on whether your current home is (a) not listed yet, (b) listed but not under contract, or (c) under contract and close to funding. The closer you are to (c), the more your contingency will be treated like a timing issue instead of a major risk. Second, confirm your numbers. If your sale nets less than expected, your down payment and cash-to-close can change fast. This is where buyers get surprised, especially if they are carrying a higher-rate mortgage on the new home or they are trying to keep reserves. We can map this alongside your pre-approval so you are not guessing. Third, line up your next step if the seller pushes back. Sometimes the right move is not “make the contingency stronger.” It is to change the plan: sell first, negotiate a leaseback, target homes with longer closing flexibility, or focus on listings that have been sitting longer. The best strategy depends on your timeline and your tolerance for risk. If you want a structured plan, start with my New Braunfels buyer guide, then tell me your current-home status and your target move date. I’ll help you build an offer strategy that fits the neighborhood and price point you are actually shopping, not a generic script.

title: New Braunfels Housing Market: March 2026 Stats Now
excerpt: New Braunfels housing market update: March 2026 Comal County stats show higher prices, more listings, and longer timelines. Here’s what to do next.

faqItems.q: 1) Is New Braunfels a buyer’s market in 2026?
faqItems.a: Parts of it are leaning that way, mainly because inventory is higher and buyers have more choices. The right answer depends on your price band and neighborhood, so you want comps plus current active competition.

faqItems.q: 2) What does 6.9 months of inventory mean?
faqItems.a: Months of inventory estimates how long it would take to sell the current supply at the current pace. Around 6–7 months typically signals a more balanced market where pricing and presentation matter a lot.

faqItems.q: 3) How long does it take to sell a home in New Braunfels right now?
faqItems.a: Timelines vary by condition, price band, and location, but March 2026 data showed days on market around 107 in Comal County. A well-positioned home can sell faster, while an overpriced home can sit much longer.

faqItems.q: 4) Are home prices dropping in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Not across the board. March 2026 Comal County data showed a median sale price of $459,900, up 6.6% year over year, but pricing pressure can still show up through concessions, repairs, or price reductions on stale listings.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I do first if I’m thinking about selling in 2026?
faqItems.a: Get a comp-backed pricing range and a realistic net proceeds estimate before you pick a list price. That one step prevents most of the expensive mistakes sellers make when inventory is higher.

opening_question: Is the New Braunfels housing market shifting in spring 2026?
quick_answer: Yes. In March 2026, Comal County’s median sale price was $459,900 (up 6.6% year over year) while closed sales were 303 (down 6.2% year over year). Active listings were 2,028 (up 11.4% year over year) and months of inventory sat at 6.9, which means buyers generally have more choices and sellers have to be more precise on price and presentation. The typical timeline also stretched, with days on market around 107 and total days (list to close) around 140. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What do March 2026 Comal County numbers mean for New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: A quick clarification before we talk strategy: the cleanest public monthly dashboard I can share for New Braunfels is reported at the Comal County level (Texas REALTORS® / Four Rivers Association of REALTORS®). New Braunfels has listings on both the Comal and Guadalupe sides, but Comal County is still the best single snapshot for the “feel” of spring 2026 locally. Here’s the headline mix for March 2026: median price $459,900 (up 6.6% YoY), closed sales 303 (down 6.2% YoY), active listings 2,028 (up 11.4% YoY), and months of inventory 6.9 (up 1.2 YoY). That combo is why so many people feel two opposing things at once: “prices still aren’t cheap” and “buyers finally have choices again.” Both can be true. When inventory is close to 7 months, you usually see a bigger spread between the homes that are positioned correctly and the ones that are not. The well-priced, clean, easy-to-show homes still move. The “we’ll just try a number” homes sit, get reduced, and then sell for less than they would have if they’d launched correctly. If you’re a seller, start with your numbers: I’d use a local CMA plus a realistic net proceeds estimate so you’re looking at reality, not just a list price. Then we tighten it with comps and adjust for what buyers are actually rewarding right now. If you want the bigger regional context too, here’s a related update I published earlier: San Antonio–New Braunfels market update (April 2026).

content_sections.h: If you’re buying, should you wait or act now?
content_sections.p: In spring 2026, the question is usually not “Should I wait for a crash?” It’s “How do I buy without overpaying or losing the home I actually want?” With 2,028 active listings and 6.9 months of inventory, buyers tend to have more leverage than they did during the peak frenzy years, but that leverage shows up in specific ways. What I’m seeing right now is that buyers win by being selective, not passive. Waiting “for a better deal” without a clear plan can backfire if rates move, if the specific neighborhood you want stays tight, or if you burn a season of family logistics. Instead, pick your criteria, pick your payment comfort zone, and then negotiate hard on the homes that actually fit. The fastest way to make this real is to model your payment and cash-to-close. Use the mortgage calculator and the closing cost breakdown, then we tailor it to your exact loan type (conventional, FHA, VA) and your timeline. Also, keep your eye on timing. With days on market around 107, you’ll see more listings go stale. That creates opportunity, but it’s not automatic. The “stale listing discount” usually only appears when (1) the home was overpriced at launch, (2) the seller has a clear next move, and (3) your offer solves a problem: certainty, timing, or hassle. I help my buyers build offers that feel low-risk to the seller without giving away the farm. One more local-only reality: a lot of out-of-area buyers still treat New Braunfels like it’s one single market. It’s not. In the same week, I’ll see one pocket where homes are moving quickly because the price point hits the demand band, and another pocket where similar homes sit because the payment is just high enough to shrink the buyer pool. That’s why you don’t want to make timing decisions off a national headline. That’s also why the “average” days on market number can mislead you. If your target home is move-in ready and priced in a high-demand band, it can attract multiple serious buyers quickly. If it is overpriced, has functional layout issues, or sits in a band where fewer buyers qualify at today’s rates, it can sit long enough that the negotiation picture changes completely. When I’m coaching buyers here, I’m less focused on national narratives and more focused on two lists: (1) what your must-haves cost right now, and (2) what your must-haves cost in the neighborhoods you would accept as backups.

content_sections.h: If you’re selling, what changes in a 6.9-month-inventory market?
content_sections.p: When inventory is low, sellers can be a little sloppy and still get rescued by demand. When inventory is higher, the market rewards precision. In March 2026, months of inventory was 6.9, and the average home’s total timeline from list to close was around 140 days. That doesn’t mean your home “will take 140 days.” It means the market is giving you a clearer penalty for mistakes. The first mistake I see is anchoring to a neighbor’s list price instead of what buyers are actually paying for comparable condition, lot, updates, and location. The second is ignoring the price band problem. If your home is priced in a range where the buyer pool gets thinner, your days on market can jump even if the home is objectively “nice.” The third is being reactive. If you launch too high and then chase the market down with reductions, you usually end up selling for less than you would have with a clean, comp-backed launch. If you’re thinking about selling in the next 30 to 180 days, the highest-leverage step is a comp-backed pricing plan plus a realistic net proceeds estimate. Start here: get a home value range for your situation. Then I’ll tell you the part most dashboards won’t: what buyers in your micro-pocket are objecting to right now (layout, lot, finishes, HOA friction, or simply payment shock). My “only Cody would say this” moment for spring 2026 is this: in New Braunfels, I’m seeing sellers lose money by chasing a “round-number” price that looks good on a screen. Buyers are shopping payments, not just prices. A $10K shift in price can move you into a better payment band for your buyer pool, and that can be the difference between a clean offer and months of carrying costs.

content_sections.h: What’s a practical game plan for May and June 2026?
content_sections.p:
If you’re a buyer: decide your max monthly payment first, then shop the best neighborhoods inside that payment band. When you find the right fit, negotiate based on the seller’s reality, not internet predictions. Your leverage tends to be strongest on homes that are (a) overpriced, (b) harder to show, or (c) sitting beyond the first wave of attention.

If you’re a seller: treat your first week on market like it matters, because it does. In a higher-inventory environment, the market’s first impression sets your negotiating position. The goal is not “the highest list price.” The goal is the best combination of price and terms you can actually close, with minimal concessions and minimal turbulence.

If you’re relocating or dealing with a hard deadline (school calendar, job start, PCS orders, lease ending): you need a timeline plan more than you need a prediction. That’s a conversation I have with clients constantly, because it’s where deals get messy fast if you wing it.

Here’s the decision filter I use with clients: if you have a non-negotiable move date, we build the plan backward from that date and treat “perfect timing” as a bonus, not the requirement. If you have flexibility, we can be more aggressive about negotiating on stale listings and asking for repairs or credits. Either way, the winning move is having a written plan: target neighborhoods, a payment ceiling, and a short list of deal-breakers so you do not make a rushed decision under pressure.
