title: Staging a House for Sale in New Braunfels (2026)
excerpt: Staging a house for sale in New Braunfels in 2026 is about photos, light, and a clean layout. In a slower market, it helps you avoid price cuts and negotiate better.

faqItems.q: 1) Do I need professional staging to sell in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Not always. If your furniture fits the space, the home is clean, and the lighting is good, owner occupied staging can be enough. Professional staging is most helpful for vacant homes, awkward layouts, or listings where you need a stronger first impression in photos.

faqItems.q: 2) What is the biggest staging mistake you see in Hill Country homes?
faqItems.a: Clutter plus dark rooms. Too much furniture and dim lighting makes rooms feel smaller online and buyers assume there are hidden issues. In practice, cleaning, bright consistent lighting, and simple furniture edits usually outperform expensive decor purchases.

faqItems.q: 3) Should I repaint before listing, or just stage?
faqItems.a: Repaint when paint is a clear objection, like heavy scuffs, bold colors, or patchy touch ups that show in photos. Staging cannot hide visible wear in person, and buyers will negotiate harder if they think the home needs work. If paint is fine, spend on cleaning, lighting, and small repairs first.

faqItems.q: 4) Is virtual staging worth it for a vacant house?
faqItems.a: It can be, especially if you need buyers to understand room scale and use. It should be disclosed and it cannot misrepresent condition or features. I generally prefer a plan that pairs strong photos, honest presentation, and pricing that matches current buyer expectations.

faqItems.q: 5) How much does staging usually change the sale price or time on market?
faqItems.a: It depends on pricing, condition, and competition, so there is no guaranteed outcome. National survey data from the National Association of REALTORS® shows many agents report staging helps buyers visualize the home and can reduce time on market, and some agents report higher offers for staged homes. Locally, I treat staging as a way to protect your pricing and reduce concessions by removing buyer objections early.

opening_question: How do you stage a house for sale in New Braunfels in 2026 without wasting money?
quick_answer: Staging a house for sale in New Braunfels in 2026 is less about trendy decor and more about making the home feel clean, bright, and easy to understand online and in person. In the Central Hill Country Board of REALTORS® February 2026 report, the broader market showed an average 82 days on market and about 6.7 months of inventory, which means buyers have options and homes that show poorly get punished. Focus first on the rooms that sell the lifestyle in photos (living area, kitchen, primary suite), then fix the friction points that trigger objections (smells, lighting, clutter, deferred maintenance). For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What matters most for staging in a slower 2026 Hill Country market?
content_sections.p: If you are selling in 2026, you are not staging for the neighbors. You are staging for two moments: the first 3 seconds on a listing photo carousel, and the first 3 minutes when a buyer walks in and decides whether the home feels like work. When buyers have choices, the homes that feel like projects get filtered out early, and that is where price reductions start to creep in. This is why I coach sellers to think about staging as a negotiation tool, not a decorating project. When your home looks clean, well cared for, and move in ready, the buyer has fewer reasons to ask for credits, repairs, and concessions. If you want the numbers side of this, I usually pair a staging plan with a comp backed pricing plan so we are not guessing. That starts with a local value range, which you can kick off here: get a New Braunfels home value estimate. Here is the part people miss. In New Braunfels, a lot of buyers are relocating from Austin or San Antonio. They are touring multiple homes in one afternoon. When a home is dark, smells like pets, or has crowded furniture, they do not interpret it as a simple clean up. They interpret it as, what else has not been maintained. That is the mental jump that costs you leverage. And in 2026, you are not only competing with other resale homes. You are competing with builder inventory and incentives that make a brand new home feel easy. If your photos and first impression are average, buyers will mentally price you below the shiny option before you ever get the showing. Staging is one of the simplest ways to keep your home in the conversation long enough for the floor plan, location, and backyard to do their job.

content_sections.h: Which rooms should you stage first (and which ones can you keep simple)?
content_sections.p: Start with the rooms that anchor price perception: the main living area, the kitchen, and the primary bedroom. Those spaces drive the emotional story and they dominate listing photos. If those three photograph well, buyers will forgive a guest room that is plain. In my experience, sellers waste money staging the wrong things. They buy new small decor pieces, but leave the big visual blockers in place. Oversized sectionals that shrink the room. A dining table that crowds the walkway. A garage that is packed wall to wall so buyers assume storage is a problem. Staging is mostly editing. You are removing confusion so the layout reads instantly. Outdoor staging matters in the Hill Country too, but keep it honest. Clean the patio, add a simple seating setup, and make sure the yard looks maintained. Do not create a resort fantasy if the reality is full sun and low shade. The goal is to show how the space functions, not to oversell. If you are already thinking about how prep costs and timing affect your bottom line, run a quick seller math check with the seller net sheet so you can decide what is worth doing before you list.

content_sections.h: What are the highest ROI fixes that make staging work in photos?
content_sections.p: Light beats decor. Replace burned out bulbs, match color temperature, open blinds, and consider brighter bulbs in darker rooms. A bright, even photo reads as newer and cleaner even if the finishes are not brand new. Clean beats upgrades. Deep clean baseboards, grout lines, and glass. Remove pet odor at the source. Buyers do not usually say, the house smells. They simply stop imagining themselves living there. If you only spend money in one place, spend it on cleaning and odor remediation. Repairs beat paint when they remove buyer objections. Loose handles, sticky doors, torn screens, and drip stains signal deferred maintenance. In 2026, buyers are slower to ignore those signals. This is the same pattern I talked about in selling when builders offer incentives in Comal County. When buyers can compare your resale home to a new build with credits, they look harder for reasons to negotiate. Staging works best when it is paired with a clean inspection narrative.

content_sections.h: When should you choose professional staging vs. owner occupied staging vs. virtual staging?
content_sections.p: Professional staging makes sense when the home is vacant, the layout is hard to read, or the price point needs a polished first impression. Owner occupied staging works when the furniture fits the scale of the rooms and you can live a little lighter for a few weeks. Virtual staging can be useful for an empty room photo set, but it has to be disclosed and it cannot misrepresent condition or features. If you are trying to decide, I use a simple question with sellers: are we solving a clarity problem or a condition problem. If the home is clean and in good shape but feels empty or awkward, staging solves clarity. If the home has visible wear, staging alone will not solve it, and buyers will still ask for credits. This is why a prep plan and pricing plan have to be built together. One more practical note. If you use virtual staging, keep it honest and consistent with the home as it will be shown. Virtual staging should never add features that are not there, and it should be disclosed so buyers are not surprised when they walk in. In a slower market, surprises create skepticism, and skepticism turns into lower offers and tougher repair negotiations. Nationally, the National Association of REALTORS® reports that 83% of buyers’ agents say staging helps buyers visualize a property as their future home, and nearly half of sellers’ agents report that staging can reduce time on market. That matches what I see locally. Staging does not replace pricing. It protects your pricing by reducing the reasons buyers hesitate. If you want a specific plan that matches your neighborhood and your home’s condition, this pairs well with my seller concessions approach in New Braunfels seller concessions strategy.

title: Comal County Homestead Exemption Deadline (2026)
excerpt: Comal County homestead exemption deadline for 2026 was April 30. If you missed it, you may still have options, but timing and paperwork matter.

faqItems.q: 1) What was the homestead exemption deadline in Comal County for 2026?
faqItems.a: The standard deadline for the 2026 tax year in Comal County was April 30, 2026. The Comal Appraisal District recommends filing between January 1 and April 30 so it can be processed before tax statements go out.

faqItems.q: 2) Where do I file a homestead exemption in Texas?
faqItems.a: You file your homestead exemption application with the appraisal district in the county where the property is located. In Comal County, that’s the Comal Appraisal District.

faqItems.q: 3) Does the homestead exemption apply automatically after closing?
faqItems.a: No. Closing does not automatically file a homestead exemption for you. You generally need to submit an application to the appropriate county appraisal district once you own and occupy the home as your primary residence.

faqItems.q: 4) Can I file late for a homestead exemption if I missed the deadline?
faqItems.a: Sometimes, yes. Texas rules can allow late applications in certain situations, and some counties note late filing may be allowed up to two years after the delinquency date for the year you want the exemption. Confirm the current rule and your eligibility with your county appraisal district.

faqItems.q: 5) Why does knowing the county matter in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: New Braunfels spans county lines, so the correct appraisal district depends on where the property is located. Filing with the wrong county can delay your exemption or require re-submitting paperwork, so verify the county and CAD early.

opening_question: What is the homestead exemption deadline in Comal County for 2026?
quick_answer: For Comal County homeowners, the standard homestead exemption application deadline for the 2026 tax year was April 30, 2026, and the Comal Appraisal District recommends filing between January 1 and April 30 so it can be processed before tax bills go out in the fall. In plain English: file as soon as you close and move in, because your exemption can materially lower the taxable value you are billed on (for example, a $20,000 exemption can reduce the taxable value used to calculate your bill). If you missed the standard deadline, Texas rules can allow late filing in some situations, but you should confirm your specific eligibility directly with the appraisal district for the county where your home is located. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Which office handles homestead exemptions for New Braunfels homes?
content_sections.p: If your home is in Comal County, homestead exemptions are handled through the Comal Appraisal District (CAD), not the title company and not the county tax office. The Texas Comptroller’s guidance is straightforward: exemption applications are filed with the appraisal district in the county where the property is located. This matters in New Braunfels because the city straddles county lines. I see buyers assume a “New Braunfels” mailing address automatically means Comal County. It does not. Parts of New Braunfels are in Guadalupe County, and the right first step is identifying which county appraisal district your property is actually in. If you file with the wrong CAD, you can waste weeks. The second detail buyers miss is timing. The title company records your deed, your lender sets up escrow, and your appraisal district processes exemptions. Those are three different systems. Nobody at closing is automatically filing your homestead exemption for you, and nobody is automatically checking whether you filed it correctly. If you are early in the buying process and want the whole timeline laid out, start with my New Braunfels buyer guide so you know what happens at closing, what happens after closing, and what paperwork is realistically on you versus handled by your lender or title company.

content_sections.h: Why does the April 30 deadline matter if you just bought the home?
content_sections.p: A homestead exemption is a partial exemption that can reduce the taxable value used to calculate your property tax bill. A simple example the Comal Appraisal District uses is this: if your home is valued at $100,000 and you qualify for a $20,000 exemption, you are taxed as if the home were worth $80,000. The dollar impact depends on your local rates, but the mechanism is the same. Texas also has some baseline homestead pieces that show up in the Comptroller’s guidance, including minimums for certain exemptions. For example, the local option exemption cannot be less than $5,000, and Tax Code Section 11.13(a) requires some counties to provide a $3,000 residence homestead exemption for specific county taxes. On top of that, school district exemptions can be large. The Comptroller’s example is useful for understanding the scale: if a home is appraised at $300,000 and you qualify for a $140,000 exemption for school taxes, you pay school taxes as if it were worth $160,000. Here’s the real-world mistake I see with relocating buyers: they wait because they think the exemption “starts automatically” when they sign at the title company. It does not. Closing is one event, but the appraisal district’s processing window is another. Filing earlier is what gives you the best chance of having it applied before statements go out later in the year. A second mistake is budgeting off last year’s tax bill without understanding how exemptions are attached to the prior owner. The prior owner’s exemptions are not your exemptions. Your payment plan needs to assume your own taxable value and your own exemptions, not the seller’s. If you want a clean, realistic cost picture for your specific price point, factor taxes alongside your lender estimate, insurance, and closing costs. I break that down in a plain-English way here: closing costs in Texas and what to expect.

content_sections.h: What if you missed the Comal County homestead exemption deadline?
content_sections.p: First, do not assume you are “out of luck” forever. Texas rules can allow some late applications, and other counties publish guidance about late filing (for example, Hays CAD notes late applications may be allowed up to 2 years after the delinquency date for the year you want the exemption). That said, the cleanest path is always filing on time, and each county’s process and documentation expectations can feel a little different in practice. Also, note the wording in the Comptroller’s guidance. It describes a general deadline of before May 1. In Comal County, the standard local deadline published by the appraisal district for this cycle was April 30. When state guidance and a county process are close but not identical, I always advise clients to treat the county’s instructions as the day-to-day operating rule, then confirm anything unusual directly with the CAD. My advice is to treat this like a three-check process: confirm your property’s county and appraisal district, confirm what documentation they want for your situation, and confirm whether there is any proration or late-filing pathway that applies to you. If you are in Comal County, start with the Comal CAD exemption page so you are working from the current rule set. If you want a bigger-picture view of how homestead exemptions and protests show up in your monthly budget, I also wrote New Braunfels property taxes: homestead and protests and Texas homestead exemption basics for 2026 buyers.

content_sections.h: What documents and details usually slow down a homestead exemption approval?
content_sections.p: Most delays I see are not because someone is doing something “wrong.” They are because the application is missing one detail the CAD needs to match you to the property, or because the buyer waits until the fall when the CAD is processing a pile of changes at the same time. Name and ID match. If your driver’s license address does not match the property address yet, you may need to update it or provide whatever documentation the CAD accepts for your scenario. The exact documentation expectations can change, so I treat the CAD’s current instructions as the source of truth. Primary residence clarity. A homestead exemption is for your primary residence. If you are buying a second home, a river weekend place, or a future move-in property, you may not qualify right away. This is one of those topics where I can give general guidance, but you should verify the details directly with the appraisal district. County line confusion. Again, New Braunfels is the classic trap. If you are in a subdivision that feels “central New Braunfels” but the parcel is actually in Guadalupe County, you are working with a different CAD and a different workflow.

content_sections.h: How should buyers plan for homestead exemptions before making an offer?
content_sections.p: If you are 30 to 180 days from writing an offer, the best time to plan for homestead exemptions is before you fall in love with a payment number. Taxes in the Hill Country are not a rounding error, and the exemption conversation is one of the easiest ways to avoid a “wait, why is my bill higher than we thought?” moment in the first year. Build your budget off conservative assumptions. When a lender gives a payment estimate, taxes are often an estimate, not a promise. If you are buying new construction, a recent appraisal district value may lag what you actually paid. If you are buying a resale, the prior owner’s exemptions can make the historical bill look lower than what you will pay. Know your county and your timeline. If you close in spring or early summer, you want your exemption application in quickly so it can be processed before statements go out in the fall. In Comal County, the appraisal district specifically points homeowners to the January 1 to April 30 filing window for pre-fall processing. Make it part of your offer strategy. I do not want you picking a home based on a “best case” payment. I want you choosing based on a payment you can live with even if taxes come in higher in year one, then using exemptions and protests (when appropriate) to improve the number going forward. If you want me to help you map that out for the neighborhoods and price ranges you are actually shopping, I can build a buyer game plan that includes the cost side, not just the search side.

title: Choose a Listing Agent in New Braunfels, TX (2026)
excerpt: Choose a listing agent in New Braunfels, TX in 2026 by comparing pricing skill, negotiation, and a clear net-proceeds plan, not just commission or promises.

faqItems.q: 1) How many listing agents should I interview before choosing one?
faqItems.a: At least two, and three is even better if your home is unique or you’re unsure on price. You want to compare pricing logic, marketing execution, and negotiation approach, not just personality.

faqItems.q: 2) Is there a ‘standard’ real estate commission in Texas?
faqItems.a: No. Commission is negotiable, and the state does not set a required rate. What matters is whether the services and strategy you’re paying for protect your net proceeds and your timeline.

faqItems.q: 3) How can I verify a Texas real estate agent’s license?
faqItems.a: Use the Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) license holder lookup. You can confirm license status, see the sponsoring broker, and review any published disciplinary actions.

faqItems.q: 4) What’s the biggest pricing mistake New Braunfels sellers make in 2026?
faqItems.a: Overpricing to ‘leave room to negotiate’ and then missing the strongest buyer window in the first couple of weeks. If the market tells you the number is off, you want a plan to adjust early and strategically, not slowly and emotionally.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I ask a listing agent to show me in writing?
faqItems.a: Ask for a comp-backed pricing range, an estimated net sheet, and a written first-14-days plan. If you’re competing with new construction, also ask how they will position your home against builder incentives and concessions.

opening_question: How do I choose the right listing agent in New Braunfels in 2026?
quick_answer: In 2026, choosing a listing agent in New Braunfels comes down to one thing: who can best protect your net proceeds with the right price, the right prep, and a negotiation plan that fits today’s market. National data shows most sellers still hire an agent (NAR reported 91% of sellers used an agent and FSBO was about 5%), which tells you the hard part is not putting a sign in the yard. It’s getting the contract terms, timing, and pricing right for your neighborhood and price band. Interview at least two agents and ask for a comp-backed pricing range, an estimated net sheet, and a written plan for what happens if you do not get traction in the first two weeks. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What should you judge a listing agent on in 2026 (besides commission)?
content_sections.p: If you only compare agents by commission, you’re shopping the wrong line item. Your real cost is the difference between a clean, competitive sale and a listing that sits, takes price cuts, and gives up leverage in negotiations. In a shifting market, the agent who protects your net is the one who can price precisely, create a clean first impression, and negotiate the details that affect your bottom line. Start with net proceeds, not the list price. A high suggested list price can feel good in the kitchen. It can also be the fastest way to end up chasing the market. Ask each agent to walk you through an estimated net sheet and explain what they assumed for concessions, repairs, title policy, and typical local fees. If you want to run the numbers yourself first, use the seller net sheet estimator and bring that to the interview so you can compare apples to apples. Pricing skill is the make-or-break factor in New Braunfels right now. Here’s what I mean in plain language: the first two weeks are your window to capture the buyers who have been watching your neighborhood and are ready to act. If you miss that window because the price is aspirational instead of comp-backed, you are usually negotiating from a weaker position later. If you want to see how I think about this locally, I break down the “why” in New Braunfels home pricing strategy (2026). Negotiation is not just the offer price. The agent you hire should be able to explain, in real scenarios, how they handle inspection credits, appraisal risk, option-period negotiations, and buyer requests that show up after you’re emotionally “sold.” If they cannot describe a repeatable negotiation process, you are betting your equity on vibes.

content_sections.h: What questions should you ask when you interview listing agents?
content_sections.p: Treat the listing appointment like a hiring interview. You are not picking a personality. You’re picking a plan. 1) “Show me the comps you’re using and tell me what you’re weighting most.” I want to hear an agent explain why a sale is truly comparable, not just that it is nearby. In New Braunfels, a half-mile can change your buyer pool. HOA rules, tax districts, builder competition, and even which side of town you’re on can move demand. A strong agent will show you the comps, explain adjustments in plain English, and give you a pricing range with a strategy for where to start inside that range. 2) “What is your first-14-days plan, and what changes if we do not get traction?” A good plan is not “we’ll put it online and see what happens.” It should include professional photos, showing strategy, feedback collection, and decision points for price or condition adjustments. If your home is competing with builder inventory, you also need a plan for how to address incentives and concessions without giving away the farm. If that’s your situation, read selling when builders offer incentives in Comal County and then ask your agent how they would apply that playbook to your neighborhood. 3) “How do you handle prep and presentation without wasting money?” Not every improvement pays back, and I’m cautious about sellers being talked into big projects that do not move the needle. A strong agent can separate “must-fix” from “nice-to-have,” then help you sequence what to do first. If you want a practical starting point, ask your agent for a room-by-room prep plan that focuses on the fixes and presentation items that actually move buyer decisions in your price range. 4) “Who will I talk to during the week, and how often?” Communication is a system, not a promise. Ask what updates look like when you are on-market, what happens after each showing, and how quickly they respond to buyers and agents. If you are relocating or traveling, this matters even more. 5) “Walk me through a recent negotiation where the contract almost fell apart.” You’re looking for judgment under pressure. The best listing agent for you is the one who can keep momentum when inspection results come back, appraisal value is tight, or a buyer gets cold feet. In Texas, the contract is full of timing and option-period details. A calm, organized negotiator can be the difference between closing and starting over.

content_sections.h: What Texas rules and consumer protections should you pay attention to?
content_sections.p: I’m not an attorney, and I’m not giving legal advice here, but Texas does have consumer-protection guardrails that can help you vet an agent’s professionalism. Verify the license and any disciplinary history. Texas has a public license-holder lookup. If an agent seems offended that you want to verify, that’s a red flag. This is normal due diligence for a six-figure transaction. Know what the required notices are. TREC requires consumer notices like the Information About Brokerage Services (IABS) and a Consumer Protection Notice to be provided and made available. Those notices exist so you understand who represents whom, what minimum duties are owed, and where to go if something is wrong. Pay attention to how an agent talks about people and neighborhoods. You should never hear language that signals preference or exclusion about who “belongs” in an area, and you should never hear neighborhood descriptions that lean on demographics. A professional agent will stick to facts that matter to real estate decisions: property features, HOA rules, tax districts, commute patterns, flood maps, lot size, and how the market is behaving. If you hear anything that makes you uncomfortable, you can end the conversation and move on. Commission is negotiable, and TREC does not set it. There is no “standard” commission mandated by the state. What matters is whether the services and outcomes you’re paying for make sense for your goals. The cheapest fee can be expensive if it costs you time, price, or contract terms.

content_sections.h: What does a truly local New Braunfels listing plan look like?
content_sections.p: This is the part most sellers don’t realize until after they’ve been on the market for a month: “New Braunfels” is not one market. It’s a set of pockets, and the buyer behavior changes by pocket. Local pricing means understanding the buyer pool by price band. A home that should sell in the mid $300Ks is often competing for a very different buyer than a home in the mid $500Ks, even if they are both technically in New Braunfels. One group may be very payment-sensitive and focused on closing costs. Another group may care more about layout, storage, and lot feel. If your agent prices you as if every buyer thinks the same way, you will feel it in showing feedback. Builder competition is real, and it shows up in subtle ways. I see sellers underestimate this all the time. They’ll say, “But my house is nicer than the model.” That may be true, but the builder may also be advertising incentives that reduce a buyer’s out-of-pocket cost. A good listing agent will build a plan around that reality: strong initial positioning, clean condition, and a negotiation posture that keeps you competitive without panicking. Here’s my “only-in-New-Braunfels” truth: the listings that go stale here are usually not “bad houses.” They’re houses that were priced like it’s still 2021, presented like it’s still 2015, and then they get stubborn about the first round of feedback. When I’m coaching a seller, I’d rather make two smart moves in week one, than take three price cuts over 60 days. If you want the fastest clarity, run two numbers early. First, get a comp-backed value range using a local analysis (start here: home value and pricing strategy). Second, estimate your walk-away proceeds so you can make decisions without emotion (a seller net sheet is the shortcut). Once you know those numbers, picking the right agent becomes much simpler because you can judge them by how well their plan protects those numbers, not by how confident they sound.

title: Crossvine PID assessment in Cibolo: what buyers pay
excerpt: Crossvine PID assessment in Cibolo can add a second line item beyond normal property taxes. Here’s how it affects 2026 payments, resale, and offers.

faqItems.q: 1) What is a PID assessment in Texas?
faqItems.a: A PID assessment is a special assessment charged to properties inside a Public Improvement District to pay for qualified public improvements. It is separate from the normal property tax rate and is typically paid along with property taxes.

faqItems.q: 2) Does a PID affect mortgage qualification?
faqItems.a: Yes. Lenders generally treat PID assessments like a real recurring cost when they estimate your monthly housing payment. The safest approach is to have your lender price the payment using the exact address and current assessment information.

faqItems.q: 3) Can you negotiate a PID assessment when buying a home?
faqItems.a: You can negotiate the home price and seller concessions, but a PID assessment attached to the property is not something the seller can remove. What you can do is factor it into your offer strategy and compare it against neighborhoods without that layer.

faqItems.q: 4) How do I find out the PID amount for a specific address?
faqItems.a: Start by requesting PID disclosure documents from the builder or seller, then confirm the figures with the taxing entities or district administrator tied to that PID. Your lender can also help validate the amount they should use for payment estimates.

faqItems.q: 5) Is a PID the same thing as an HOA?
faqItems.a: No. A PID is a public special assessment tied to a district, while an HOA fee is a private association due that funds neighborhood rules and amenities. Some neighborhoods have both, which is why the all-in payment needs to be modeled early.

opening_question: Buying in Crossvine (Cibolo) and seeing “PID” on the tax side, what does it actually do to your monthly payment and resale plan in 2026?
quick_answer: A PID (Public Improvement District) is a special assessment layered on top of your normal property taxes, and lenders treat it like a real recurring cost. Even if the city tax rate is only part of your total tax picture, Cibolo’s rate is currently about $0.5226 per $100 of taxable value, and a PID assessment would be in addition to that. The practical takeaway is this: if you are payment-sensitive, you want to know the PID term (how many years), what the annual assessment is today, and whether there is also an ongoing operations and maintenance layer. In Crossvine, I tell buyers to assume the advertised list price is only half the affordability story until we confirm the tax and special district stack on that exact lot. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What is a PID assessment, in plain English?
content_sections.p: A Public Improvement District (PID) is a financing tool allowed under Texas law that lets a city fund qualified public improvements and then recover the cost from property owners inside the district through a special assessment. Think of it like a second tax-style bill line. It is not your base property tax rate. It is a separate assessment that shows up alongside your normal property taxes, and it can run for years. When a buyer tells me “I can afford the payment on a $400K house,” my next question in Cibolo, Schertz, and New Braunfels-adjacent growth corridors is: “What does the tax stack look like on that specific address?” That is where a PID or MUD layer can change the payment more than negotiating $5,000 off the price. If you want a quick example of how special districts can change the math, I wrote a practical breakdown on Veramendi MUD taxes and monthly cost and how to model it in your budget.

content_sections.h: How does a PID change your monthly payment in 2026?
content_sections.p: It raises the all-in monthly cost that your lender underwrites. Even if you plan to refinance later, your lender qualifies you on today’s recurring costs: principal, interest, taxes, insurance, HOA, and any known special assessments. Here is the part buyers miss: you can negotiate a purchase price, but you cannot negotiate away a PID assessment that is already attached to the property. That means the PID affects affordability the same way a higher tax rate does. My practical rule in this area: before you fall in love with the floor plan, confirm the tax rate estimate on that exact lot and confirm whether the neighborhood has a PID, MUD, or both. If you want a fast gut-check, have your lender quote two scenarios: the same home price with the Crossvine estimate and the same home price with a nearby non-PID estimate. Seeing the payment side-by-side is what makes the decision feel clear.

content_sections.h: What should you verify before you write an offer in Crossvine?
content_sections.p: Insight: Ask for the assessment disclosure early. With PIDs, the useful documents are usually the service plan, assessment roll, or the most recent annual assessment notice that shows the current amount and how long it is expected to last. Insight: Confirm whether the PID is capital only, O&M, or both. Some districts are designed to pay for infrastructure over time, while others also include an operations and maintenance layer. The label matters because it changes whether the assessment naturally tapers off or could continue. Insight: Compare it against nearby “no PID” options. In practice, a PID neighborhood can still be a good fit if the home checks every other box, but you want to make that decision with your eyes open. I would rather you pick Crossvine on purpose than pick it by accident. If you want the neighborhood context, start with the Cibolo–Schertz area guide. I can narrow it to Crossvine-adjacent options at your price point.

content_sections.h: Does a PID help or hurt resale in Crossvine?
content_sections.p: A PID does not automatically make a neighborhood a “bad deal.” It can be the reason the community has the infrastructure and amenities it has. Where it can hurt is on the margin. When two similar homes compete and one has a cleaner monthly payment, payment-sensitive buyers lean toward the one with less friction. That is especially true when rates move up and buyers are watching their monthly budget more than they are watching list price. The second resale issue is buyer confidence. If the PID details are vague, or the listing agent cannot answer basic questions about the assessment, buyers assume the worst. The fix is simple: have the documents ready and show the numbers clearly. When I help sellers in a PID neighborhood, I want the buyer to see the math in writing, not in a verbal “it’s not that much.” A clean approach is to share the most recent assessment notice or budget summary, then pair it with a lender-style payment example at a few common down payments. That reduces friction and keeps the negotiation focused on the home, not uncertainty. If you want to see how I frame this with buyers and sellers, the same “payment story” thinking shows up in my write-up on builder incentives in New Braunfels, because incentives and special districts both change buyer behavior through monthly cost.

content_sections.h: What I see buyers get wrong in this corridor (Market Reality)
content_sections.p:
When buyers are relocating from Austin or out of state, they often assume “newer neighborhood” equals “simple taxes.” In this corridor, newer often means more layers.

I also see buyers fixate on interest rate changes and ignore what is right in front of them: a tax and assessment stack that can be the difference between feeling comfortable and feeling stretched every month.

Here is the only-Cody moment: if you show me two identical payments, I will take the house with the cleaner long-term tax story almost every time, because it gives you more flexibility when you need to sell, rent it out, or move for work. That flexibility matters around JBSA-driven moves.

If you want, I can also point you to the right city and county pages for the current tax rate pieces, then we will focus on the one part most buyers cannot guess: the special district layers tied to the lot.

content_sections.h: How do you protect yourself in the contract when taxes feel unclear?
content_sections.p: Texas gives buyers a tool most other states do not: the Option Period. Use it to verify the tax and assessment story while you still have an uncomplicated exit. In the option window, you can: - Ask the builder or seller for any PID disclosure or annual assessment notice - Verify the current tax estimate with the lender using the exact address - Confirm HOA dues and any transfer or resale certificate fees One more practical tip: ask your lender to quote both the current year estimate and a “what if the appraisal district resets the value closer to market” estimate. I am not giving financial advice here, but I do not want you surprised by the first full tax bill after closing. That last point sounds small, but in neighborhoods with multiple layers, the “little” recurring costs add up.

title: Buying Acreage in Texas Hill Country: What to Check (2026)
excerpt: Buying acreage in Texas Hill Country in 2026 can be a great move, but the win is in the details: water, access, restrictions, and real monthly costs before you commit.[…]

faqItems.q: 1) Is buying acreage in the Texas Hill Country more expensive in 2026?
faqItems.a: In many pockets, it is still expensive compared to earlier years, and the market has not snapped back to pre-boom pricing. The bigger issue is that raw land can look cheaper than it really is once you add water, septic, power, and access costs.

faqItems.q: 2) Do I need a well to buy Hill Country acreage?
faqItems.a: Not always. Some tracts are served by water systems, and some buyers plan on wells. The right answer depends on the pocket you are in and what is available at the tract, so you want to confirm the actual service options early.

faqItems.q: 3) How do deed restrictions affect what I can do on my land?
faqItems.a: Restrictions can limit building size, outbuildings, animals, RV storage, and even construction rules in some communities. Do not rely on what a listing says or what a neighbor believes. Get the documents and read what is actually enforceable.

faqItems.q: 4) What is the Option Period and why does it matter for land offers in Texas?
faqItems.a: The Option Period is a negotiated window where you can cancel for any reason in exchange for an option fee. For acreage, it matters because access, septic feasibility, and utility timelines can take time to verify, and you want enough runway to confirm the deal before you are locked in.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the fastest way to choose between New Braunfels, Canyon Lake, and Bulverde for acreage?
faqItems.a: Start with your weekly routine and commute needs, then narrow to pockets that match how often you want to be in town versus how rural you want daily life to feel. From there, compare tract-level feasibility, because the land details can matter more than the city name on the listing.

opening_question: Thinking about buying acreage in the Texas Hill Country in 2026, but not sure what can quietly blow up the deal after you fall in love with the view?
quick_answer: In 2026, Hill Country acreage is still in demand and pricing is still elevated. The Texas Real Estate Research Center reported an average of $7,704 per acre for the Hill Country and Austin–Waco regions in Winter 2026, up 3.4% year over year. Your real cost depends less on the list price and more on water, septic feasibility, utility extension, access, and deed restrictions, plus how quickly you can verify all of that during your Option Period. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does "buying acreage" mean in the Hill Country, practically?
content_sections.p:
Acreage in the Texas Hill Country is not one thing. You can be five minutes from H-E-B in New Braunfels on a 1 acre homesite, or you can be 25 to 45 minutes from town on 10 to 30 acres where your "neighbors" are mostly fences and gates. Those are totally different lifestyle choices, and they come with different due diligence.

Here is the practical part I see relocators underestimate. In many Hill Country pockets, the land is the easy part. The hard part is confirming what you can actually do with it without turning your first year into a construction project you did not plan for. That means verifying access, utilities, water, and restrictions early, not after you are emotionally attached.

If you are still at the "which area fits me" stage, I would start with a clear comparison of pockets and tradeoffs, not with scrolling listings. Start with the areas that fit your routine, then tour with a plan.

content_sections.h: How much are Hill Country acres costing in 2026?
content_sections.p: The best baseline I have found for the land market is Texas A&M's Texas Real Estate Research Center (TRERC) reporting, because it gives you a consistent regional snapshot. In Winter 2026, TRERC reported an average of $7,704 per acre in the Hill Country and Austin–Waco regions, which they note is a new record for that region and a 3.4% increase year over year. That number is not a promise for any specific tract. It is a quick reality check. A build-ready homesite in a gated neighborhood with paved roads and utilities can price very differently from raw land with no improvements, limited access, and unknown water. Location inside the Hill Country matters too. The closer you are to major corridors and job centers, the more buyers compete for convenience, and that tends to keep pricing firm even when the broader market cools. If you want to translate the land price into "what does this do to my payment," start with a budget and work backwards. The mortgage calculator is a quick way to sanity-check monthly numbers before you spend weekends touring properties that were never going to pencil.

content_sections.h: What are the hidden deal-killers when you buy acreage?
content_sections.p: Most acreage deals do not fall apart because someone lied. They fall apart because a buyer learns something late that they should have verified early. The top categories are access, restrictions, and feasibility. Access sounds simple until it is not. Does the property have deeded access from a public road? Is the drive you see on the ground actually on the tract you are buying, or is it a neighbor's easement? Can you bring in a builder and concrete trucks, or is it a narrow private road with maintenance costs and limitations? I have seen buyers fall in love with a tract, then realize the practical access does not match the Instagram version. Restrictions are the other big one. Some tracts are very "do what you want" and others have tight deed restrictions or HOA rules that impact building size, RV storage, animals, outbuildings, and even which builders can be used. If you want a quick primer on how I structure early exits in Texas when something does not check out, read Texas option period basics before you write your first land offer.

content_sections.h: How do water, septic, and power change your true cost?
content_sections.p:
This is the part I wish every acreage buyer would treat as a first-class decision, not a line item. Water drives lifestyle. Septic drives feasibility. Power drives timeline and cost.

Water can mean a well, a water system, or hauling. Each has tradeoffs. A well can be fantastic, but you want to know depth, yield history if available, and what it will cost if you need to improve the system. A water system can be convenient, but you want to understand the fees and whether you are in an area with planned capacity changes. If you are comparing areas, the Texas Water Development Board is a solid starting place for general groundwater context and terminology. You still need tract-level confirmation, but having the vocabulary helps you ask the right questions.

Septic is where the "cheap" tract can get expensive fast. In many Hill Country areas, you need a soil evaluation to determine the right system type and where it can be placed. If you cannot place it, you cannot build the home you planned, even if the land is beautiful. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality has plain-language guidance on on-site sewage facilities that is worth skimming before you are under contract.

content_sections.h: How do you pick the right Hill Country pocket near New Braunfels?
content_sections.p:
If you are using New Braunfels as your hub, I usually break the conversation into three practical questions: How often do you need to be on IH-35, how much do you care about being close to the rivers and lake, and how rural do you really want day-to-day life to feel.

For example, Canyon Lake area properties can give you views and water access vibes, but the lake is a real variable. If lake proximity is part of your dream, you should understand how lake levels can affect perception and pricing so you set expectations the right way from the start.

On the north side toward Bulverde and Spring Branch, you often see a different mix of custom homes, larger tracts, and commuting patterns. Toward Seguin, you can get more land for the money in some areas, but you want to be honest about drive times and your weekly routine. If you are not sure which direction fits, it is completely normal. That is why I like to start with a short list of "best-fit" pockets and then tour with a plan.

content_sections.h: What should you verify during the first week after you find "the one"?
content_sections.p: When a buyer tells me, "Cody, we found the perfect land," my next question is always the same: "Perfect for what, and have we proven it yet?" That is my only-Cody moment because I see the same pattern on repeat. People buy the view, then spend the next year trying to make the utilities and restrictions match the dream. During the first week, you are trying to turn unknowns into knowns. Confirm access and easements with the title company and survey. Confirm restrictions and any HOA rules with documents, not hearsay. Start the water and septic feasibility conversation immediately, because those timelines can eat your Option Period if you wait. If you want the most practical version of this, I also recommend skimming the New Braunfels area utility providers guide so you know what questions to ask about electric providers, service lines, and who actually supplies what in the pocket you are looking at.

content_sections.h: Is Hill Country acreage a smart move for you right now?
content_sections.p: It can be, but it depends on what you are trying to buy: a lifestyle, a long-term homesite, a weekend place, or a future build. The more your plan depends on utilities, build timing, and flexibility, the more you should treat due diligence as part of the purchase price. I am also very direct with buyers about the timeline. If you are 30 to 180 days out, you have time to compare areas and run the numbers. If you are trying to buy and build fast, you need a tract with fewer moving parts, even if it costs more. The wrong land is not a bargain. It is an expensive delay. If you are still deciding whether the Hill Country lifestyle itself is the right fit, this older post, Is Hill Country living right for you?, lays out the real tradeoffs I see clients weigh before they commit.

title: Texas Earnest Money Rules 2026: New Braunfels Buyers
excerpt: Texas earnest money rules 2026 can protect New Braunfels buyers, but only if your deadlines and notices are clean. Here’s how to keep your deposit refundable.

faqItems.q: 1) Is earnest money required in Texas?
faqItems.a: Earnest money is not a separate Texas “law requirement.” It is a contract term the buyer and seller negotiate, and it is commonly used in Texas resale transactions.

faqItems.q: 2) When do I have to deliver earnest money after the contract is effective?
faqItems.a: The TREC resale contract sets a delivery timeline tied to the Effective Date and also addresses what happens if the last day falls on a weekend or legal holiday. Your safest move is to treat the deadline as strict and deliver early.

faqItems.q: 3) If I terminate during the option period, do I get earnest money back?
faqItems.a: If you properly terminate within the option period, the contract provides that the option fee is not refunded, and the earnest money is refunded to the buyer. This is why the option period is such an important buyer protection tool in Texas.

faqItems.q: 4) Is the option fee the same thing as earnest money?
faqItems.a: No. The option fee is paid for the unrestricted right to terminate during the option period and is generally not refunded if you terminate. Earnest money is held by the escrow agent and may be refundable depending on your contract terms and deadlines.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the biggest mistake that causes earnest money disputes?
faqItems.a: Missed deadlines and unclear notice language. Most problems are avoidable when you calendar the deadlines up front, schedule inspections early, and send clear written termination notices when needed.

opening_question: If you wire earnest money in Texas, when is it actually refundable?
quick_answer: In Texas, earnest money is not “non-refundable by default.” It is a negotiable deposit held by the escrow agent, and whether you get it back usually comes down to deadlines, notices, and how your TREC contract is filled out. The two big buyer protections are (1) the Option Period, which gives you an unrestricted right to terminate if you pay the option fee on time, and (2) contingencies and contract timelines (financing, title, appraisal, HOA docs, and other addenda) that can make earnest money refundable when they are properly followed. Most earnest money problems I see are not about the dollar amount. They are about missed delivery windows, vague termination emails, or assuming “inspection contingency” works the same way it does in other states. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does earnest money actually do in a Texas contract?
content_sections.p: Think of earnest money as a performance deposit, not a penalty. In most Texas resale transactions, the buyer deposits earnest money with the escrow agent named in the contract. The seller does not automatically get it just because you sign the contract. What matters is how the contract says it can be released. The contract sets the delivery deadline, and it also spells out when a refund is required, when the seller may claim it, and what happens if there is a dispute. Earnest money is not your down payment. It is separate from your loan down payment and separate from your closing costs. If you want to understand your total cash needs, start with a payment and cost plan (here is my New Braunfels closing costs breakdown). If you are relocating to New Braunfels from out of state, this is where buyers get tripped up. They treat Texas earnest money like a universal “deposit you lose if you cancel,” and then they do not focus enough on the paperwork and timing that keeps it refundable.

content_sections.h: When is earnest money due, and what happens if it is late?
content_sections.p: The contract has a delivery deadline, and sellers watch it closely. Under the TREC resale contract, the buyer must deliver earnest money (and the option fee, if negotiated) within a set number of days after the Effective Date. The form also addresses what happens when that last day falls on a weekend or legal holiday. Late earnest money creates leverage for the seller. If the buyer fails to deliver on time, the seller may have the right to terminate or pursue remedies as allowed by the contract. In a fast-moving pocket of New Braunfels, I have seen deals die over an “easy” miss like a wire not arriving before cutoff. If you are writing offers in competitive neighborhoods, your agent should treat earnest money delivery like a closing-critical deadline, not a clerical task.

content_sections.h: How does the Texas Option Period protect your earnest money?
content_sections.p: The Option Period is the cleanest buyer safety valve in Texas. When the seller agrees to an option period, you get an unrestricted right to terminate within the option window if you pay the option fee within the required time. Option fee and earnest money behave differently. If you terminate within the option period, the option fee is not refunded, and the contract requires the escrow agent to refund the earnest money to the buyer. That is why the option period is often the difference between “I can walk away” and “I might have to fight for my deposit.” If you want a deeper explanation of how this works in a real New Braunfels transaction, start with Texas option period basics for earnest money protection.

content_sections.h: What other contract timelines can make earnest money refundable?
content_sections.p: Most refunds happen through contract performance, not conflict. Beyond the option period, your contract and addenda can create situations where earnest money is refundable if you follow the exact steps. Common examples buyers run into in New Braunfels: loan approval timelines, appraisal-related amendments, title objections, HOA document delivery, and survey or commitment delivery deadlines. Each one has a clock, and the refund depends on sending the right notice on time. Contingency language matters more than people think. A simple example is selling a home at the same time. If your offer is written with a home-sale contingency, the refund and timing mechanics change. Here is my guide to home-sale contingency offers in New Braunfels if that is your situation. This is also where buyers benefit from reading the full process once, not learning it under pressure. If you have not already, skim the step-by-step home buying process so you understand which deadlines are truly make-or-break.

content_sections.h: What happens to earnest money if there is a disagreement?
content_sections.p: The escrow agent cannot guess who is right. If the buyer and seller disagree about who should receive the earnest money, the escrow agent usually requires written instructions that match the contract before releasing funds. Most disputes are really paperwork disputes. One side thinks a deadline was met. The other side thinks it was missed. Or the termination was sent, but it was not sent the way the contract requires. Practical reality in Comal and Guadalupe County transactions: if you are in a tense negotiation, the easiest way to protect yourself is to keep your notices simple, timely, and confirmable. Keep the email chain. Get a receipt or confirmation. Do not rely on a casual text message. I am not a lawyer, and I cannot give legal advice, but I can tell you this. The buyers who avoid earnest money drama are the ones who treat notice and deadline management like a real part of the strategy, not an afterthought.

content_sections.h: What are the most common earnest money mistakes buyers make?
content_sections.p: Missing delivery deadlines. If the contract says 3 days, treat it like 3 days. Get wiring instructions early, confirm cutoff times, and do not assume a weekend buys you time without checking the contract language. Not separating “termination notice” from “repair negotiation.” Asking for repairs is not the same thing as terminating. If you intend to terminate, do it clearly, in writing, with the proper timing. Assuming the title company automatically “knows what you mean.” The escrow agent is not there to interpret intent. Clean instructions and clean notice language prevent the most expensive misunderstandings. Only Cody would say this: in New Braunfels, the deals that get messy are rarely the complicated ones. It is the simple resale where the buyer thinks the option period is “just the inspection window,” waits to schedule inspections until day 6, and then realizes they have no practical time left to negotiate or walk away cleanly.

content_sections.h: Should you offer more earnest money to win in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: Sometimes it helps, but it is not the lever most buyers think it is. In a seller’s market, buyers often assume higher earnest money automatically makes an offer “safer” to the seller. In reality, sellers usually care more about certainty of close, clean timelines, and whether you can perform. What I look at first: closing date realism, lender readiness, appraisal risk, and whether your option period and inspection plan match the neighborhood’s typical negotiation pace. In some New Braunfels pockets, a strong offer is the one that feels organized, not the one that simply swings harder on deposits. If you want to strengthen an offer without creating unnecessary deposit risk, I will walk you through which terms actually move the needle for the seller in your specific price range and neighborhood.

content_sections.h: How can you protect your earnest money in a New Braunfels offer?
content_sections.p: Start with a contract plan, not a deposit amount. I would rather see a buyer with a clean option period, realistic inspection scheduling, and lender timelines that match the closing date than a buyer who simply increases earnest money to “look stronger.” Use the right tool for the right question. If you are trying to understand your total cash needs, use a mortgage payment estimate and cost-to-close planning. If you are trying to reduce the risk of losing earnest money, focus on the option period, addenda deadlines, and clean written notices. Make wiring security part of your plan. Wire fraud attempts happen. Always verify wiring instructions with a known phone number and do not trust last-minute “updated instructions” emails without verification. If you want me to sanity-check your offer strategy before you submit, that is exactly what I do with buyers. We will map deadlines, negotiation levers, and the simplest path to a refundable outcome if the home does not check out.

title: Buying a Second Home in Texas Hill Country: 2026 Guide
excerpt: Buying a second home in Texas Hill Country in 2026 can work if you price the total monthly cost, taxes, and STR rules first. Here's a practical plan for your area.

faqItems.q: 1) How is financing different on a second home in Texas?
faqItems.a: Second-home financing often comes with different down payment rules and pricing than a primary residence. Your lender will look closely at occupancy intent, your debt-to-income ratio, and reserves. Talk with your lender early so your budget reflects the loan terms you can actually get.

faqItems.q: 2) Do I get a homestead exemption on a second home in Comal County?
faqItems.a: Generally, homestead exemptions apply to your primary residence, not a second home. That means your tax estimate for a second home should not assume the same exemptions you may have on your main house. Confirm your specific situation with the Comal Appraisal District.

faqItems.q: 3) Can I use short-term rental income to qualify for a second home purchase?
faqItems.a: Some lenders may consider rental income, but it depends on the loan program, documentation, and how the property will be used. Even when it is allowed, you should build a conservative plan that works without perfect occupancy. Treat STR income as upside, not the foundation of your budget.

faqItems.q: 4) What should I check first for a Hill Country second home on acreage?
faqItems.a: Start with water source, septic system, access roads, fencing, and the cost to maintain the land. Insurance and inspection items can be very different than a newer neighborhood home. If you do not want extra upkeep, choose a property type that matches your lifestyle.

faqItems.q: 5) Is 2026 a good time to buy a second home in the Hill Country?
faqItems.a: It can be, especially if you shop with a monthly payment target and negotiate based on your specific area and price band. Statewide indicators like months of supply and days on market suggest buyers may have more room to negotiate than in peak years. The right answer depends on the property, your financing, and how you plan to use the home.

opening_question: Should you buy a second home in Texas Hill Country in 2026?
quick_answer: Buying a second home in the Texas Hill Country in 2026 can make sense if you start with the boring math first: financing terms, property taxes without a homestead exemption, and whether you will actually use it enough to justify the carrying cost. Rates are still a real part of the decision. One Texas-market guide cited a 6.54% 30-year fixed rate as of May 2026, and second-home pricing can be higher depending on down payment, credit, and lender rules. Use the lifestyle upside to choose the area, but use the monthly payment and "non-homestead" tax reality to choose the budget. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does the Hill Country market feel like going into summer 2026?
content_sections.p: If you are considering a second home, your first instinct is usually lifestyle. River weekends. Lake time. A place to reset without being stuck in a condo tower. That part matters, but 2026 buyers are also walking into a market that has been uneven by pocket and price point. Some neighborhoods still feel tight. Others give you room to negotiate, especially when resale listings are competing with builder incentives. Here is the practical lens I use with my New Braunfels relocators: don’t ask “Is it a buyer’s market?” Ask “Is my exact price band getting price cuts, and what does that do to my leverage?” That is especially true for second homes because you are often picking from higher-maintenance properties (views, acreage, older homes, waterfront-adjacent) where condition and insurance costs can swing your monthly number. One statewide indicator is supply. A Texas-market summary cited 10.07 months of supply as of March 31, 2026, along with a median 82 days on market. That does not mean your specific Hill Country area will behave exactly like the state. It does mean you should expect more listings to sit long enough for you to negotiate, and you should be ready to walk away when the numbers do not work. If you want a fast reset on how Texas contracts work, re-read Texas option period basics for New Braunfels buyers. Second-home buyers make the same expensive mistake first-time buyers do: they fall in love with the view and forget the exit plan in the contract.

content_sections.h: What costs surprise second-home buyers in the Hill Country?
content_sections.p: The tax bill is different when it is not your homestead. A second home generally does not get the same homestead exemptions you would use on your primary residence, so you need to run your estimate with that in mind. In Comal County, the appraisal district explains the homestead exemption concept with simple examples, and it also notes that homeowners who qualify for the homestead exemption receive at least a $140,000 exemption for school district taxes. That is a big deal. If the property is not your homestead, you should not assume you will get those savings. This is one of the most common “we didn’t know” moments I see when someone is moving from Austin or out of state and buying a weekend place. Insurance and water risk can be the quiet deal-killer. Hill Country properties can come with flood-map questions, wind and hail exposure, older roofs, and longer response times for some services. I am not saying “avoid” anything. I am saying you should ask the questions early. For river-adjacent or low-water crossings, you want to know what insurance will actually cost before you anchor your budget. If you are eyeing Canyon Lake because it feels like a vacation every weekend, also read Canyon Lake water levels and the real estate impact so you do not buy based on a photo from a wet year. Short-term rental plans need a reality check. A lot of second-home buyers start with “We’ll use it sometimes and rent it out the rest.” That can work, but only if the property, HOA, and local rules allow it and the numbers still work when you are not booked. Before you lean on STR income to justify the purchase, build a conservative plan that assumes slower seasons, higher maintenance, and a management fee. If the purchase only works in the best-case scenario, it is not a plan. If you treat the monthly cost like a payment you will make even in the off-season, you will make better decisions. That means you pick a budget you can carry comfortably, then you only shop the homes that fit that number.

content_sections.h: How do you choose the right Hill Country area for a second home?
content_sections.p: I like to start with your use pattern. Is this a true weekend place you will drive to twice a month, or is it a future primary home you will “test drive” for a year? Those are different decisions. A true weekend place should be easy to reach, easy to lock up, and located where you will actually go. A future primary should be chosen for daily-life logistics: commute routes, groceries, medical, and how you feel on a random Tuesday, not just a Saturday. Here is my “only a local would say this” moment: out-of-town buyers often underestimate what IH-35 feels like at the wrong time, especially between San Antonio and New Braunfels. If your second home is supposed to reduce stress, but you are sitting in traffic every Friday at 4:30, you will stop using it. When we build a move plan, I ask clients to do one test drive in the exact time window they would typically travel. It sounds obvious, but it changes what areas actually fit. Next, match the property style to the maintenance you want to live with. Hill Country acreage is a different lifestyle than a newer neighborhood home, and it comes with different questions (water source, septic, fencing, wildlife, access, and who maintains what). If acreage is on your short list, read buying acreage in Texas Hill Country: what to check (2026) and decide whether you want a place to relax or a second job. If you are not sure which pockets make sense, start with a short list first and then shop inside it. Narrow the areas first, then shop inside that lane. That is how you avoid the common trap of shopping “everywhere” and never getting confident enough to move forward.

content_sections.h: What is the safest step-by-step plan to buy a second home in 2026?
content_sections.p: Step one is deciding what the home is for. If it is lifestyle only, your budget should be based on what you can comfortably carry even if it never produces a dollar of rental income. If it is a hybrid second home and STR, your plan should still cash-flow under conservative assumptions. If it is a future primary, you need a plan for timing and how you will sell or convert your current home. Step two is building the true monthly number. That means payment, insurance, HOA (if any), utilities, and property taxes with the right exemptions applied or not applied. Comal County’s tax office also notes that it maintains over 122,000 tax accounts and collects and disburses over $164 million in property taxes annually. The point is not the big number. The point is that property taxes are a real monthly cost here, and second-home buyers should treat them like a payment, not a once-a-year surprise. Step three is writing an offer with an exit plan. That is where the option period matters, inspections matter, and due diligence matters. You can love the property and still protect yourself. This is exactly the kind of conversation I have with clients before we even schedule showings, because the contract strategy needs to match the property type. If you want, I’ll help you build the plan before you tour. That way you are shopping with a clear budget, a tight area list, and a contract strategy that fits the property.

title: Living in Canyon Lake Year Round: Texas Hill Country
excerpt: Living in Canyon Lake year round is less “vacation mode” and more about water, roads, utilities, and taxes. Here’s what day-to-day really feels like […]

faqItems.q: 1) Is Canyon Lake a good place to live year round?
faqItems.a: It can be, especially if you want a lake-and-Hill-Country lifestyle and you are comfortable planning around utilities, roads, and maintenance. The “right” answer depends on which pocket you choose and what your day-to-day routine looks like.

faqItems.q: 2) How far is Canyon Lake from New Braunfels and San Antonio?
faqItems.a: Many drives are very manageable, but exact times vary a lot by where you are on the lake and which route you take. If commute time is a deciding factor, verify your specific routes at your actual commute hours before you choose a home.

faqItems.q: 3) What should I check before buying a home at Canyon Lake?
faqItems.a: Beyond the inspection, focus on flood and drainage questions for the exact lot, road access, and utility setup (city services vs. septic/well when applicable). Also read HOA rules early if you care about boat storage, RV parking, or building a shop.

faqItems.q: 4) Do lake level changes affect Canyon Lake real estate?
faqItems.a: They can influence how buyers feel about lakefront and lakeview homes, and they can change how people use the property day to day. The best strategy is to buy a home that still works for your lifestyle even when you are not on the water.

faqItems.q: 5) What does it cost to live in Canyon Lake besides the mortgage?
faqItems.a: Owners typically budget for property taxes, insurance, utilities, and ongoing maintenance. The totals vary by home type, lot, and systems, so it is smart to estimate the full monthly and annual cost before you commit.

opening_question: What is it actually like to live at Canyon Lake year round, not just visit for the weekend?
quick_answer: If you want lake access, Hill Country views, and more breathing room than the IH-35 corridor, living in Canyon Lake year round can be a great fit, as long as you go in with eyes open about utilities, roads, and maintenance. As a baseline data point, Data USA reports a $389,300 median property value in Canyon Lake (2024). That number is a useful reference, but your real decision usually comes down to which pocket you choose (lakefront, lakeview, or further out) and what kind of daily routine you want. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Are you picturing weekends, or everyday life at the lake?
content_sections.p:
Most people fall in love with Canyon Lake on a Saturday. The water is the headline, the views are the hook, and the pace feels like it gives your brain room to breathe.

Year round life is different. Your happiness is usually tied to the unglamorous stuff: where you grocery shop, what your commute actually feels like at 7:30 AM, how reliable your internet is for work, and whether your property is set up for Texas summers and sudden storms.

If you are new to the area, I always recommend you start by narrowing your “daily-life” must-haves first (commute, errands, views, lot size), then you tour with that filter. It saves time and keeps you from falling for the wrong pocket just because the photos look great.

content_sections.h: What does “Canyon Lake” mean in real estate terms?
content_sections.p: In conversation, people say “Canyon Lake” as if it is one neighborhood. In reality, you are choosing between multiple pockets that feel very different. Lakefront or close-to-the-water pockets. These are the spots where you pay for proximity and the lifestyle. Expect more emphasis on views, access, and sometimes tighter lots. Hill Country view corridors and larger-lot areas. Many buyers end up here because they want space, privacy, or a shop, and they are fine being a short drive from the lake. Newer builds vs. older housing stock. Newer homes can reduce immediate maintenance, but older homes sometimes have better tree canopy, established lots, or closer in locations. The tradeoff is systems, roof age, and renovation scope. Another overlooked reality is access. A home can be “near the lake” and still feel far from what you actually do. Boat ramps, marinas, and your preferred part of the shoreline can change your routine more than the map suggests. If you plan to be on the water weekly, we should match your home location to the part of the lake you will actually use. This is the first place I see relocators make an expensive mistake: they pick a listing online first, then try to justify the area later. Flip that. Pick the daily-life pocket first, then shop within it.

content_sections.h: How much does it cost to own in Canyon Lake compared to nearby areas?
content_sections.p: The price you see online is only part of the story. In the Hill Country, the ownership costs that surprise people are usually taxes, insurance, and ongoing maintenance. Data USA reports a $389,300 median property value in Canyon Lake (2024) and a high homeownership rate. That does not mean every home is “around $389K,” but it gives you an anchor for what the area has looked like recently. On the tax side, Comal County’s own information makes it clear that property taxes are a major piece of the annual budget. If you are moving from out of state, do not guess. Run the numbers early, and consider how a homestead exemption could change your long-term plan. One practical tip that saves time: get your utility questions answered early. Not every home is set up the same way, and some service setups are more “hands on” than others. If you want the Texas-specific walkthrough for what to expect when you set things up, use: utility providers in the area.

content_sections.h: What do year-round residents wish they checked before buying?
content_sections.p: These are the due diligence themes I keep circling back to with Canyon Lake buyers who plan to live here full-time. Water, drainage, and flood questions. Even if a home is not “on the lake,” water moves fast in the Hill Country. The right next step is verifying floodplain and drainage realities for the exact address and lot, not relying on general assumptions. Roads and routes. Two homes that are five miles apart can feel completely different based on road type, access to main routes, and how quickly you can get to your usual errands. Septic and well realities (when applicable). Some properties are on systems that require more hands-on ownership than city utilities. If that is new to you, it is not a deal-breaker, but it is something to plan for. Connectivity. If you work from home, do not assume the listing’s “high-speed internet available” note means the same thing you are used to. Ask what service is actually available at that address, then verify with the provider. The same goes for cell coverage. It is not fun to discover you have dead spots after you move. HOA rules and short-term rental dynamics. Some sections have tighter rules than others. If you care about boat storage, RV parking, building a shop, or future plans, read the restrictions early so you do not fall in love with a home that will fight your lifestyle. Insurance and maintenance expectations. Wind, hail, and heat are not theories here. Roofing condition, tree management, and drainage control are not “nice to have” items. They are part of owning a Hill Country home without constant surprises.

content_sections.h: Does Canyon Lake still make sense if the lake level changes?
content_sections.p: If the lake is your primary reason for moving, it is smart to talk through how water conditions affect your enjoyment and resale options. Some buyers want to be able to see the water from the back porch. Others just want to be near it for weekends and sunsets. Those are different needs. I wrote a deeper, local-only breakdown here: Canyon Lake water levels and real estate impact. It is one of the most common “I’m not sure” questions I get from buyers who are comparing Canyon Lake to New Braunfels, Bulverde, or other Hill Country options. A practical way to think about it: do you need “walk to the water,” “see the water,” or “be near the water”? Those are three different budgets and three different resale audiences. If the lake is the whole point, we should get very clear on which of those you actually mean before you shop. My honest take: if your plan is year-round living, you will be happiest when the home works even on the days you do not go to the lake. The view is a bonus. The daily routine is the foundation.

content_sections.h: How do you decide if Canyon Lake is the right Hill Country fit for you?
content_sections.p: If you are moving in the next 30 to 180 days, the goal is not to collect more opinions. The goal is to build a short list of areas that match your daily life, then pick the best property within that lane. A good comparison set for many relocators is: Canyon Lake (lake lifestyle), New Braunfels (more city services and quick IH-35 access), and Bulverde or Spring Branch (Hill Country feel with different commute patterns). If you are coming from Austin, Houston, or out of state, your commute tolerance and your “I need city conveniences” level matter a lot. Here’s the part I see people underestimate: once you live at the lake, you stop thinking like a vacationer. You start thinking like an owner. You care about where packages get delivered, how fast you can get to the hardware store, whether you have a realistic place to store a trailer, and what your “I’m going to be gone for three days” plan is for pets and plants in July. Those are boring questions, but they are the questions that make year-round life feel easy. If you are deciding between more land vs. more neighborhood convenience, this is the Hill Country checklist I use with buyers: buying acreage in Texas Hill Country.
