title: Moving to Garden Ridge TX from California: 2026 Plan
excerpt: Moving to Garden Ridge TX from California in 2026? Here is a practical plan for budgeting, timing, taxes, and the Texas buying process so you move with fewer surprises.

faqItems.q: 1) Is Garden Ridge closer to San Antonio or New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Garden Ridge sits between both, and the “feel” of the commute depends on the specific address and your daily route. When we build your plan, we anchor your search to your most common drives so you do not buy a great house in the wrong spot for your schedule.

faqItems.q: 2) Do you need an attorney to close on a home in Texas?
faqItems.a: In Texas, closings are typically handled through a title company rather than an attorney-required closing model. You can still use legal counsel if you want, but most transactions are structured around the standard Texas contract process and title-company-led closing.

faqItems.q: 3) What is the option period in Texas and why does it matter?
faqItems.a: The option period is a short window after contract where you can terminate for any reason, typically used to complete inspections and decide on repairs. It matters because it is your main protection for finding issues and renegotiating or walking away without turning it into a fight.

faqItems.q: 4) How do property taxes affect affordability in Comal County areas like Garden Ridge?
faqItems.a: Property taxes can materially change your monthly payment because they are often escrowed into the mortgage payment. The exact amount depends on the address, taxing jurisdictions, exemptions, and how values change after purchase, so we budget conservatively and verify the specific home before you commit.

faqItems.q: 5) When should you start planning a relocation if you are moving from California?
faqItems.a: If you are 30 to 180 days out, start now. The best time to plan is before you travel to tour homes so your trip is efficient and you are ready to write quickly if the right home shows up.

opening_question: Thinking about moving to Garden Ridge, TX from California in 2026, and want a real plan instead of a vibe?
quick_answer: Garden Ridge is a small, low-density Comal County community near San Antonio and New Braunfels with about 4,332 residents (recent ACS estimates), and it tends to attract buyers who want more space and a quieter setup without being far from I-35 access. The biggest 2026 “gotchas” for California movers are usually property tax budgeting, how Texas contract timelines work (option period, earnest money, inspections), and how quickly the right homes can move when inventory is tight. If you build a numbers-first plan and line up your financing and timing early, the move is very manageable. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What should you know about Garden Ridge before you decide?
content_sections.p: Garden Ridge sits in Comal County with quick access toward San Antonio, Schertz-Cibolo, and New Braunfels. It is not a master-planned “one big neighborhood” market. It feels more like a patchwork of established pockets and newer builds, with a lot of larger lots compared to what many California buyers are used to. The first thing I tell California movers. Do not treat Garden Ridge like a zip-code-only decision. Two homes that look similar on paper can have very different day-to-day realities based on road access, HOA structure (or no HOA), septic versus city services, and how close you are to your most common drives. If you want a broader orientation first, start with my New Braunfels relocation guide. Then we can narrow your search using the things that actually move the needle: lot size, commute pattern, property tax exposure, and whether you want an older home with mature trees or something newer with modern mechanicals.

content_sections.h: How do you build a 2026 budget that will not surprise you after closing?
content_sections.p: Most California movers have a strong feel for purchase price and interest rate. The pain usually shows up in the monthly “all-in” number once Texas property taxes and insurance are stacked into the payment. Budget like a Texan, not like a headline. In this part of the Hill Country, your property tax bill depends on the taxing jurisdictions tied to that specific address (county, city, ISD, and any special districts) and whether you qualify for exemptions like the Texas homestead exemption. Two homes a mile apart can carry different effective tax burdens. Before you fall in love with a house, run the payment two ways: one with the current tax and one with a realistic “year-two” assumption after the appraisal district updates values. If you want a quick starting point, use the mortgage calculator to sanity-check payment ranges, then we tighten it with address-specific tax data once you have a short list. My local reality check. The “best deal” is not always the lowest price. Sometimes the right move is paying a little more for the home that keeps your monthly carry cost predictable and your resale demand broader later.

content_sections.h: What is different about buying a home in Texas compared to California?
content_sections.p: Texas contracts are timeline-driven and very process-specific. The three terms California buyers usually need to internalize fast are the option period, earnest money, and the fact that closings are typically handled by a title company. Option period is your inspection protection. You pay an option fee for the unrestricted right to terminate during the option period. That is the window where inspections happen and big decisions get made. If you want a deeper breakdown, read Texas option period basics for New Braunfels buyers. Earnest money has rules and deadlines. Earnest money is typically held by the title company and timing matters. If you are writing competitive offers, we make sure the dates and delivery steps are clean so your contract does not accidentally create risk. Practical takeaway. The buyer who wins and then stays calm through inspection and appraisal is the buyer who planned the timeline in advance. That is what we build before you start touring seriously.

content_sections.h: How do you choose the right search strategy for Garden Ridge (not just the right house)?
content_sections.p: Garden Ridge inventory can feel “thin” because the area does not produce listings at the same pace as larger master-planned zones. That means your strategy matters as much as your criteria. Decide your non-negotiables in the right order. For most relocators, the best order is: monthly payment comfort, commute pattern, lot size, home condition tolerance (move-in-ready vs. willing to remodel), then style preferences. If you start with granite colors or floorplan vibe, you will waste time and miss the homes that actually fit your life. Use a two-list method. Create (1) a “must-have” list that is truly binary, and (2) a “nice-to-have” list that you are willing to trade. This sounds basic, but it is the difference between seeing 6 homes that all feel wrong and seeing 6 homes where 2 are worth writing on. If you want the step-by-step process, I will map it to your exact relocation timeline so your tours, offers, and inspections happen in a clean sequence.

content_sections.h: What should you verify about property systems and insurance before you commit?
content_sections.p: A lot of the stress relocators feel comes from treating the inspection as the start of the process. In reality, the easiest moves happen when you pre-decide what you care about and what you are willing to maintain. Utilities and systems. Depending on the specific home, you might be evaluating septic, private well components, propane, or other rural-adjacent features. None of that is automatically “bad,” but it changes your ownership rhythm. You want clarity on age, service history, and what a normal maintenance year looks like so you can budget time and money realistically. Insurance and risk factors. In the Hill Country, you also want to understand insurance pricing and any factors that can change it, like roof age, prior claims, and whether the property sits near a mapped floodplain. The goal is simple: no last-minute surprises that blow up your monthly number or your comfort level. My rule of thumb. If you are relocating, plan to over-communicate with your lender, your inspector, and the title company early. The move gets easier when everyone is working off the same timeline and the same “this is what matters” list.

content_sections.h: What are the biggest 2026 relocation mistakes you can avoid up front?
content_sections.p: Mistake 1: Assuming property taxes are “fixed.” In Texas, taxable value and exemptions matter. If you are buying as a primary residence, plan how and when you will file homestead. If you missed the timing for this year, you plan for next year. For context on the annual cycle, see Comal County homestead exemption deadlines. Mistake 2: Treating incentives like free money. Builder incentives and rate buydowns can shift buyer demand between new construction and resale, which changes negotiation leverage. Even if you are not buying new, incentives can impact how aggressive a resale seller has to be to compete. Mistake 3: Waiting to get tactical until you land in Texas. If you are 30 to 180 days out, you can do the heavy lifting now: lender pre-approval, down payment plan, tax assumptions, and a tour plan that stacks the best candidates into one efficient trip. Mistake 4: Forgetting the “property systems” questions. Depending on the home, you may be evaluating septic, well components, or other rural-adjacent features. Those are not dealbreakers. They just require a different inspection mindset and a clear plan for what you will repair versus what you will negotiate.

title: Student Loans and Mortgage Approval in New Braunfels
excerpt: Student loans can change your mortgage approval in New Braunfels by shifting the payment lenders count in DTI, especially with IDR, deferment, or $0 reporting.

faqItems.q: 1) Can I buy a house in New Braunfels with student loans?
faqItems.a: Yes. Student loans usually affect your approval through your debt-to-income ratio, not as an automatic disqualifier. The key is documenting the monthly payment your lender is required to count so your pre-approval matches reality.

faqItems.q: 2) If my student loan payment is $0 on IDR, will a lender count $0?
faqItems.a: Sometimes, but typically only with documentation that verifies the actual required payment is $0. If the credit report shows $0 or no payment and the file cannot document the payment properly, some loan programs may require an assumed qualifying payment.

faqItems.q: 3) What happens if my student loans are deferred or in forbearance?
faqItems.a: This is where lenders often have to calculate a qualifying payment if the credit report does not show a usable monthly payment. Depending on the loan program and documentation, that assumed payment can be higher than what you are currently paying, which can reduce what you qualify for.

faqItems.q: 4) Do conventional, FHA, and VA loans treat student loans the same way?
faqItems.a: No. Each program can have different rules for what monthly payment must be used in DTI, especially when the credit report shows $0 or no payment. Your lender can tell you which rule applies based on your program and underwriting findings.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I do before I start touring homes in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Gather your student-loan documentation and ask your lender what payment they will be required to count for qualifying. Then set your shopping range based on a conservative scenario, and make sure your cash-to-close and closing-cost plan match that range.

opening_question: How do student loans affect mortgage approval in New Braunfels in 2026?
quick_answer: Student loans do not automatically stop you from buying a home in New Braunfels, but they can change the monthly debt payment a lender has to count in your debt-to-income ratio. On many conventional loans, if your credit report shows a monthly student loan payment, that payment is typically used, but if it shows $0 or no payment, lenders may need extra documentation or they may calculate a qualifying payment using rules like 1% of the balance for certain scenarios. The practical move is to get the right student-loan paperwork lined up early so your lender is not forced to use a higher assumed payment at the worst possible time. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: How do lenders treat student loans when qualifying for a mortgage?
content_sections.p: Start with the payment your credit report shows. In real life, the biggest swing is not your student-loan balance. It is the monthly payment the lender is required to count when they calculate your debt-to-income ratio (DTI). If your credit report shows a monthly student loan payment, many conventional lenders can use that number for qualifying. If the credit report is wrong, lenders may be able to use your most recent student-loan statement instead, as long as it supports a different payment amount. $0 payments are possible, but documentation is the difference between “counts as $0” and “we have to assume a payment.” One common misconception I hear from buyers relocating along the I-35 corridor is, “My loans are on IDR and the payment is $0, so it does not affect me.” Sometimes that is true, but only if your loan file can document it. If a lender cannot document the actual required payment, they may be required to use an assumed qualifying payment that is much higher than what you are currently paying. Deferred or forbearance student loans can trigger an assumed payment. For example, Fannie Mae guidance allows a lender to calculate a qualifying payment on deferred/forbearance student loans using either 1% of the outstanding balance or a fully amortizing payment based on documented repayment terms when the credit report shows $0 or no payment. That is why two buyers with the same income can get very different pre-approvals depending on how their student loans are documented. Program rules vary. Conventional, FHA, and VA loans can treat student loans differently. The main point is not to memorize every guideline. The point is to walk into your lender conversation with the right documents so the payment that gets counted matches reality as closely as guidelines allow. If you want a quick way to pressure-test your numbers, you can start with my mortgage calculator, then confirm the actual qualifying payment rules with your lender for the specific program you are using.

content_sections.h: What student-loan documents should you gather before you talk to a lender?
content_sections.p: Bring your latest student-loan statement, not just a screenshot. If the credit report is missing the payment, shows the wrong payment, or shows $0, the lender will usually need documentation to support what payment should be counted. A clean PDF statement, a servicer letter, or official account history beats a phone screenshot every time. If you are on an income-driven repayment (IDR) plan, bring the IDR proof. I have seen buyers lose days during an option period because their lender needed to verify the IDR payment amount and the buyer did not have the documentation ready. That is preventable. If your loans are deferred or in forbearance, expect extra questions. This is the scenario where lenders often default to an assumed payment if the file does not show a clear monthly obligation. If you have a documented repayment schedule or a letter showing what the payment will be when repayment resumes, bring it. If you are pursuing forgiveness or an employment-contingent plan, your lender may ask for documentation that you are eligible and approved. Do not wait until you are writing an offer. In New Braunfels, the speed of your financing clarity matters because it affects how confidently you can structure earnest money, option fee, and deadlines. If you have not read my breakdown of how Texas handles these pieces, this is a good companion: Texas earnest money rules for New Braunfels buyers. Then you can ask your lender, “Here is my documentation. What payment will you be required to count for my student loans on this program?”

content_sections.h: How does student-loan qualification affect what you can afford in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: DTI is the lever. Your student loan affects affordability because it changes the monthly debt number that gets counted against your income. When that counted payment goes up, your maximum mortgage payment usually has to go down. That can reduce your price range, reduce how competitive you want to be on repairs or closing costs, or push you toward new construction incentives versus resale, depending on what is happening in the neighborhood you are shopping. Use a simple test, but treat it as a draft. Here is a clean way to think about it without pretending this is exact underwriting. If your student loan payment that gets counted is $0, your DTI might support one price range. If the counted payment becomes $400, $800, or an assumed amount based on your balance, your supported housing payment can change noticeably. That is why I like to run two scenarios early: your “best case” documented payment and your “conservative case” assumed payment. You can sketch both scenarios using the mortgage calculator, then confirm the lender’s rules before you get emotionally attached to a house. In New Braunfels, the pain shows up at the edges of a price band. The difference between qualifying for a home in the upper end of your range versus the middle of your range often shows up in negotiations and inspection decisions. It also affects whether you want to pursue seller concessions, and that ties directly into closing costs. If you have not looked at the cost side yet, treat closing costs like part of the affordability conversation, not a separate topic. Every lender overlays guidelines differently. Two lenders can both be “right” and still calculate your qualifying payment differently depending on the loan program, automated underwriting, and what the credit report shows. The win is not chasing the most permissive answer. The win is building an offer strategy that still works if your qualifying payment comes in higher than you hoped.

content_sections.h: What’s the biggest student-loan mistake I see New Braunfels buyers make?
content_sections.p: They assume the lender will automatically count their “real” payment. The most expensive version of this mistake is when a buyer shops homes based on one assumed student-loan payment, then the lender has to count a different payment when the file is underwritten. That can happen when the credit report shows $0, the buyer is in deferment, or the file is missing IDR documentation. Then the timeline gets tight. In Texas, your option period is short by design. If you are under contract and your approval amount changes, you are suddenly deciding whether to renegotiate, walk, or switch properties while the clock is running. This is also where “home-sale contingency” planning matters. If you are selling and buying at the same time, read home-sale contingency offers in Texas so you understand how lenders and contracts interact. Only Cody would say this. New Braunfels has a lot of buyers who are relocating from Austin or San Antonio and they are used to fast pre-approvals and “we will figure it out later” underwriting. Here, the market can still move quickly in certain pockets and price points, and the part that trips people up is not the house. It is the paperwork. If you want to avoid the surprise payment issue, I would rather you spend one hour this week gathering student-loan docs than spend three stressful days in an option period trying to fix it. Your next best move is a plan, not a pep talk. If you tell me your target monthly payment, the neighborhoods you are considering, and how your student loans are structured (IDR, deferment, forgiveness track), I can help you frame the right questions for your lender and build a buying strategy that matches your real numbers.

title: VA Loan in Schertz TX (2026): PCS Checklist for JBSA
excerpt: VA loan in Schertz TX in 2026 can be a strong JBSA PCS move, but the timeline matters. Here’s a step-by-step checklist from COE to keys so you avoid surprises.

faqItems.q: 1) Can I use a VA loan to buy in Schertz or Cibolo on a short PCS timeline?
faqItems.a: Yes. The biggest success factor is starting the lender process early so the file is clean before you go under contract. When the paperwork is solid, the timeline is usually about the property, not your eligibility or documentation.

faqItems.q: 2) Do I need a COE before I start shopping for homes?
faqItems.a: You do not have to wait for the COE to tour homes, but you should start the COE process early so there are no surprises later. A lender can often pull the COE for you, and VA.gov also lets you request it directly.

faqItems.q: 3) How much is the VA funding fee in 2026?
faqItems.a: It depends on the loan type and your situation, and some borrowers are exempt. The VA publishes the current funding fee and closing cost guidance, and it is the best source for the exact rates that apply to your loan.

faqItems.q: 4) Can a seller help pay closing costs on a VA loan in Texas?
faqItems.a: Often yes, but the structure matters. Some costs are treated differently under VA rules, and the way concessions are written in the contract can affect what the VA considers allowable. This is a good reason to coordinate the offer strategy with a VA-experienced lender and agent.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I compare when choosing between Schertz, Cibolo, and New Braunfels for a JBSA commute?
faqItems.a: Compare your real commute window, not the map distance, and compare the all-in monthly payment including taxes and HOA or assessment fees. Then weigh lifestyle and daily logistics like shopping, amenities, and how much you want to drive for work and weekends.

opening_question: PCS orders in hand and thinking Schertz or Cibolo? Want to use your VA loan and still close on time?
quick_answer: Yes, a VA loan can work very well in Schertz, Cibolo, and the northeast JBSA corridor, even on a PCS timeline. The key is to start early on the COE and lender setup so you are not trying to fix eligibility or documentation after you are under contract. One number to plan for is the VA funding fee, which ranges from 0.5% to 3.3% depending on the loan type and your situation, and some borrowers are exempt. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why do so many JBSA buyers look at Schertz and Cibolo first?
content_sections.p: It is the corridor math. For a lot of JBSA assignments, Schertz and Cibolo sit in a spot that can make the daily drive workable to JBSA Randolph and JBSA Fort Sam, while still giving you newer housing options than many central neighborhoods. In practice, this area gives you a mix of newer subdivisions, established neighborhoods, and a steady pipeline of new construction. That matters on a PCS timeline because you can pick the tradeoff that fits you: a resale home that can close faster, or a new-build that can line up with a reporting date if the builder timeline is real. One Texas-specific note that surprises relocating buyers is how quickly taxes and special districts can change the monthly number. Property taxes are a big piece of the payment in this region, and some neighborhoods also have MUD or PID-style assessments. Before you fall in love with a floor plan, you want to confirm what the total monthly payment looks like with taxes and any HOA or district fees, not just principal and interest. If you want to run payment scenarios quickly, use my mortgage calculator as a starting point.

content_sections.h: When should you start the VA loan process if you are on PCS orders?
content_sections.p: Earlier than you think. The fastest VA closings I see are the ones where the borrower did the unglamorous setup before touring homes. If you are about 90 to 180 days out, the goal is a clean pre-approval and a clear plan for how your housing allowance and any shift work schedules affect your shopping range. If you are 30 to 90 days out, the goal is to be fully underwritten (or as close as your lender can get) so the contract-to-close window is about the property, not your paperwork. If you want a simple path, start with two steps: (1) pick a lender who does VA daily, and (2) get your COE handled early. The other key is to understand the Texas contract timeline so you are not surprised by the option period, inspection window, and closing steps. PCS reality check: your timeline will feel tight even when it is not. That is why I like to build a checklist that lines up your lender milestones, your inspection window, and your appraisal timeline around your reporting date instead of hoping it all works out.

content_sections.h: How do you get your COE without slowing down underwriting?
content_sections.p: The COE is not the hard part, but waiting on it can be. Many buyers assume they will deal with the Certificate of Eligibility after they find a home. On a PCS timeline, that is backwards. You can request a COE through VA.gov, and in many cases the lender can also retrieve it through the VA system as part of the loan setup. Either way, the point is to surface any eligibility or documentation friction early, not after the option period clock is ticking. If you are missing docs or you are not sure what your status is, do not guess. Get it clarified early, then you are shopping with confidence. If you want to see the exact VA steps, here is the official COE request page: How to request a COE. This is one of those places where a tight lender and agent team matters. I would rather spend 20 minutes this week building a clean file than lose a house next month because the file was still fuzzy when underwriting got serious.

content_sections.h: What numbers should you know before you write an offer in Schertz?
content_sections.p: In this market, the payment is the strategy. Before you write, you want to know three numbers: the monthly payment range you are truly comfortable with, your cash-to-close target, and your concession plan. On the VA side, the funding fee is a one-time fee that can be financed in many cases. The VA publishes the current funding fee and closing cost guidance here: VA funding fee and closing costs. The big takeaway is that it is not a single flat number for every borrower. It varies, and some borrowers are exempt. On the contract side, Texas uses an option period that out-of-state buyers often misread. If you have not bought in Texas before, skim this before you write: Texas option period basics. Finally, understand how seller help actually works on VA. Not every credit is the same, and the way concessions are structured can change what the VA considers allowable versus what must be paid by the seller. If that topic is on your mind, I wrote a plain-English breakdown here: VA seller credits and the 4% rule.

content_sections.h: How do VA appraisals and repairs tend to go in this corridor?
content_sections.p: Most VA appraisals are normal, but you want to avoid preventable repair flags. The VA appraiser is not trying to fail a deal, but they do have minimum property requirements focused on safety and basic habitability. In Schertz and Cibolo, the issues I see most often are not exotic. They are things like missing smoke detectors, peeling paint on older exteriors, roof condition questions, or straightforward safety items. In rural edges outside the core subdivisions, you can also see septic or well-related questions. That does not mean you should avoid those homes. It means you should plan for the inspection and repair conversation from day one. If you are buying a resale home, I like to walk the property with a VA lens before we write. Not to nitpick, but to spot obvious fixes that keep underwriting smooth. If the home is borderline on condition, we talk about whether it is the right fit for a VA timeline, or whether a different property will be less stressful. And if you are comparing new construction versus resale, remember this: a builder can fix a punch list quickly, but they can also drag out closing dates. Your best path depends on your reporting date and how much schedule risk you can tolerate.

content_sections.h: Should you use a VA loan on new construction in Schertz or Cibolo?
content_sections.p: Sometimes yes, but only with eyes open. New construction can look like the cleanest PCS solution, and it can be, but it introduces a different risk: the calendar. If you go new-build, you want to confirm the builder timeline in writing, understand how incentives are structured, and make sure your lender is set up for new construction draws and change orders if they come up. I also like to confirm which fees are truly optional and which are baked into the neighborhood (HOA, special districts, and any assessment structures). One local nuance: some newer neighborhoods in the area use additional assessments that can surprise a relocating buyer who is used to a simpler tax structure. Before you commit, ask for the full fee picture in writing so you can compare the all-in monthly payment across neighborhoods. If you are deciding between two neighborhoods with similar prices, do not pick based only on the builder incentive. Pick based on the all-in monthly payment, the reporting-date risk, and the resale reality two to five years from now. That is the part that protects you when life changes and you need options.

content_sections.h: What do PCS buyers usually get wrong about the Schertz corridor?
content_sections.p: They underestimate the commute reality and overestimate how fast “close to base” feels. Here is the honest, local version: the map distance is not the drive time when you hit IH-35 or Loop 1604 at the wrong time. This is my “only a local would say it” advice for JBSA moves. If you are leaving the house at 7:15 a.m., I want you to test that commute in the real window you will drive it. Not at noon on a Saturday. If your shift is off-peak, your world is different. The goal is not to scare you. It is to make sure the neighborhood you pick matches your actual day. The second thing PCS buyers miss is that the cheapest list price is rarely the cheapest monthly payment. Taxes, HOA, and assessment structures can swing the payment enough to change your comfortable range. If you want a sanity check, send me the addresses you are considering and I will map the commute pattern, the tax picture, and the realistic payment range so you can compare apples to apples. If you are torn between staying closer to San Antonio or moving into New Braunfels, I can help you compare the commute reality and the all-in payment so you pick the area that fits your day, not just your search results.

content_sections.h: What is the simplest next step if you are 30 to 180 days from moving?
content_sections.p: Get a VA-ready game plan, then shop with leverage. The cleanest PCS purchase is rarely the one with the most optimism. It is the one with the best plan. Start by getting a VA-focused pre-approval and your COE process underway, then build a short list of neighborhoods that fit your reporting date, your commute window, and your payment comfort zone. From there, we can time showings, write offers with the right concessions strategy, and protect your exit options if your orders change. If you want to talk through your specific situation, I can help you build a JBSA-to-Hill Country roadmap and a realistic offer strategy for the neighborhoods you are actually considering. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

title: Best Time to Sell a House in New Braunfels (2026)
excerpt: Best time to sell a house in New Braunfels depends on your price band, builder competition, and timing. Here’s how to pick your strongest 30–90 day window.

faqItems.q: 1) What month is best to sell a house in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: For many sellers, late winter through early summer tends to be a strong window because more buyers are actively touring homes. The best month for your home depends on your price range, prep timeline, and how much competition you have from similar listings and new construction.

faqItems.q: 2) Should I wait to sell until mortgage rates drop?
faqItems.a: I would not base your plan on predicting rates. If you need to move within the next 30–180 days, you can still sell successfully by pricing to today’s buyer behavior, presenting well in week one, and setting terms that attract qualified buyers.

faqItems.q: 3) How long does it usually take to sell a house in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: It depends on your neighborhood pocket, condition, and price band. A well-positioned home often finds its strongest buyer early, while an overpriced home can sit and then chase the market with price cuts.

faqItems.q: 4) What is the biggest mistake sellers make when timing their sale?
faqItems.a: Waiting until everything is perfect and then launching late, or pricing too high and “testing the market.” Your best leverage is usually in the first week. Preparation and correct pricing are the two levers you control.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I do before listing to get a better offer?
faqItems.a: Start with a comp-backed value range, then focus on first-week presentation: deep cleaning, small repairs, and staging choices that help buyers feel the home is move-in ready. If you want to be extra strategic, plan your option period and closing window so the contract is easy for a strong buyer to accept.

opening_question: When is the best time to sell a house in New Braunfels if you want the best mix of price, leverage, and a clean contract?
quick_answer: For most New Braunfels sellers, your best window is late winter through early summer, when buyer activity is typically stronger and you have more shots at clean terms. Right now, the market is moving but not sprinting. Cody’s March 2026 dashboard snapshot shows a median price around $346,115 and roughly 5.5 months of inventory, which is a more negotiated environment than the ultra-tight years. The real answer is not a single month on the calendar. It is the best time for your home type, your neighborhood pocket, and your next move timeline. If you are 30–180 days from listing, the smart play is to work backward from (1) your target closing date, (2) your prep timeline, and (3) the price band you need to hit. If you want, I can map the likely buyer profile for your price range, the comps that will actually set your ceiling, and the two or three weeks you are most likely to get your strongest offers. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What actually changes season-to-season in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: A lot of sellers think “best time” is just spring versus summer. In New Braunfels, the seasonality that matters most is the buyer pool that shows up, and what they are willing to negotiate on. Here is what tends to shift through the year: Showings and urgency. Spring generally brings more active buyers. That can mean more showings, faster decisions, and fewer “let’s wait and see” offers. In a negotiated market, momentum matters. Competition from new construction. Builder incentives often ramp up when a community is trying to hit quarterly targets. If your neighborhood is competing with a brand-new home down the street offering rate buydowns or closing cost help, the “best time” for you might be when incentives are quieter or when your home is positioned as the better value. Contract cleanliness. The strongest offers are not always the highest price. The best time to list is when you can attract qualified buyers who bring clean terms: realistic option periods, fewer repair battles, and financing that actually closes. If you want a quick baseline for where we are right now, see my recent update: New Braunfels housing market March 2026 stats.

content_sections.h: Is spring still the best time to sell in 2026?
content_sections.p:
Often, yes. Spring is still the season when more buyers are actively touring homes, comparing neighborhoods, and writing offers.

But in 2026 the bigger question I’m getting is: “Do I list now, or do I wait for rates to drop?” The truth is you cannot build a selling strategy on a prediction. What you can do is build a plan that performs in today’s buyer behavior.

If you are in a price band that is saturated with inventory, waiting can backfire because you are stepping into more competition later. If you are in a scarcity pocket (a floor plan, lot type, or neighborhood that does not come up often), you can win almost any month as long as you price correctly and you look better than the alternatives.

In other words: spring helps, but it does not save a pricing mistake. A clean, comp-backed price plus strong first-week presentation is what wins you leverage.

content_sections.h: How do you pick your ideal list date if you need to close by a certain time?
content_sections.p: Most sellers have a “move by” deadline even if they do not say it out loud. School calendars, job changes, new construction completion dates, and lease end dates all create pressure. A practical way to pick the best time to sell is to work backward from your real deadline: Step 1: Choose your target closing window. If you need to be out by August 15, do not plan to accept an offer on August 1. Give yourself buffer. Step 2: Back up 30–45 days for the contract-to-close timeline. This can vary based on lender and terms, but you want a realistic runway. Step 3: Back up 7–14 days for the first-week market test. In New Braunfels, the first 7–10 days tells you almost everything about whether the market agrees with your price. Step 4: Back up 2–6 weeks for prep. This is where sellers win. Cleaning, paint touch-ups, small repairs, and staging choices can be the difference between “nice house” and “I have to have this one.” If you want a prep playbook that matches how buyers actually shop here, this pairs well with: Staging a house for sale in New Braunfels.

content_sections.h: What price range is most sensitive to timing in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: Timing sensitivity is usually strongest where buyers have the most alternatives. In New Braunfels, that often shows up in the broad mid-range where many homes “feel similar” in photos, and in neighborhoods where builders are still delivering new inventory. Here’s the pattern I see over and over: Entry to mid-range listings compete on payment, not just price. If your likely buyer is payment-sensitive, the season you list matters less than whether your home is positioned as the best value versus similar homes and new construction incentives. Move-up listings compete on lifestyle and condition. Buyers at higher price points often have more flexibility, but they also get picky. A dated home can sit in any season. Unique homes compete on scarcity. If your home has a rare lot, a layout that is hard to replace, or a location that does not come up often, your leverage comes from scarcity. Timing still matters, but the bigger lever is “Are we priced where the next-best alternative looks worse?” Want the fastest way to pressure-test your number? Get a comp-backed value range for your exact neighborhood pocket, not just an online estimate.

content_sections.h: What’s the biggest timing mistake New Braunfels sellers make?
content_sections.p: They wait to list until everything is perfect, then they miss their best leverage window. This is the “only a local would say this” moment: in a lot of New Braunfels neighborhoods, buyers forgive small cosmetic flaws if the home is priced right and shows well. What they do not forgive is a home that feels overpriced in week one and then starts chasing the market with price cuts. I see this most with sellers who are trying to time the market like a stock. They hold off, hoping for a magical week when buyers will pay a premium. Meanwhile, the comparable homes that actually set the price ceiling are selling, and new listings are replacing them. If you want to sell with leverage, the move is usually: Prepare earlier than you think. Even if you list later, preparation done early gives you control. Price for week one, not week six. Your best buyer is almost always the one who finds you early. Pick terms that attract strong buyers. A clean, realistic option period and clear disclosures often beat a slightly higher price with messy terms. If you want, I can lay out a simple listing plan for your home: value range, prep priorities, timing, and the negotiation guardrails we will use when offers come in.

content_sections.h: How should you think about the Texas option period when timing your sale?
content_sections.p:
In Texas, the option period is not just a formality. It is leverage.

When you list in a stronger demand window, you are more likely to see buyers accept shorter option periods and cleaner inspection negotiations. When you list in a slower window, buyers often ask for more time and more concessions.

That does not mean you should avoid a slower season. It means your pricing and terms need to be even more intentional. The goal is to attract serious buyers, not just traffic.

If you are planning to sell soon, I recommend deciding your “terms comfort zone” before you list: the option period length you can live with, the closing window that fits your move, and what kinds of repair requests you will negotiate versus decline. That clarity keeps you from reacting emotionally when the first offer hits your inbox.

content_sections.h: What should you do in the 30–90 days before listing?
content_sections.p: If you are trying to pick the best time to sell a house in New Braunfels, the 30–90 days before you go live is where you earn your result. Here is the order I recommend most sellers follow: 1) Nail the value range with real comps. Not just online estimates. Real comps, adjusted for condition, location, lot, and updates. 2) Identify the “buyer objections” before you list. Every neighborhood pocket has them. Road noise, stairs, dated finishes, older roofs, septic concerns outside city limits. When we plan for objections ahead of time, the listing feels more confident and buyers negotiate less. 3) Build a prep list that matches ROI. Not every update pays back. Paint, flooring fixes, lighting, and deep cleaning often outperform expensive remodels when timing is tight. 4) Decide your terms strategy. Preferred closing window, leaseback needs, and how you will handle repair requests. 5) Launch with a first-week plan. Great photos, accurate pricing, and a showing strategy that makes it easy for serious buyers to see the home. If you want to run the math before we even talk about list price, I can estimate a net sheet so you know what the numbers look like after typical costs.

title: Comal County Median Sale Price and DOM: Spring 2026
excerpt: Comal County median sale price and days on market are key timing signals. Here’s what Spring 2026 numbers suggest for New Braunfels buyers and sellers.

faqItems.q: 1) Is Comal County’s median sale price the same as New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Not necessarily. New Braunfels spans Comal and Guadalupe counties, and even within Comal, the mix of homes that sell each month can change the county median. For decisions, use a neighborhood-specific comp set.

faqItems.q: 2) Does “118 days to sell” mean my home will sit four months?
faqItems.a: No. “Time to sell” can be measured different ways and can include the whole path to closing. A well-priced, well-prepped home can still go pending much faster than an average.

faqItems.q: 3) What matters more right now: price or condition?
faqItems.a: Both, but price sets the conversation and condition keeps buyers moving forward. In a slower pace environment, buyers compare your home to the cleanest alternatives, so visible maintenance and inspection signals matter.

faqItems.q: 4) How can a buyer use higher days on market without losing the right home?
faqItems.a: Use DOM to negotiate smarter terms, not to assume every seller is desperate. If a home is priced correctly and shows well, it can still attract strong offers even in a slower market.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the fastest way to get a real market answer for my address?
faqItems.a: Request a local market analysis based on recent, similar sales and active competition in your pocket of New Braunfels. You can start with the home value form and include your timeline and priorities.

opening_question: Are Comal County home prices still climbing in 2026, and how long are homes really taking to sell?
quick_answer: As we move through Spring 2026, Comal County’s pricing is still holding in the mid-$400s in many public market snapshots, but the bigger story is pace. One widely cited spring snapshot shows a median sale price around $464,000 with an average time to sell around 118 days, which is a very different feel than the 2021–2022 sprint. In plain terms: sellers need a pricing-and-prep plan, and buyers can often be more selective if they understand which homes are actually positioned to move. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What do the latest Spring 2026 Comal County numbers show?
content_sections.p: If you only look at price, it is easy to miss what is actually changing. In several Spring 2026 market snapshots, Comal County’s median sale price clusters in the mid-$400s. One spring snapshot commonly referenced by consumers shows a median sale price around $464,000 and an average time to sell around 118 days. Two quick notes so you do not overreact to a single number. First, different sites define time-on-market differently. Some measure from list date to pending, others from list date to close, and some blend in different property types. Second, median sale price is extremely sensitive to the mix of what sold that month. A few more custom homes or acreage closings can move the median without meaning your neighborhood suddenly “went up.” If you want a number you can actually use, the move is to translate county stats into your pocket of New Braunfels. That is exactly what a local market analysis does. It takes the county headline and narrows it to your subdivision, school district boundary (as a property feature, not a rating), price band, and current competition. If you are selling, start with your value range at my home value page. If you are buying, we can map your payment comfort to the right neighborhoods and price bands before you ever tour houses.

content_sections.h: Why do median sale price and days on market tell different stories?
content_sections.p: Median sale price answers “what did people pay,” but it does not answer “how hard was it to get under contract.” Days on market is the friction metric. When DOM stretches, it usually means buyers have more choices, sellers have more competition, and pricing needs to be tighter to get the same result. This is where I see people make expensive mistakes. Sellers sometimes chase the highest number they saw online last month, even if that sale was a different product in a different pocket. Buyers sometimes assume every listing is desperate because DOM is up, then they lose the one home that was actually priced correctly and had clean condition. Here is the practical takeaway: use price to set your guardrails, then use DOM to set your expectations and strategy. If you want to sell in the next 30–180 days, your question is not “what is the county median?” It is “what is the shortest path to a clean offer in my neighborhood, at my price point, given today’s competition?” If you want a good example of how competition shifts when builders are aggressive, read my Spring 2026 builder incentives guide for New Braunfels.

content_sections.h: What does a ~4-month selling pace mean for sellers in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: A 3–4 month “average time to sell” headline does not mean every seller waits four months. It means the middle of the market is not automatically bailing you out anymore. In a faster market, a home that was slightly overpriced could still get rescued by urgency. In a slower market, that same home sits long enough for buyers to start asking, “What is wrong with it?” Insight: the first price is your best price opportunity. The first 7–14 days is when you get the most honest buyer feedback. If showings are thin, the market is telling you something early. Waiting 30–45 days before adjusting usually costs more than the adjustment itself because you lose momentum and you invite tougher negotiations later. Insight: condition competes when price bands are tight. When buyers have options, the “average” house gets compared against the cleanest house, not the other average houses. In New Braunfels, that means small things matter: roof age disclosure clarity, HVAC age and service records, obvious deferred maintenance, and whether inspection items look like a pattern. The “only locals notice this” part: New Braunfels is not one market. In Spring 2026, I see pace change by pocket and by price band. A home in one of the established, commutable pockets can still move quickly when it is priced right, while another home at the same price but with a different commute pattern, HOA structure, or lot situation can sit. Buyers relocating from Austin often assume every well-staged home will get multiple offers automatically. That is just not how 2026 is behaving in many pockets. Strategy matters again. If you want to sanity-check your numbers before you list, I can run the same comp-backed pricing conversation I use in listing appointments, so you know what buyers will compare you against before you pick a number.

content_sections.h: How should buyers read price and DOM in Spring 2026?
content_sections.p: If you are buying, higher DOM can be a gift, but only if you use it correctly. The goal is not to “lowball everything.” The goal is to spot which listings are misaligned (price, condition, terms, or marketing) versus which listings are actually strong and simply operating in a slower environment. Insight: negotiation power shows up in terms, not just price. In a slower market, you will often do better by targeting seller-paid closing costs, repair credits, or rate-buydown conversations than by forcing a dramatic price cut that breaks the deal. Your lender can tell you what matters most for your payment. Insight: days on market is not the same as days to close. If a “time to sell” metric includes the full path to closing, it can look long even when the home went pending in a normal timeframe. That is why I track both. The question you care about is whether buyers are writing offers, not just whether the file finally closed. If you are newer to Texas, make sure you understand earnest money and the Option Period rules before you write offers. That one detail changes how you negotiate and how you protect yourself while you inspect.

content_sections.h: What should you do next if you are making a move in 30 to 180 days?
content_sections.p:
County headlines are useful, but you do not buy or sell “the county.” You buy or sell one home, on one street, competing against a handful of real alternatives right now. The fastest way to make the market feel simple again is to get a neighborhood-specific plan.

If you are selling, we start by mapping your competition and the buyer objections that show up in your price band. If you are buying, we start by narrowing your search to the pockets that make sense for your commute and lifestyle, then we build an offer plan that matches the reality of each listing.

If you want the cleanest starting point, request a value range, then tell me your timeline and what you want to net, and I will translate the market into options.

title: River vs Lake Property in Texas Hill Country (2026)
excerpt: River vs lake property in Texas Hill Country comes down to flood risk, access, and the lifestyle you actually use. Here is how I help buyers compare the tradeoffs in 2026.[…]

faqItems.q: 1) Is river property or lake property better in Texas Hill Country?
faqItems.a: Neither is automatically better. Lake property usually fits buyers who want boating, broad views, and a weekend lake culture. River property often fits buyers who want shade, current, swimming, and float culture, but it typically requires more careful flood and access verification.

faqItems.q: 2) How do I check flood risk for a riverfront home near New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Start with the FEMA flood maps to see the flood zone and floodplain boundaries, then talk with your insurance professional about pricing and coverage options. In practice, I like to do this early so the flood story does not surprise you during option period.

faqItems.q: 3) Do lake levels matter for lakefront property value near Canyon Lake?
faqItems.a: Yes, because levels can influence shoreline usability, views, and buyer perception. The experience depends on the shoreline slope, how far you have to walk to reach water, and how you plan to use the lake. It is smart to evaluate the property as a view and access purchase, not only as a “waterfront” label.

faqItems.q: 4) What costs are different between riverfront and lakefront homes in Hill Country?
faqItems.a: Riverfront homes can come with different flood-related insurance and mitigation considerations depending on flood maps and structure elevation. Lake homes may have different maintenance and equipment costs tied to boating and shoreline exposure. Either way, utilities and infrastructure can be a bigger cost driver than buyers expect.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the best way to choose the right Hill Country water area to live?
faqItems.a: Build a shortlist based on your weekly routine, then tour river and lake options with the same must-haves so you can compare the real feel side by side. I also recommend verifying access, utilities, and flood map context early so you are choosing with clear numbers, not assumptions.

opening_question: Trying to decide between river property and lake property in the Texas Hill Country for 2026?
quick_answer: If you want predictable boating and a classic “dock and weekends” feel, lake property usually fits better. If you want float culture, shade, and a front-row seat to Hill Country river life, river property can be incredible, but you need to underwrite flood risk and access much more carefully. Around New Braunfels, Canyon Lake’s conservation pool elevation is about 909 ft msl, but day-to-day usability depends on the shoreline, slope, and water levels, not just the address. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What do you actually mean by “riverfront” or “lakefront” in Hill Country listings?
content_sections.p: First, I translate the marketing language into real access. In the New Braunfels and Canyon Lake area, “waterfront” can mean true deeded frontage, it can mean an HOA-owned strip you can use, or it can mean you are simply near the water. Those three experiences price very differently. River property is often about proximity plus usability. With the Comal and Guadalupe, some homes have direct bank access, some have a shared neighborhood park, and some back up to a greenbelt that feels like water access but is not. Before we fall in love with a view, I confirm where the lot line ends, where any easements begin, and whether access is walkable year-round. Lake property is often about slope, shoreline, and rules. On reservoirs like Canyon Lake, a “lakeview” lot can be amazing even without shoreline. A “lakefront” lot can be steep enough that you rarely go down to the water. And dock rules vary by lake and jurisdiction. I like to treat “lakefront” as a starting point, then verify the real shoreline path, the grade, and what you can legally install or store.

content_sections.h: Which lifestyle do you want to use every month, not just on vacation?
content_sections.p: Lake life is usually about boating and broad open water. If you picture a long day on a boat, bigger horizon views, and a second-home vibe, the lake tends to deliver. It also tends to have a clearer “weekend culture” with marinas, ramps, and predictable recreation patterns. River life is usually about shade, current, and a shorter feedback loop. People who love river property usually want to swim, fish, kayak, or float. They want the sound of moving water, big cypress trees, and a setting that feels more tucked in. In New Braunfels, that can also mean being close to the tubing economy and seasonal traffic patterns. My local reality check. The part relocating buyers miss is how different a Saturday feels in peak season. A house that feels peaceful on a February showing can sit in the middle of tubing traffic and parking overflow in July. That is not “good” or “bad.” It is just a real-use question we should answer before you commit.

content_sections.h: How does flood risk show up differently for river property vs lake property?
content_sections.p: River risk is usually fast and localized. Rivers rise and fall with storms upstream, and the risk profile can change a lot from one bend to the next. In practice, that means I prioritize understanding the property’s flood zone designation, base flood elevation context, and any local floodplain requirements before we even talk about cosmetics. Lake risk is usually about water level variability and shoreline usability. Reservoir levels can swing. A lakefront home can still be “waterfront,” but the usable shoreline can shift. That matters for your view, your path to the water, and how you imagine using the property. What I do with clients. We pull FEMA flood maps early, then we talk through what that means for insurance quotes, improvements, and resale. If the numbers do not make sense, you would rather know before option period and inspections. If you want context on how Canyon Lake levels can influence buyer perception, this post pairs well with Canyon Lake water levels and real estate impact.

content_sections.h: What are the practical costs and constraints most buyers miss?
content_sections.p: Insurance and maintenance are not equal between river and lake. Riverfront homes can carry higher flood-related insurance or mitigation costs depending on the flood zone and structure elevation. Lake property can come with different wind exposure, shoreline erosion concerns, and equipment maintenance if you own boats or store watercraft. Utilities and infrastructure can become the real deciding factor. A lot of the best-feeling Hill Country water properties are outside city limits. That can mean septic, well, or a different water system. It can also mean different internet options and travel times to everyday errands. When we compare river and lake homes, I like to price the whole lifestyle, not just the purchase. Boundaries and easements decide your real access. For water-adjacent lots, I want a survey, I want to understand any easements, and I want to confirm what “access” looks like on foot. It is easy to assume you will use the water weekly, then realize the best route is a steep scramble or crosses land you do not control. Access is a negotiation topic. I see deals where “easy access to the water” is assumed, then the buyer realizes the path is steep, rocky, or eroded. If access is your main reason for buying, we treat it like a required feature, just like a garage or a home office.

content_sections.h: How do you pick the right Hill Country area for your water lifestyle near New Braunfels?
content_sections.p: Start with your normal week. Are you commuting to San Antonio? Are you trying to be close to New Braunfels amenities? Do you want to be closer to Canyon Lake, or closer to the Comal and Guadalupe corridors? The “right” answer depends on what you will do on Tuesday, not just on the weekend. Then match the area to your tolerance for seasonality. Some pockets feel sleepy in the off-season and busy in peak season. Others feel steady year-round but come at a higher price point. If you want a structured way to compare, I use a simple shortlist approach and then we confirm the tradeoffs in person. Two quick internal links that help buyers frame the decision. If you are considering a second home, read buying a second home in Texas Hill Country. If you are weighing rural water property with land, also read buying acreage in the Texas Hill Country. If you want the broad comparison view, start here: explore Texas Hill Country areas near New Braunfels.

content_sections.h: What is a smart “river vs lake” decision framework for 2026?
content_sections.p: Step 1: Decide what you want to use most. Boating and big water views tends to pull you toward the lake. Shade, current, and float culture tends to pull you toward the river. Step 2: Underwrite risk and access as hard requirements. With river properties, flood risk and access can make or break the deal. With lake properties, water level variability and shoreline path can change the experience more than buyers expect. Step 3: Price the whole lifestyle. Insurance, utilities, maintenance, and travel time to the things you do every week can swing the “real cost” more than a small change in the purchase price. Step 4: Make a shortlist and tour with intent. The fastest way to pick the right fit is to tour 2–3 river options and 2–3 lake options with the same must-haves, then compare how you feel and what the numbers say.

title: Texas VLB Home Loan Benefits 2026 in New Braunfels
excerpt: Texas VLB home loan benefits in 2026 can stretch your buying power in New Braunfels. Here’s what the $832,750 max means, who qualifies, and how to use it.

faqItems.q: 1) Is the Texas VLB home loan the same as a VA loan?
faqItems.a: No. VA benefits are federal, and the VLB program is a Texas benefit administered through the Texas General Land Office. A lender can help you compare both options side by side for the same property and timeline.

faqItems.q: 2) What is the maximum Texas VLB home loan amount in 2026?
faqItems.a: The Texas GLO’s VLB home loan information lists a maximum loan amount up to $832,750 for eligible Veterans, military members, and spouses. Your actual approved amount depends on lender underwriting and your financial profile.

faqItems.q: 3) Do I need a disability rating to use VLB home loan benefits?
faqItems.a: No. Disability is not a requirement for eligibility. However, the program notes that a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or higher can qualify you for a discounted interest rate, which is worth discussing with your lender.

faqItems.q: 4) Can I use VLB for new construction in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Potentially, yes. The program notes that new construction loans must meet applicable building standards required by local jurisdictions. The key is to confirm the lender process early so your contract deadlines and the loan timeline stay aligned.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the best first step if I’m PCS’ing to the New Braunfels area?
faqItems.a: Start by confirming your financing options and timeline with a lender, then narrow your neighborhood targets based on commute, taxes, and HOA structure. If you want help mapping that plan, call Cody Posey Real Estate at 830.360.5569.

opening_question: Are Texas VLB home loan benefits worth using in 2026 if you’re buying in New Braunfels?
quick_answer: For many eligible Veterans and military households, Texas VLB home loan benefits can be a strong complement to your overall financing plan in 2026, especially if you are comparing VA, FHA, and conventional options with a local lender. The Texas General Land Office lists a maximum VLB home loan amount up to $832,750, which matters in New Braunfels where price points vary a lot by neighborhood and whether you’re considering new construction. If you have a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or higher, the program notes a discounted interest rate benefit, which can shift the math depending on your scenario. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What is the Texas Veterans Land Board (VLB) home loan program in 2026?
content_sections.p: When people say “VLB loan,” they’re usually talking about the Texas Veterans Land Board home loan benefit administered through the Texas General Land Office (GLO). In plain English, it’s a Texas-specific veteran benefit that can provide competitive fixed-rate financing and other advantages for eligible Veterans, active-duty service members, and certain spouses. Here’s the misconception I hear all the time. PCS buyers moving into the New Braunfels and JBSA orbit often assume “VA and VLB are the same thing.” They are not. The VA benefit is federal. VLB is Texas. In practice, that means your lender, your eligibility checks, and your timeline can look a little different. The right move is to treat VLB as a tool inside your bigger plan, not a magic product that replaces everything else. If you’re relocating, start with the big picture first: your duty location or commute, your target move window, and what monthly payment you want to live with. Then you and a lender can compare VA versus VLB versus other options side by side using the same property, the same price, and the same insurance and tax assumptions. If you want a local starting point before you call a lender, my New Braunfels relocation guide is built for that exact roadmap conversation.

content_sections.h: How big is the VLB home loan amount, and what does $832,750 actually mean locally?
content_sections.p: One of the most important numbers in the 2026 VLB conversation is the maximum home loan amount the program lists: up to $832,750 for eligible Veterans, military members, and spouses. That does not mean you should borrow that much, and it does not mean every borrower will qualify for that amount. It does mean the program is positioned to support a wide range of price points, including many move-up options in New Braunfels, Canyon Lake, and the north Comal County corridor. In New Braunfels, the same price can buy a very different “feel.” I see buyers compare a newer neighborhood in the Veramendi or FM 1101 side of town against an older area closer to Gruene, downtown, or other established pockets. The home may be the same size on paper, but the taxes, HOA structure, commute patterns, and what you can negotiate can be totally different. That’s why the loan amount headline is only step one. The real question is whether the loan product fits the property type and the timeline you are working with. If you want to pressure-test your target payment range, run a few scenarios with your lender using the same home price, taxes, and insurance assumptions. That way your VA versus VLB comparison stays apples to apples.

content_sections.h: Do you need a VA disability rating to get VLB benefits (and what is the 30% detail)?
content_sections.p: You do not need a disability rating to be eligible for VLB home loan benefits. The program is designed for eligible Veterans, active-duty military members, and certain spouses based on program rules. That said, there is one detail that can matter a lot for budgeting: the GLO notes that Veterans with a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or greater qualify for a discounted interest rate. Whether that discount is the deciding factor depends on the spread between rate options available to you at the time you apply, your credit profile, and how long you expect to keep the loan. Practical guidance. If you have a disability rating at or above that threshold, bring it up early. Do not wait until you are under contract. I have seen buyers lose time because the benefit conversation started after the offer was accepted, and then the lender needed additional documentation. Your goal should be to confirm the benefit, confirm the documents, and confirm the timeline before you write an offer, especially in neighborhoods where a clean financing path is the difference between winning and losing. If you want a refresher on how VA financing costs can work in general, you may also want to skim my earlier post on VA funding fee rates in 2026 and then ask your lender how those costs compare to your VLB options.

content_sections.h: How does VLB interact with VA loans, new construction, and the reality of New Braunfels contracts?
content_sections.p: Insight: treat this like a timing strategy, not just a rate decision. The VLB pages and press materials emphasize the program’s goal of expanding homeownership opportunities for Texas Veterans, and they reference how Veterans may pair benefits and work with participating lenders. In the real world, what matters is whether VLB fits your contract timeline and the property type you’re targeting. New Braunfels has two markets running at once. Resale homes operate on a familiar Texas contract rhythm, where the Option Period and the financing approval timeline drive the pace. New construction, especially with national builders, can introduce different deadlines, incentive structures, and lender preferences. If you want to buy a new build, the VLB program also notes that new construction loans must meet building standards required locally by the applicable jurisdictions. That is not a red flag, but it is another reason to get your lender lined up early. Here’s what I see PCS buyers miss. They focus on “getting the best rate” and forget that the best deal is the one that closes on time without drama. In a builder contract, delays can cost you incentives. In a resale negotiation, a shaky financing story can cost you the house. If you’re unsure which path fits you best, start with a clear offer strategy and let financing support that strategy, not the other way around. If you are actively PCS’ing into the area, my PCS checklist for JBSA-area buyers will help you map the moving parts. Then we can tailor it to New Braunfels neighborhoods and your commute.

content_sections.h: What should you do before you write an offer if you want to use VLB in 2026?
content_sections.p: The best time to handle the VLB decision is before you fall in love with a house. Once you are emotionally attached to a property, it is harder to make calm, strategic choices. Insight: your lender choice is part of your offer strength. If you are using a specialized benefit, you want a lender who can close on time and explain the program clearly to a listing agent when needed. In New Braunfels, there are plenty of great homes that get multiple offers, and the offer that wins is usually the one that feels the most certain. Start by clarifying your “must-haves” and “nice-to-haves” so you can write an offer that fits your real life. Then align the loan path, the timeline, and your cash-to-close estimate. If you are not sure who to call first, my recommended lenders list is a solid starting point because it’s built around communication and closing performance, not flashy promises. And if you want a second set of eyes before you take the next step, that is what I do. I will help you match the right neighborhoods and price bands to your commute, your move window, and the kind of monthly payment you want to live with, so the financing decision supports the overall plan.
