title: VA Seller Credits Texas: 2026 Rule for New Braunfels
excerpt: VA seller credits Texas buyers can negotiate are more flexible than many people think. The 4% cap applies to concessions, not every closing cost credit.

faqItems.q: 1) Can a seller pay all my closing costs on a VA loan in Texas?
faqItems.a: The VA allows sellers or builders to offer credits toward some or all buyer closing costs, and VA guidance says it does not limit credits for a loan's closing costs. Your lender may still apply stricter rules, and the contract and Closing Disclosure need to label the credits correctly. Always have the lender review the credit structure before submitting the offer.

faqItems.q: 2) What is the 4% VA seller concession cap based on?
faqItems.a: The VA concession cap is no more than 4% of the home's reasonable value, which is tied to the VA Notice of Value. It is not a blanket cap on every seller-paid closing cost. If the appraised value changes, the lender should re-check the concession calculation.

faqItems.q: 3) Does the VA funding fee count as a seller concession?
faqItems.a: Yes. If the seller pays the buyer's VA funding fee, that payment is treated as a seller concession and counts toward the 4% cap. Buyers who are exempt from the funding fee may have a different credit strategy, so confirm your status with your lender early.

faqItems.q: 4) Do temporary buydowns count as seller concessions on VA loans?
faqItems.a: VA guidance says temporary buydowns funded by the seller or builder are considered seller concessions. That means they generally need to fit within the 4% concession limit. Because buydown rules and lender overlays can be specific, ask your lender to document how the buydown will be treated before you write the offer.

faqItems.q: 5) Are VA offers with seller credits harder for sellers to accept?
faqItems.a: Not always. A VA offer with seller credits can still be strong if the price, appraisal outlook, buyer qualification, and closing timeline make sense. Sellers should compare net proceeds and risk, not just react to the words VA loan or seller credit.

opening_question: How do VA seller credits work in Texas when you are buying near New Braunfels?
quick_answer: VA seller credits in Texas can help a New Braunfels or JBSA-area buyer reduce cash due at closing, but the key is separating normal closing cost credits from VA-defined seller concessions. The VA says it does not limit credits for a loan's closing costs, but it does limit seller concessions to no more than 4% of the home's reasonable value shown on the Notice of Value. That means the seller may be able to pay allowable closing costs separately from the 4% concession bucket, while items like the VA funding fee, debt payoff, certain prepaid costs, or temporary buydown funds need careful lender review. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does the VA 4% seller concession rule actually limit?
content_sections.p: The biggest mistake I see with VA seller credits is treating every dollar from the seller as if it belongs in one pile. That is not how the VA describes it. The VA draws a line between credits toward loan closing costs and seller concessions, and that line matters when you are trying to write a clean offer in New Braunfels, Schertz, Cibolo, or anywhere in the JBSA orbit. The lead rule is straightforward: seller concessions are capped at 4% of the home's reasonable value. The reasonable value is tied to the VA appraisal and Notice of Value, not just the number everyone negotiated on day one. If the appraisal comes in lower than expected, your lender has to re-check the concession math before closing. Normal closing cost credits are different. VA guidance says sellers or builders can offer credits to cover some or all buyer closing costs, and the VA does not put the same percentage cap on those closing cost credits. Your lender can still have overlays, the contract still has to be written correctly, and the final Closing Disclosure has to label things properly. But the VA rule itself is not a blanket 4% cap on every seller-paid dollar. For a military buyer using a VA loan, this distinction can change the whole offer strategy. A seller-paid title charge, appraisal fee, recording fee, or allowed lender fee may be handled differently from a seller paying your VA funding fee or paying off a credit balance. If you are comparing this with other financing choices, it helps to read Cody's FHA vs conventional loan Texas guide because each loan type treats seller help differently.

content_sections.h: Which seller-paid items count as concessions on a VA loan?
content_sections.p: The items that usually need the most attention are the extras beyond routine closing costs. The VA gives examples such as credits for the VA funding fee, debt payoff, or prepayment of the buyer's hazard insurance. The VA also says temporary buydowns funded by the seller or builder are considered seller concessions, so those funds need to fit inside the 4% cap unless your lender documents them another way under current VA guidance. This matters in New Braunfels because builder incentives and resale seller credits can look similar in marketing, but they do not always work the same way on a VA file. A builder may advertise money toward closing costs, rate buydowns, or upgrades. A resale seller may agree to help a PCS buyer preserve cash for the move. The contract language should say what the credit is actually for, because the lender has to decide what goes in the closing cost bucket and what goes in the concession bucket. Here is the local reality Cody would point out before you write the offer: relocating buyers often ask for the largest credit they can get, but the smarter move is usually to ask for the credit that solves the actual problem. If your cash-to-close is the issue, closing cost help may be the first priority. If your payment is the issue, a documented rate buydown may help, but you need to confirm whether it counts as a concession. If your debt-to-income ratio is tight because of a car payment or credit balance, a targeted payoff may help your qualification, but that is clearly a concession and must fit the cap. That is why I do not like vague contract language on VA credits. A line that says seller to contribute a large flat amount can create confusion once the lender, title company, and VA appraisal are all in play. A better offer separates the purpose of the seller credit, keeps a little buffer below the cap, and lets the lender confirm the structure before everyone is emotionally committed to the wrong number.

content_sections.h: How should New Braunfels VA buyers use seller credits in 2026?
content_sections.p: A good VA seller-credit plan starts before you tour homes. You want your lender to show estimated closing costs, funding fee status, likely prepaid taxes and insurance, and any payment strategy you are considering. If you are exempt from the funding fee, your credit strategy may look different than a buyer who needs to finance or negotiate that fee. If you are not exempt, the seller may be able to pay the VA funding fee, but that payment counts toward the concession bucket. In Texas, closing is normally handled through a title company, and the title company, lender, and agent all need the numbers to line up. Property taxes are also a real part of the monthly payment conversation here. New Braunfels spans Comal and Guadalupe counties, and buyer costs can shift depending on tax rates, escrow setup, HOA dues, MUD or PID assessments, insurance, and whether the home is new construction or resale. For a bigger picture on monthly payment pressure, Cody's New Braunfels property tax and payment guide is worth reviewing before you decide how much seller help to request. For a PCS buyer, the goal is usually not just getting the most concession possible. The goal is keeping the move stable. You may be trying to protect cash for temporary lodging, movers, utility deposits, child care, repairs after closing, or the gap between reporting dates and the first full local paycheck. The VA loan can be powerful because it may allow no down payment and no PMI, but no down payment does not mean no planning. The cleanest structure is usually a written side-by-side estimate. One column shows seller-paid allowable closing costs. The other shows VA-defined concessions. Then the lender confirms which items count against the 4% cap and whether the lender has any stricter overlay. That is the same kind of practical planning behind Cody's VA loan PCS checklist for Schertz and JBSA buyers, because military buyers need timing, financing, and contract terms working together.

content_sections.h: What should sellers know when a VA buyer requests credits?
content_sections.p:
A VA buyer asking for seller credits is not automatically a weak buyer. Sometimes the credit is a smart way to make the offer work while preserving the buyer's cash and keeping the sale price where both sides can live with it. The key for sellers is understanding what the credit is solving and whether the home's price, condition, days on market, and competing options support that request.

In 2026, the New Braunfels and Hill Country market is not one single negotiation environment. A well-prepared home in the right price band may have less reason to give away a large credit. A home competing against builder incentives, a home needing repairs, or a listing that has already missed the first wave of buyer attention may need a sharper concession strategy. Texas Real Estate Research Center housing data is useful here because local activity, inventory, and pricing pressure can shift by metro and county, but your exact answer still depends on the property.

For sellers, the mistake is saying no to the credit before understanding the net. A VA buyer may ask for seller-paid closing costs, a temporary buydown, or help with a funding fee. Those are not the same thing from the lender's perspective, and they are not the same thing from your net-proceeds perspective. You need to know the actual dollar impact and the likelihood that the buyer can close cleanly with that structure.

This is where a local offer review matters. I would rather help a seller compare net price, appraisal risk, repair risk, and financing terms than react to the words VA loan or seller credit. Sometimes the VA offer is not the highest gross price, but it is the better net and the smoother closing. Other times the requested credit is too aggressive for the home's position in the market. Either way, guessing is expensive.

title: Texas Buyer Agent Commission Rules in New Braunfels
excerpt: Texas buyer agent commission rules now require clearer written agreements, fee terms, and negotiation planning before New Braunfels buyers tour homes.

faqItems.q: 1) Are buyer agent commissions still negotiable in Texas?
faqItems.a: Yes. Buyer-agent compensation is negotiable, and buyers should review the amount, timing, and payment options before signing a representation agreement. The important change is that those terms need to be clearer up front instead of assumed from old market habits.

faqItems.q: 2) Can a seller still pay my buyer agent in 2026?
faqItems.a: Yes, a seller may still agree to pay buyer-agent compensation or provide concessions, but offers of compensation are no longer published through MLS compensation fields under the NAR settlement rules. Whether the seller contributes depends on the property, market conditions, offer terms, and seller instructions.

faqItems.q: 3) Do I have to sign a buyer representation agreement before seeing homes in Texas?
faqItems.a: If you want an agent to represent you, Texas buyers should expect a written agreement that explains the representation relationship and fee terms. TREC guidance says Texas law changed as of January 1, 2026 to require written agreements for buyer representation.

faqItems.q: 4) What happens if the seller will not pay the buyer-agent fee?
faqItems.a: Your options depend on your buyer agreement, loan type, and available cash. You may be able to ask for a seller concession, adjust the offer structure, bring the amount yourself, choose another property, or renegotiate within the limits of the agreement and contract.

faqItems.q: 5) How should New Braunfels buyers budget for commission changes?
faqItems.a: Build the fee conversation into your cash-to-close plan before touring. Ask your lender and agent to model multiple scenarios so you understand down payment, closing costs, seller concessions, rate strategy, and possible buyer-agent compensation before making an offer.

opening_question: What do Texas buyer agent commission rules mean for New Braunfels buyers in 2026?
quick_answer: Texas buyer agent commission rules in 2026 mean you should expect a written buyer agreement before serious home shopping, clear language about how your agent is paid, and no assumption that a seller will automatically cover your buyer-agent fee. TREC says Texas law changed as of January 1, 2026 to require written agreements for buyer representation, while NAR settlement rules removed offers of compensation from MLS fields. In New Braunfels, that makes your offer strategy, closing-cost plan, and fee negotiation more important before you fall in love with a house. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What changed about buyer agent commissions in Texas?
content_sections.p: The biggest change is not that buyer agents suddenly stopped getting paid. The real change is that the conversation moved out of the background and into the open. Buyers now need to understand the written agreement, the compensation amount, who may pay it, and what happens if the seller does not offer enough to cover it. Under the post-settlement rules, MLS systems can no longer be the place where listing brokers publish blanket offers of buyer-agent compensation. That does not mean sellers are forbidden from helping with buyer-agent compensation. It means the fee has to be discussed, negotiated, and documented through the right channels instead of treated as an invisible MLS field. Texas added another layer in 2026. TREC's guidance says changes passed by the 89th Texas Legislature require written agreements for buyer representation as of January 1. In plain English, if you're going to be represented by an agent, you should expect to sign something that spells out the relationship and the compensation terms before the work gets too deep. That is a good thing when it is explained clearly. It gives you a chance to ask, "What do I owe? When would I owe it? Can it be negotiated into the offer? What happens if the seller says no?" Those questions belong near the beginning of the process, right alongside lender approval, down payment planning, and your closing-cost estimate.

content_sections.h: Does this mean New Braunfels buyers have to pay their agent out of pocket?
content_sections.p: Sometimes yes, sometimes no. The honest answer is that it depends on the listing, the seller's strategy, your loan type, your available cash, and how the offer is written. There is no automatic rule that says the seller must pay the buyer-agent fee, and there is no automatic rule that says the buyer must bring it separately in cash at closing. In the New Braunfels and Hill Country market, this is where local strategy matters. A home sitting longer, a builder inventory property, or a listing with room for negotiation may create more opportunity to ask the seller to contribute toward buyer costs. A well-priced home in a tight pocket, or a house with multiple strong offers, may give you less room to ask for extra concessions without weakening your position. What I see buyers miss is that this is not just a commission question. It is a total cash-to-close question. If you are buying around the sub-$400K price band, the same dollar can only do one job: down payment, lender costs, title charges, rate buy-down, repairs, or buyer-agent compensation. Before we write an offer, I want that math on the table so you know what is negotiable and what is non-negotiable for your situation. This is why a buyer game plan matters before the first full weekend of showings. The right answer for a VA buyer near Schertz-Cibolo may not match the right answer for a conventional buyer comparing Gruene, Veramendi, and Solms. If financing is still part of the puzzle, Cody's New Braunfels buyer guide is a better starting point than guessing from social media posts about commissions.

content_sections.h: How should the buyer agreement shape your offer strategy?
content_sections.p: Your buyer agreement should make the fee terms clear enough that you can build them into the offer strategy. That means you need to know the compensation amount, whether it is a percentage or flat fee, what services are covered, when it is owed, and how seller-paid compensation or concessions are credited against it. For example, if your agreement says your broker is paid a certain amount and the seller offers less than that, you need to understand whether you are responsible for the difference. If the seller offers nothing, you need to know whether you will ask for a concession, adjust price, use lender credits where allowed, or choose a different property. None of that should be a surprise three days before closing. The local wrinkle in New Braunfels is that not every property type negotiates the same way. New construction can have builder incentives that look generous but come with lender, timing, or inventory tradeoffs. Resale homes may have more seller flexibility when days on market stretch, but condition and appraisal still matter. If you are comparing builder inventory with resale options, the commission conversation belongs in the same comparison as incentives, inspection leverage, rate buy-downs, and the points covered in new construction versus resale in Cibolo. The agreement also protects the conversation from vague promises. "The seller usually pays it" is not a plan. "Here is what this agreement says, here is what this listing appears to allow, here is what we will ask for, and here is your fallback if the seller counters" is a plan. That is how I want buyers approaching offers in 2026.

content_sections.h: What should buyers ask before signing a representation agreement?
content_sections.p: Start with the basic fee questions. Ask how the buyer agent is paid, whether the amount is negotiable, whether seller-paid compensation reduces what you owe, and what happens if the seller does not agree to cover it. You should also ask how long the agreement lasts, what property types or areas it covers, and how cancellation works if the fit is not right. Then connect the agreement to your real buying plan. If you are using FHA, conventional, VA, or a low-down-payment program, ask how buyer-agent compensation might affect your cash-to-close estimate. Buyers who are still comparing loan types may want to revisit FHA versus conventional loan tradeoffs in New Braunfels before deciding how aggressive they can be with concessions. You should also ask what the agent will actually do for the fee. A strong buyer agent is not just opening doors. The work includes pricing analysis, neighborhood and property-fit guidance, contract strategy, repair negotiation, lender and title coordination, deadline tracking, appraisal conversations, and keeping you from making expensive emotional decisions when the house feels right but the numbers do not. Here is the part I tell buyers directly: if someone is uncomfortable explaining their fee, their value, and your options in normal language, slow down. You do not need legal advice from an agent, and you should read any contract carefully, but you do deserve a plain-English explanation before you sign.

content_sections.h: How do commission rules affect total buying costs in New Braunfels?
content_sections.p:
They make the early budget conversation more important. Your lender approval may tell you the maximum price you can buy, but it does not always show the cleanest way to structure an offer when buyer-agent compensation, closing costs, rate strategy, and repair requests are all competing for limited dollars.

In Texas, buyers already need to plan for earnest money, option fee, inspection costs, lender charges, title-related costs, prepaid taxes and insurance, and possible HOA or POA transfer fees. If buyer-agent compensation might not be fully covered by the seller, that needs to be modeled with the rest of the cash-to-close estimate instead of treated as a last-minute line item. The same mindset applies to option money and earnest money, because those early contract dollars affect how much breathing room you have later.

The practical move is to run more than one scenario. One scenario assumes the seller pays the agreed buyer-agent compensation. One assumes the seller pays part. One assumes you bring the fee yourself or adjust the offer terms to protect cash. That does not mean every scenario is likely. It means you know the pressure points before negotiations start.

This is where I want buyers to feel calm, not cornered. The rule changes did not make buying impossible. They made vague buying more expensive. If you understand the agreement, the fee structure, the closing-cost stack, and the local negotiation environment before touring, you can make a stronger offer without walking blind into a cost surprise.

title: Seller Closing Costs Texas: New Braunfels 2026 Guide
excerpt: Seller closing costs Texas homeowners pay in 2026 usually depend on commissions, title costs, concessions, taxes, payoff timing, and strategy.

faqItems.q: 1) What are typical seller closing costs in Texas in 2026?
faqItems.a: Texas seller closing costs often run about 6% to 10% of the sale price when commissions, title costs, concessions, prorated taxes, and payoff-related items are included. The non-commission portion is usually much smaller, but it depends on the contract and property. Sellers should review a net sheet before listing, not after they accept an offer.

faqItems.q: 2) Does Texas have a real estate transfer tax?
faqItems.a: Texas does not have a state real estate transfer tax. That helps reduce one cost category compared with states that charge transfer taxes. Sellers can still have title, escrow, recording, payoff, tax-proration, commission, and negotiated concession costs.

faqItems.q: 3) Who pays for the owner's title policy in Texas?
faqItems.a: The Texas contract controls who pays for the owner's title policy. In many resale transactions the seller pays when the contract says so, but it is negotiable. Texas title insurance premiums are set by the Texas Department of Insurance, so the basic premium is not something title companies freely discount.

faqItems.q: 4) Can a Texas seller pay buyer closing costs?
faqItems.a: Yes, a Texas seller can agree to contribute toward certain buyer expenses when the contract is written that way. TREC's Paragraph 12 separates seller expenses, buyer expenses, and brokerage-fee language more clearly than many sellers realize. The amount and purpose should be reviewed carefully with your agent and title company.

faqItems.q: 5) How do I estimate my net proceeds before selling?
faqItems.a: Start with a realistic sale-price range, then subtract mortgage payoff, commissions, likely title and escrow charges, tax prorations, repairs, HOA or lien payoffs, and possible buyer concessions. The best estimate uses local comparable sales and current buyer behavior, not a single online value. A seller net sheet lets you compare price and terms before you commit.

opening_question: What seller closing costs should New Braunfels homeowners expect in Texas in 2026?
quick_answer: Seller closing costs in Texas in 2026 often land around 6% to 10% of the sale price when commissions, title charges, negotiated concessions, prorated taxes, and payoff-related items are all included. The true non-commission closing cost portion is usually much smaller, but the final number depends on your contract, payoff, repairs, survey needs, title policy, and whether you agree to help the buyer with expenses. Texas does not have a state real estate transfer tax, and Texas title insurance premiums are set by the Texas Department of Insurance, with 2026 basic rates effective March 1, 2026. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What counts as a seller closing cost in Texas?
content_sections.p: When New Braunfels sellers ask me what they'll pay at closing, the first thing I do is separate three buckets: commission, true closing costs, and negotiated credits. Most online estimates lump everything together, which is why sellers get surprised when their net sheet looks different from a quick calculator. Commission is usually the largest line item. That can include the listing broker fee the seller agreed to pay in the listing agreement, and it may also include a buyer-broker contribution if the seller agrees to one in the contract. TREC's 2025 contract changes made Paragraph 12 more specific about which expenses each party agrees to pay, so sellers should not treat buyer-side compensation or buyer credits as automatic. They are strategy decisions and contract decisions. True seller closing costs are the title, escrow, recording, release, document, tax, and payoff-related items that show up on the settlement statement. In many Texas transactions, the seller also pays for the owner's title policy when the contract says so, but that is negotiable. Texas title premiums are not random. The Texas Department of Insurance sets the basic premium rates, and the 2026 title rate chart applies to closings after March 1, 2026. The third bucket is negotiated help for the buyer. That might mean a contribution toward buyer expenses, repair credits, rate buydown help, or a specific amount toward buyer-broker compensation if properly written in the contract. If you're already comparing price reductions, repair requests, and buyer credits, it helps to review New Braunfels seller concessions before you decide what to offer.

content_sections.h: How much should a seller budget on a New Braunfels sale?
content_sections.p: A practical planning range for seller closing costs in Texas is 6% to 10% of the sales price when commissions are included. On a $400,000 sale, that broad range would be $24,000 to $40,000. That does not mean every seller pays the high end. It means your net proceeds plan should account for the full stack before you commit to a list price or accept an offer. Here is the part sellers often miss: the offer with the highest price is not always the offer with the best net. A buyer asking for a large seller credit, a survey amendment, a home warranty, repairs, and a later closing date can quietly eat into proceeds. A slightly lower offer with cleaner terms may leave you with more certainty and a better bottom line. In New Braunfels, this matters even more because buyer expectations can change by price band and property type. A clean resale near IH-35 may compete differently than a Hill Country home on acreage, a newer home near builder inventory, or a property with septic, well, floodplain, or HOA documentation questions. I see sellers focus on the headline price first, but the contract terms are where the real net number is built. If you're starting with an online value estimate, use it as a rough signal, not a net proceeds plan. A better next step is pairing value range with seller-cost math through a local pricing review. Cody's custom home value strategy is built for that, and this related guide on New Braunfels home pricing strategy explains why the first price has to match the negotiation plan.

content_sections.h: Which closing costs are easiest to underestimate?
content_sections.p: Title policy and escrow charges. If the contract says the seller pays for the owner's title policy, that line can be meaningful, especially as the sale price rises. Because Texas regulates title insurance pricing, the rate is not a shopping contest between title companies, although other settlement fees and service details can still vary. Property tax prorations. Texas property taxes are usually prorated between buyer and seller based on the closing date. If you close before the tax bill is final, the title company uses the best available figures and the contract governs how those prorations are handled. In Comal and Guadalupe counties, sellers should pay close attention to exemptions, current-year values, and whether the home is in the city, an ETJ, a MUD, a PID, or another taxing setup. Payoff and lien release items. Your mortgage payoff is not just the visible principal balance from an app. It can include interest through the payoff date, escrow adjustments, recording fees, and release-related charges. If there is a HELOC, solar lien, judgment, tax lien, or old unreleased lien, those issues can slow closing or change the net sheet. Repairs and concessions. This is where sellers can lose control if they wait until after inspection to think strategically. Some repairs make sense before listing. Some are better handled through price or credits. Some should be rejected or reframed depending on the buyer's loan, the property's condition, and the competitive set. If you're deciding whether to fix items before listing, the as-is versus fix-it decision is usually tied directly to your closing-cost and negotiation plan.

content_sections.h: How should closing costs shape your pricing and negotiation plan?
content_sections.p:
Seller closing costs should not be treated as an afterthought. They should shape the listing price, the concession strategy, the inspection response, and the offer review process from the beginning. If you price the home as if every dollar of list price will become proceeds, you're setting yourself up for frustration.

The New Braunfels mistake I see most often is a seller saying, "I'll just leave room to negotiate," without knowing what that room is supposed to cover. Is it buyer closing costs? A rate buydown? An appraisal gap concern? Builder incentives down the road? A roof issue? A property-tax objection? Those are different problems, and they require different pricing moves.

A strong seller strategy starts with a projected net sheet at multiple price points. One scenario should show a clean offer. One should show a concession-heavy offer. One should show a lower price with stronger terms. That lets you compare real outcomes instead of reacting emotionally when an offer comes in below list or asks for help.

This is exactly the kind of question I walk my clients through before we list. We look at comparable sales, current competition, likely buyer objections, and the cost of each negotiation path. If the numbers show that a pre-listing repair protects more equity than a later credit, we plan for that. If the numbers show that a seller credit could attract more qualified buyers without damaging the net, we price around it.

title: Texas Inspection Requests: New Braunfels 2026 Guide
excerpt: Texas inspection requests should focus on defects, safety, and cost exposure, not cosmetic wish lists. Here is how New Braunfels buyers should negotiate.

faqItems.q: 1) What repairs should I ask for after a Texas home inspection?
faqItems.a: Ask for repairs tied to safety, function, financing, insurance, or major cost exposure. Common examples include roof damage, HVAC defects, active leaks, unsafe electrical conditions, plumbing problems, foundation concerns, drainage issues, septic issues, or lender-required repairs. Cosmetic items usually weaken the request unless they point to a larger defect.

faqItems.q: 2) Can a Texas buyer ask for seller credits instead of repairs?
faqItems.a: Yes, buyers can negotiate seller credits when the contract, lender, and closing structure allow it. Credits may help with allowed closing costs, but lender limits and loan-program rules matter. Always confirm the amount and wording with your lender before sending an amendment.

faqItems.q: 3) Do sellers have to make repairs after a Texas inspection?
faqItems.a: No, sellers generally do not have to agree to buyer-requested repairs unless the contract requires a specific item or the parties agree in writing. The buyer can ask, the seller can agree, counter, or refuse, and the buyer must decide based on the contract deadlines. During the option period, the buyer may have termination rights if the option fee was properly paid and notice is given on time.

faqItems.q: 4) How long do I have to negotiate inspection repairs in Texas?
faqItems.a: Your timing depends on the option period and the deadlines in your contract. TREC explains that the option period can be used to inspect the property and negotiate an amendment for necessary repairs. Because the right to terminate is deadline-sensitive, buyers should schedule inspections immediately and negotiate before the option period expires.

faqItems.q: 5) What inspection issues are common around New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: New Braunfels buyers should watch roof condition, HVAC age, drainage, foundation movement signs, plumbing, electrical, septic, well systems, floodplain questions, and prior renovation quality. The exact concerns depend on the property type, age, location, and whether the home is inside city services or on a more rural setup. A local review helps separate normal maintenance from real negotiation issues.

opening_question: What should you ask the seller for after a Texas home inspection in New Braunfels?
quick_answer: After a Texas home inspection, ask the seller for repairs, seller credits, or a price adjustment tied to real defects, safety concerns, lender-required items, or expensive systems. In 2026, TREC lists Amendment to Contract Form 39-10 as effective January 3, 2025, with Form 39-11 effective July 1, 2026, so your agent needs to use the current form for the timing of your contract. In New Braunfels, the strongest requests usually involve roof condition, HVAC age, foundation signs, drainage, electrical, plumbing, septic, well, or flood-related concerns, not paint colors or loose cabinet pulls. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What kinds of inspection requests are reasonable in Texas?
content_sections.p: Reasonable inspection requests usually connect to habitability, safety, insurability, financing, or a meaningful cost the buyer did not know about when the offer was written. That means roof damage, active plumbing leaks, unsafe electrical conditions, HVAC problems, wood-destroying insect concerns, foundation movement signs, missing permits, drainage issues, septic concerns, or lender-required repairs usually belong in the conversation. Cosmetic issues usually don't, unless they reveal a larger defect or were misrepresented before the offer. Texas buyers also need to keep the contract structure in mind. TREC explains that contract forms are public records, but they are intended primarily for trained license holders, and mistakes in their use can create financial loss or an unenforceable contract. That matters after inspection because the words in the amendment matter just as much as the inspection report. A vague request like "seller to fix roof" can create confusion. A cleaner request identifies the issue, the expected standard, the deadline, who performs the work, and what documentation transfers before closing. In New Braunfels, I coach buyers to separate the report into three buckets: items that affect the deal, items to watch after closing, and items you accept as normal wear. The part relocating buyers from Austin or out of state sometimes miss is that a Hill Country inspection can look scarier than a suburban inspection because of drainage, limestone, pier-and-beam additions, older downtown homes, septic, or well systems. Not every note is a crisis. The job is to decide what changes your risk, your cost, or your willingness to move forward. This is where a buyer game plan matters. If you're still early in the process, my Texas option period guide for New Braunfels buyers explains why inspection timing and termination rights need to be lined up before you start negotiating. Inspection requests are strongest when they come from a clear strategy, not a reaction to a long report.

content_sections.h: Should you ask for repairs, seller credits, or a price reduction?
content_sections.p: The right ask depends on the problem, the seller's situation, your loan type, and how close you are to closing. Repairs can make sense when the defect is specific, the work is easy to verify, and the seller can complete it before closing. A seller credit can make more sense when you want control over the contractor or when the fix may uncover more work. A price reduction helps your long-term equity position, but it does not always solve a cash problem at closing. For buyers watching monthly payment, the difference matters. A $5,000 price reduction usually does not feel like $5,000 in your pocket on closing day. A properly structured seller credit may help with closing costs or allowed loan costs, but lender limits apply and credits have to be written correctly. This is why I do not want buyers guessing after the inspection. You should run the numbers with your lender before you decide whether to ask for repairs, credits, or price. There are also practical seller-side realities. Some sellers will agree to a clean credit faster than managing contractors while packing. Others prefer repairs because they don't want the price changed. Some will say no if the request reads like a remodel list. The better your request is tied to the inspection findings and the real cost of ownership, the more serious it feels across the table. If closing costs are part of the negotiation, review the numbers before you send the amendment. My plain-English closing cost breakdown is a helpful starting point, and this recent guide to Texas buyer agent commission rules in New Braunfels shows why buyers need to understand all cash-to-close pieces before they negotiate credits.

content_sections.h: How does the Texas option period affect inspection negotiations?
content_sections.p:
The option period is the pressure point. TREC says a buyer who pays the agreed option fee has the unrestricted right to terminate for any reason by giving written notice during the option period. TREC also notes that buyers can use that time to inspect the property and negotiate an amendment for necessary repairs. Once that clock is running, you do not have unlimited time to think, price, negotiate, and re-negotiate.

That is why I want the inspection scheduled immediately after the effective date, especially in New Braunfels and nearby Hill Country areas where specialty follow-ups can take time. If the general inspector flags possible roof damage, HVAC failure, drainage concerns, septic issues, or foundation movement, you may need a specialist opinion before you know what to ask for. Waiting until day five of a short option period can leave you negotiating with incomplete information.

The amendment should also match the current form and contract timing. TREC's contracts page lists Amendment to Contract Form 39-10 with an effective date of January 3, 2025, and Form 39-11 with an effective date of July 1, 2026. For a June 2026 contract, the date matters because forms update. The safest path is to work with an agent who checks the current TREC form and coordinates with the lender, title company, and inspector before the deadline.

One local mistake I see is buyers treating the inspection as a second round of price shopping instead of a due-diligence checkpoint. If the house was already priced for condition, a long repair list may not move the seller. If the report reveals a major hidden cost, the conversation changes. That distinction is exactly what I walk buyers through before they decide whether to ask, accept, renegotiate, or terminate.

content_sections.h: What New Braunfels inspection issues deserve extra attention?
content_sections.p: New Braunfels buyers should pay close attention to the systems that create the biggest ownership surprises. Roof condition matters because hail, age, insurance underwriting, and lender concerns can collide quickly. HVAC matters because Texas heat turns a weak system into a real comfort and cost issue. Drainage matters because Hill Country lots can move water fast, and water moving toward the foundation is not something to ignore. Older homes near downtown, properties near the rivers, acreage outside city services, and newer subdivisions can all create different inspection questions. An older home may raise electrical, plumbing, foundation, or prior-renovation questions. A rural or semi-rural property may require extra attention to septic, well, water pressure, access, fencing, and drainage. A newer build or resale in a fast-growing corridor may still need close review of grading, attic ventilation, workmanship, and warranty transfer. Floodplain and water-adjacent questions deserve careful treatment. A property does not have to be waterfront for drainage or flood insurance questions to matter, and a buyer should verify flood zone information through proper sources rather than relying on listing remarks. This is not about scaring anyone away from a house. It is about knowing which risks are normal, which are negotiable, and which could change your budget after closing. The best request is specific and defensible. Instead of asking for every minor item, prioritize what affects value, safety, insurance, financing, or cash flow. If your budget is already tight, use the mortgage calculator to pressure-test the payment, then compare the inspection findings against your cash reserve. A strong offer strategy gets you under contract, but a strong inspection strategy helps you decide whether the contract still makes sense.

title: Bridge Loan Texas: New Braunfels Move Plan 2026
excerpt: Bridge loan Texas options can help New Braunfels homeowners buy before selling, but the right plan depends on equity, timing, risk, and payment comfort.

faqItems.q: 1) What is a bridge loan in Texas real estate?
faqItems.a: A bridge loan is short-term financing that can help a homeowner buy a new property before the current home sells. In a Texas move, it is often used to access equity or cover the down payment gap while waiting for the sale proceeds. Terms vary by lender, so buyers should compare fees, loan-to-value limits, repayment deadlines, and qualification rules before relying on one.

faqItems.q: 2) Is a bridge loan better than a home-sale contingency?
faqItems.a: A bridge loan and a home-sale contingency solve different problems. A bridge loan may make your purchase offer cleaner because it can reduce dependence on selling your current home first. A home-sale contingency can protect you financially, but it may be less attractive to a seller because another transaction has to close before your purchase can finish.

faqItems.q: 3) Can I sell and buy on the same day in Texas?
faqItems.a: Yes, selling and buying on the same day can happen in Texas, but it requires careful coordination between both contracts, lenders, agents, and title companies. The risk is that a delay on the sale side can affect the purchase side. A same-day closing plan should include backup options such as leaseback terms, temporary housing, or extra time between closings.

faqItems.q: 4) What should New Braunfels sellers check before using a bridge loan?
faqItems.a: New Braunfels sellers should check current home value, likely net proceeds, mortgage payoff, market competition, repair needs, and how quickly similar homes are moving. They should also ask the lender whether they can qualify while carrying both homes. The bridge loan is only one part of the plan. The current home's pricing and preparation still decide how much timing risk you are taking.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the safest way to buy before selling?
faqItems.a: The safest path depends on your equity, cash reserves, lender approval, replacement-home urgency, and comfort with double payments. For some homeowners, selling first with a leaseback is safer than buying first. For others, a bridge loan or HELOC can make sense if the current home is market-ready and the next home is hard to replace.

opening_question: Should you use a bridge loan in Texas to sell and buy at the same time in New Braunfels?
quick_answer: A bridge loan in Texas can help you buy your next home before your current one sells, but it is not the only way to solve the timing problem. Some lenders cap bridge financing around 75% of the current home's market value, and many buyers compare that against a sale-first plan, HELOC, leaseback, or home-sale contingency. In New Braunfels, the best answer depends on how quickly your current home is likely to sell, how much equity you have, and whether the next purchase needs to compete without a sale contingency. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What problem does a bridge loan actually solve in a New Braunfels move?
content_sections.p:
A bridge loan solves a timing problem, not a budgeting problem. It gives you temporary access to equity or short-term funds so you can purchase the next home before the current home closes. That can matter when the right house appears in Veramendi, Mission Hills Ranch, Gruene, Garden Ridge, or Canyon Lake before your current listing has a buyer.

The core issue is simple: most people need the equity from the sale to buy the next home. Without a plan, you either sell first and risk needing temporary housing, or you write an offer that depends on your current home selling. A bridge loan may let you move first, then sell, which can make your purchase offer cleaner because it may remove the sale contingency.

That does not mean it is automatically the best move. You still have to qualify with a lender, understand the short repayment window, and be comfortable with the possibility of carrying two housing costs for a period of time. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau tells buyers to compare official loan offers and understand their mortgage choices before committing, and that advice matters even more when you are stacking short-term financing on top of a move.

This is where I see New Braunfels homeowners get caught off guard. They focus on whether they can buy the next house, but the better question is whether the current house is priced and prepared well enough to sell on schedule. If your existing home needs work, sits near a builder-heavy price band, or competes with new construction incentives, the bridge loan does not fix that. It just gives the sell side a deadline.

content_sections.h: How do the three main sell-and-buy playbooks compare in Texas?
content_sections.p: The first playbook is sell first, then buy. This is usually the cleanest financially because you know your net proceeds, you remove uncertainty from your next budget, and your lender can underwrite the next purchase with clearer numbers. The tradeoff is housing logistics. You may need a leaseback, temporary rental, family stay, or a short move into storage if the right home is not ready when your sale closes. The second playbook is buy first, then sell. This is where bridge loans, HELOCs, cash reserves, and other short-term tools enter the conversation. It can be powerful when you have enough equity, strong income, and a specific home you do not want to miss. It can also create pressure if the current home takes longer than expected to sell, especially in a market where resale homes are competing against builder concessions. The third playbook is a same-day or closely coordinated closing. You sell your current home in the morning, use the proceeds, and close on the next home later that day or soon after. This can work, but it depends on both contracts, both lenders, the title company, appraisal timing, repairs, funding, and buyer performance. One delay can push the entire chain. Texas also has contract tools that matter here. A home-sale contingency can protect the buyer, but it may weaken the offer because the seller is depending on another transaction closing first. If you want a deeper explanation of that exact issue, Cody's guide to home-sale contingency offers in Texas is a smart companion to this move-planning decision. For sellers, the related question is your real net number. If the plan depends on proceeds from the current home, do not guess from a Zestimate or the neighbor's sales price. Start with likely sale price, payoff, taxes, title fees, commissions, concessions, moving costs, and payoff timing. Cody's Texas seller closing costs guide can help you understand the pieces that reduce gross price into usable equity.

content_sections.h: When does a bridge loan make sense, and when should you slow down?
content_sections.p: It can make sense when the next home is unusually hard to replace. If you are downsizing into a specific one-story layout, moving closer to family, trying to stay near a commute route, or relocating around a PCS timeline, losing the right property may cost more than the financing cost. A bridge loan can help you act when the replacement home is the real constraint. It can make sense when your current home is truly market-ready. I do not mean you have a few phone photos and a hopeful price. I mean repairs are handled, prep is done, pricing is backed by current comps, and the likely buyer objections have already been addressed. In New Braunfels, this matters because buyers compare across resale, new construction, Comal County, Guadalupe County, and sometimes Schertz or Cibolo in the same weekend. You should slow down if the bridge loan is being used to avoid a pricing conversation. This is the part I walk clients through before they make a big move. If your current home is overpriced by even a small amount in a price band with active builder incentives, you may not feel the mistake on day one. You feel it three weeks later when you are making payments, showing traffic is soft, and the next home clock is already running. You should also slow down if the payment stack is uncomfortable. Bridge financing is temporary, but temporary can still be stressful. You need to understand the bridge payment, the new mortgage payment, the old mortgage payment, insurance, taxes, HOA dues, and any payoff deadline. The National Association of Realtors has noted that bridge loans can help buyers avoid a sale contingency, but the benefit is only useful if the financing risk is manageable for your household. A good move plan compares the financing options side by side: bridge loan, HELOC, cash reserves, sale-first leaseback, home-sale contingency, and same-day closing. Then it ties that plan to the sell-side strategy. If you need a starting point for the purchase side, Cody's New Braunfels buyer guide can help frame the payment conversation before you talk with a lender.

content_sections.h: What should New Braunfels homeowners do before choosing the timing strategy?
content_sections.p: Start with a realistic value range on the home you already own. The Texas Real Estate Research Center is a useful source for broad market context, but your decision should be made at the neighborhood and price-band level. A home in a builder-heavy pocket near the IH-35 corridor may need a different strategy than a well-prepared home in Gruene, an acreage property outside city limits, or a Canyon Lake-area home with water-level questions in the buyer's mind. Next, ask your lender for the real financing menu. Do not assume every lender offers bridge loans, and do not assume the terms will match an online article. Ask about maximum loan-to-value, repayment timeline, interest-only periods, fees, required reserves, whether you must qualify with both payments, and whether your current home must be listed or under contract. Then build the transaction calendar backward. In Texas, the title company coordinates closing, earnest money is held by the title company, and option periods give buyers a defined window to inspect and terminate. If your sale and purchase overlap, inspection negotiations, appraisal timing, title funding, repairs, and lender conditions all matter. Cody's guide to Texas earnest money rules explains one piece of that contract timeline. Finally, choose the strategy that protects your real goal. If your goal is certainty, sell-first may beat buy-first. If your goal is not missing a rare replacement home, buy-first may be worth exploring. If your goal is minimizing temporary housing, a coordinated closing or leaseback may be the cleanest path. The right answer is not the same for a PCS move, a divorce transition, a retirement downsize, or a move-up purchase with kids, pets, storage, and work schedules in the mix. My practical advice: do not start with the bridge loan. Start with the move plan. Price the current home, estimate net proceeds, get lender options, identify the replacement-home constraints, and decide how much timing risk you are willing to carry. That is how you turn a stressful two-transaction problem into a sequence you can actually manage.

faqItems.q: 1) Is Indian Springs in Bulverde or San Antonio?

faqItems.q: 2) Are there still new homes for sale in Indian Springs in 2026?

content_sections.h: What does Indian Springs Bulverde mean for buyers in 2026?
content_sections.p: Indian Springs is one of those local search terms that can confuse buyers before they ever tour a house. Online portals often group it with San Antonio 78261, Bulverde Road, Bulverde Village, and the north Bexar County edge near the Comal County line. Some buyers say "Bulverde" because the road, commute pattern, and Hill Country feel point that direction, even when the mailing address may still say San Antonio. For a 2026 buyer, that distinction matters because your search results may mix true Indian Springs resale homes, nearby 78261 subdivisions, and new-home communities that are close by but not actually inside the original Indian Springs sections. That can make the inventory look broader than it is. It also changes how you compare HOA rules, tax estimates, commute patterns, and builder incentives. The current takeaway is simple: treat Indian Springs as a specific neighborhood search, then treat Bulverde Road and Highway 281 as the broader comparison zone. If you want a wider Hill Country shortlist, use Cody's Hill Country area guide to compare the nearby pockets instead of relying on one portal label. That gives you a cleaner way to decide whether Indian Springs, Kinder Ranch, Johnson Ranch, Bulverde, Garden Ridge, or Cibolo better matches your budget and timeline. This is also where I see relocating buyers get tripped up. They think "Indian Springs Bulverde" means one big active new-construction master plan. In reality, the name often points to a built-out neighborhood with resale options, plus surrounding corridors where new inventory may still exist.

content_sections.h: How much new construction is actually left in Indian Springs?
content_sections.p: The original Indian Springs new-construction story is mostly a past-tense story in 2026. Livabl lists Preserve at Indian Springs by Meritage Homes as sold out and complete, with home sizes shown from 2,885 to 3,468 square feet. Livabl also lists The Colony at Indian Springs by Highland Homes as sold out and complete. That doesn't mean there are no homes to buy in the area. It means the active new-build pipeline inside those named Indian Springs communities is not the same as a brand-new subdivision with rows of available lots. That matters because resale homes and builder homes behave differently in negotiations. A resale seller may be protecting equity, responding to inspection requests, and comparing your offer to recent neighborhood comps. A builder may be focused on closing out a phase, moving spec inventory, protecting headline pricing, or offering rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. Those are different conversations. Zillow's Indian Springs 78261 page showed 21 results at the time of research, with examples ranging from the low $400Ks to the upper $700Ks and higher. Those numbers are a snapshot, not a promise of what will be available when you shop. They do show the practical point: Indian Springs still has choices, but a buyer expecting a deep menu of fresh builder inventory inside the original community may be disappointed. If your real goal is a newer home, you should compare Indian Springs resale against nearby new-home options before you narrow too fast. Cody's recent guide to new construction vs resale in Cibolo explains the same tradeoff in another fast-growing corridor: new homes can bring warranties and incentives, while resale homes may offer established locations, completed landscaping, and a clearer read on neighborhood value.

content_sections.h: What should buyers compare before choosing Indian Springs?
content_sections.p: First, compare location reality, not just the subdivision name. Indian Springs sits in the 78261 search area near Bulverde Road, with access patterns that may involve Highway 281, TPC Parkway, Evans Road, or Stone Oak depending on your destination. A home can look close on a map and still feel different during school-hour, work-hour, or weekend traffic. If you are moving from New Braunfels, Schertz, Cibolo, or out of state, test the drive at the time you would actually make it. Second, compare total monthly cost. Newer corridors can carry HOA dues, special district costs, higher tax assessments after improvements, or builder price adjustments that change the payment more than the list price suggests. The right number is not just the advertised price. It's principal and interest, taxes, insurance, HOA, and any community-specific costs. Buyers should pressure-test the full payment before touring aggressively. Third, compare property condition and timing. A resale home in Indian Springs may have mature landscaping, finished window coverings, completed patios, and a known block-by-block feel. A nearby new build may offer fresh systems, builder warranties, and financing incentives, but you still need to inspect workmanship, lot slope, drainage, orientation, and upgrade pricing. I walk buyers through this before they fall in love with a model home because model-home emotion can hide real monthly-cost math. Fourth, compare the school district as a factual property feature only. Indian Springs Elementary lists its campus at 25751 Wilderness Oak, San Antonio, TX 78261, and buyers should verify attendance boundaries directly with the applicable district before making a decision. Boundaries can matter for logistics, but Fair Housing rules are clear: you should not choose a home based on subjective school rankings or coded neighborhood claims. Focus on the property facts you can verify. The practical move is to build a side-by-side shortlist: Indian Springs resale homes, nearby 78261 resale homes, and nearby active builder communities. If you are still deciding whether the Hill Country side, Schertz-Cibolo side, or New Braunfels side is a better fit, Cody's moving to Texas Hill Country from Austin guide is a helpful comparison for buyers who are weighing lifestyle, commute, and price tradeoffs.

content_sections.h: When does Indian Springs make sense over nearby new-home communities?
content_sections.p: Indian Springs can make sense when you want a newer-feeling resale neighborhood, a north-side San Antonio address, and access to the Bulverde Road and Highway 281 corridor without waiting on a builder timeline. It may also make sense if you find a resale home where the seller has already absorbed the cost of fencing, blinds, landscaping, appliances, and post-closing improvements that a new build may leave to you. Nearby new-home communities can make more sense when you want builder financing options, a fresh warranty package, a specific floor plan, or the ability to choose from remaining lots. But those benefits need to be measured against location, taxes, commute, lot size, and the real cost of upgrades. A builder incentive is not automatically a better deal if the base price, tax load, or commute tradeoff cancels it out. This is where local context helps. I don't want buyers chasing the newest house just because the online photos look clean. I want them comparing the home they will actually live in: the drive, the payment, the lot, the maintenance, the resale position, and the concessions they can negotiate. Sometimes Indian Springs resale wins that comparison. Sometimes a nearby builder does. The answer depends on the house, the numbers, and your timing. If you are within 30 to 180 days of buying, the best next step is not to ask whether Indian Springs is "good" or "bad." The better question is whether the specific homes available right now beat the nearby alternatives for your budget. Cody's builder incentives guide can help you understand how to compare headline incentives with the full offer package.

title: New Construction vs Resale Prices in New Braunfels
excerpt: New construction vs resale prices in New Braunfels shows a real 2026 tradeoff: resale often wins on sticker price, while builders compete on payment.

faqItems.q: 1) Are new construction homes cheaper than resale homes in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Usually, no. In 2026 snapshots, resale pricing in New Braunfels often shows a lower median sale price than new construction listing prices. However, a builder incentive, rate buydown, or closing-cost credit can make the monthly payment closer than the sticker price suggests.

faqItems.q: 2) Is resale a better value than new construction in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Resale can be a better value when the home has a stronger location, mature lot, useful upgrades, and limited near-term repair risk. It can be less attractive if inspection issues, older systems, or unrealistic pricing erase the savings. The right answer depends on the specific home and the buyer's payment target.

faqItems.q: 3) Why do builders offer incentives instead of lowering prices?
faqItems.a: Builders often use incentives because they can help buyers with payment or cash to close while protecting published prices in the community. A price cut can affect future appraisals and nearby inventory, while a closing credit or rate buydown may solve the buyer's immediate affordability problem. Buyers should still read the terms carefully.

faqItems.q: 4) Should sellers worry about builder competition in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Yes, especially if the resale is near active new-home communities or priced in the same range as builder inventory. Sellers need to show why their home is the better choice through price, condition, location, lot features, or total monthly cost. Ignoring builder incentives can make a resale sit longer than expected.

faqItems.q: 5) What is the best way to compare a new build and a resale?
faqItems.a: Compare total ownership cost, not just price. Include loan terms, property taxes, HOA or MUD dues, insurance, repair costs, builder credits, inspection findings, and commute patterns. A local market read can help you compare the homes the way a serious buyer or seller would see them.

opening_question: Are new construction homes more expensive than resale homes in New Braunfels in 2026?
quick_answer: Yes, in most side-by-side comparisons, new construction in New Braunfels is priced above resale, but the better deal depends on payment, concessions, taxes, condition, and timing. Redfin reported a New Braunfels median sale price near $340K for the three months ending May 2026, while Realtor.com showed new construction listing around $368,995. That spread is meaningful, but builder rate buydowns and closing-cost help can narrow the monthly payment gap. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What does the 2026 price gap really show?
content_sections.p: The simple answer is that resale usually looks cheaper first, and new construction usually asks you to look deeper. As of the latest available 2026 market snapshots, Redfin showed New Braunfels home prices near a $340K median sale price over the three months ending May 2026. Realtor.com showed new construction homes in New Braunfels with a median listing price of about $368,995. Zillow's New Braunfels market page showed a broader median list price above $413K at the end of May 2026, which reinforces the same point: list price and sale price are not the same conversation. That difference matters because buyers do not shop only in averages. A buyer under $400K may compare a resale in an established part of 78130 with a builder inventory home east of I-35, along FM 1101, or in a newer master-planned pocket. On paper, the resale may come in lower. In practice, the new home may include a rate buydown, closing-cost credit, appliance package, or builder warranty that changes the first two years of ownership. This is where I see people make the wrong comparison. They compare the resale list price against the new-build list price, then stop. In New Braunfels, that misses the real math. You have to compare monthly payment, tax estimate, insurance, HOA or MUD cost, likely repairs, commute pattern, and how long you plan to keep the home. If you're still early in the decision, start with the New Braunfels mortgage calculator so the payment side is not just a guess. For sellers, the same gap can either help you or hurt you. If your resale is priced like a brand-new home but has older flooring, a tired roof, or no meaningful updates, the buyer will use nearby builder inventory against you. If your home is priced with condition in mind, the resale advantage can be real because buyers still value mature trees, larger lots, established streets, and finished outdoor space.

content_sections.h: Why can new homes cost more and still compete?
content_sections.p: New construction competes differently than resale. Builders can protect headline price while moving buyers through incentives. That can mean money toward closing costs, interest-rate buydowns, design-center credits, or inventory-home discounts that do not always show up cleanly in public price data. The buyer sees a higher list price, but the lender worksheet may tell a more useful story. That does not make every new build a better deal. It means the comparison needs to be payment-based. A $385K new home with a strong builder incentive might compete against a $350K resale if the monthly payment lands close and the buyer wants lower near-term maintenance. But a resale can still win if it has better location, lower tax burden, a more flexible seller, or upgrades the buyer would otherwise have to pay for after closing. The local dashboard tells the same cautionary story from a countywide angle. The April 2026 Comal County single-family dashboard from Texas REALTORS Data Relevance Project showed a median price of $429,990, 4.0 months of inventory, and a median price per square foot of $206.98. The time-and-value view also showed 106 days on market and 139 total days from listing to close. Those numbers are not a guarantee for any one home, but they show buyers have more time to compare options than they did during the fastest pandemic-era market. I would not tell a buyer to chase a builder incentive without checking the fine print. Sometimes the rate buydown requires the builder's preferred lender. Sometimes the advertised payment assumes a specific loan structure, credit profile, or down payment. Sometimes the lot premium, MUD taxes, HOA dues, or appliance upgrades erase part of the savings. That is why a clean comparison should include lender numbers, not just a model-home sign.

content_sections.h: Where do resale homes still have the advantage?
content_sections.p: Resale homes can still be the better value when the buyer cares about location, lot character, mature landscaping, or a street that already feels settled. In New Braunfels, older resale pockets may put you closer to downtown, Gruene, Landa Park, the Comal River, or established daily routines. Newer construction can offer efficiency and fresh systems, but it may place you farther from the exact lifestyle pattern you thought you were buying. The part buyers relocating from Austin or California often miss is that New Braunfels is not one market. I-35 access, FM 306 traffic, the west side toward 78132, the east side toward Seguin, and the Comal versus Guadalupe County line can change the monthly cost and daily experience. Two homes with the same price can feel completely different once you add commute, tax rate, HOA structure, floodplain questions, and where the home sits in relation to grocery runs and weekend traffic. Condition is the big resale variable. A resale with a recent roof, updated HVAC, clean inspection profile, and realistic price can beat a new build for a practical buyer. A resale with deferred maintenance needs a bigger value gap. That is why the Texas option period matters so much in this market. If you want a deeper look at the due-diligence piece, Cody's guide to Texas inspection requests in New Braunfels explains how buyers can use inspection findings without turning the negotiation into a fight. Sellers should pay attention here. If your resale is in a location buyers already want and the home shows well, you do not have to apologize for not being new. But you do have to price against today's alternatives, not last year's memory. Builder inventory is part of your competition, especially when buyers can tour a fresh home, get a lender credit, and avoid a repair list.

content_sections.h: How should buyers and sellers use this market data?
content_sections.p: Buyers should treat the new construction vs resale decision as a total-cost comparison. Start with price, then add taxes, insurance, HOA or MUD costs, lender terms, closing-cost credits, inspection risk, warranty coverage, commute, and the cost of making the home fit your life. The lower sticker price is not always the lower cost, and the newer home is not automatically the smarter purchase. Sellers should use the same data from the other side of the table. If you are listing a resale near active builder communities, your pricing strategy needs to answer the buyer's next question before they ask it: why this house instead of the new one down the road? The answer may be lot size, location, mature outdoor space, upgrades, no waiting period, lower tax profile, or a cleaner total monthly cost. If you cannot name the advantage, the price has to do more work. This is also why automated value estimates can miss the decision point. They may catch broad price movement, but they do not always account for a builder's temporary incentive, a resale's inspection risk, or a neighborhood-level buyer objection. If you're preparing to list, use a local pricing conversation alongside the New Braunfels home value tool so the number is tied to what buyers are actually comparing this month. For buyers who want a structured path, the right move is to narrow the search by payment first, then compare two or three realistic homes across both categories.
