title: Interest Rate Impact on Seguin Home Buyers in 2026
excerpt: Interest rate impact in Seguin is changing what buyers can afford, but 2026 inventory and negotiation room may help offset higher payments.

faqItems.q: 1) Are interest rates making Seguin homes unaffordable in 2026?
faqItems.a: Interest rates are making Seguin homes more payment-sensitive, but not automatically unaffordable for every buyer. The key is to compare total monthly cost, not just the list price. A lower-priced home can still carry a higher-than-expected payment once taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and loan terms are included.

faqItems.q: 2) Should I wait for mortgage rates to drop before buying in Seguin?
faqItems.a: Waiting can make sense if your timeline and finances are flexible, but it is not risk-free. If rates drop and more buyers re-enter the market, competition could rise and seller concessions could shrink. The better question is whether today's payment and negotiation room create a plan that works for your budget.

faqItems.q: 3) Can seller concessions help offset higher interest rates?
faqItems.a: Yes, seller concessions can help with closing costs, temporary rate buydowns, or other buyer expenses when the contract and loan program allow it. They do not make every home affordable, but they can reduce cash pressure or improve the short-term payment. The right concession strategy depends on the property, seller motivation, and lender rules.

faqItems.q: 4) Is Seguin cheaper than New Braunfels for home buyers?
faqItems.a: Seguin can offer different price points than parts of New Braunfels, but cheaper is not the whole story. Buyers should compare commute, property taxes, insurance, home condition, subdivision costs, and long-term fit. A good Seguin purchase is one where the total cost and lifestyle plan both make sense.

faqItems.q: 5) How do higher rates affect Seguin home sellers?
faqItems.a: Higher rates can make buyers more selective because each price increase affects monthly payment. Sellers may need sharper pricing, stronger presentation, cleaner inspection preparation, or a concession plan. The goal is to reduce buyer friction before the listing sits and loses momentum.

opening_question: How are interest rates impacting Seguin home buyers in 2026?
quick_answer: Interest rates are keeping Seguin buyers payment-sensitive in 2026, with Freddie Mac reporting the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49% on June 25, 2026. That rate level makes monthly payment planning more important than list price alone, especially for buyers comparing Seguin, New Braunfels, Cibolo, and Schertz. The upside is that more inventory and slower buyer urgency can create room to negotiate price, repairs, rate buydowns, or closing-cost help when the house has been sitting. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why do 2026 interest rates change the Seguin buying decision?
content_sections.p: For Seguin buyers, the biggest 2026 change is not that homes suddenly became impossible to buy. It's that the same home price now has to be tested against a tighter monthly payment. A buyer who felt comfortable at one payment level during a lower-rate window may need to adjust price, down payment, loan type, seller concessions, or timing now that rates are sitting in the mid-6% range. Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey showed the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.49% as of June 25, 2026, compared with 6.77% a year earlier. That is better than the late-2023 peak environment, but it is still much higher than the 3% and 4% memories many buyers keep in their heads. That gap matters because buyers do not live inside a purchase price. They live inside the monthly payment after principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any HOA or special district cost. This is why I would not tell a Seguin buyer to shop by price range alone. I would rather start with payment range, cash-to-close, commute pattern, and the kind of home they actually need. Then we can compare Seguin against nearby options without pretending a $320K home in one area carries the same monthly cost as a similarly priced home with different taxes, insurance assumptions, concessions, or HOA dues. If you're early in the process, Cody's New Braunfels mortgage calculator is a good first pass for testing payment ranges before you start touring. Once you know the payment ceiling, the real work is deciding whether the right move is a lower list price, a stronger concession ask, or a different neighborhood fit.

content_sections.h: What is the local market giving Seguin buyers that lower-rate markets did not?
content_sections.p: The trade-off for higher rates is that buyers are not always fighting the same level of urgency they faced when money was cheaper. In the San Antonio-New Braunfels region, the Texas Real Estate Research Center tracks sales, listings, prices, and inventory so buyers can see whether the market is moving toward more choice or more pressure. For Seguin and Guadalupe County buyers, that regional context matters because demand is tied to New Braunfels overflow, Cibolo-Schertz growth, JBSA-related movement, and buyers looking for more space along the IH-10 and SH 46 corridors. Realtor.com market data for Guadalupe County showed a median listing price around $320K and a median rent around $1.8K per month in its recent county snapshot. Those are not the only numbers that matter, but they frame the decision many buyers are trying to make: whether the higher monthly mortgage payment is worth the stability, space, and long-term plan compared with renting. The answer depends on your timeline, cash reserves, and whether you can buy without stretching so far that every maintenance surprise becomes a crisis. The part I see buyers miss is that Seguin is not just a cheaper substitute for New Braunfels. Some buyers are drawn to newer subdivisions and a different commute pattern. Others want a more established feel closer to downtown Seguin, Texas Lutheran University, or the Guadalupe River corridor. A lower purchase price can help, but if you ignore taxes, insurance, commute cost, and resale appeal, you can win the price and lose the plan. That is where negotiation strategy becomes practical. A higher-rate buyer may be better served asking for seller-paid closing costs, a temporary rate buydown, inspection repairs, or a lower price depending on the property and seller motivation. This connects directly with Cody's guide to new construction vs resale prices in New Braunfels, because builder competition nearby can affect how resale sellers in Seguin think about concessions.

content_sections.h: How should Seguin buyers compare payment, concessions, and loan type?
content_sections.p: The smartest Seguin buyers in 2026 are not asking only, "Can I afford this house?" They are asking, "Which structure gives me the best total position?" A small price reduction, a seller credit, and a rate buydown can each change the numbers differently. The right answer depends on the loan program, how long you expect to own the home, how much cash you want to keep after closing, and whether the property needs work right away. For example, a buyer using FHA or conventional financing may compare mortgage insurance, down payment, and seller credit limits. A VA buyer may care more about cash-to-close, funding fee treatment, appraisal condition, and whether the seller is open to credits. Cody's FHA vs conventional loan guide is useful here because the loan choice changes more than the interest rate. It changes how strong the offer looks, what repairs may become lender issues, and how much flexibility you have after inspection. There is also a timing decision. Some buyers want to wait for rates to fall. That can work if your lease, savings plan, and life timeline support it. But if rates fall and buyer demand jumps at the same time, you may face more competition, fewer seller concessions, and less time to think. A lower rate with a higher price and fewer concessions is not automatically better than a higher rate with a stronger negotiated deal today. This is the conversation I walk clients through before we write. We look at the payment, the cash needed, the likely inspection asks, and the property's competition. If the listing has been sitting, if comparable homes are adjusting price, or if a builder down the road is offering incentives, we may have room to ask. If the home is priced well and fits a hard-to-find need, the strategy may be different.

content_sections.h: What should sellers understand about rate-sensitive Seguin buyers?
content_sections.p: Sellers need to pay attention to interest rates too, because today's buyer is not just comparing your home to another home. They are comparing the total monthly cost of your home against every other option in the search area. If a buyer's lender says the payment is too high, your list price, property taxes, insurance estimate, HOA dues, and repair condition all become part of the same objection. This is where some Seguin sellers get in trouble. They look at what a neighbor sold for during a more aggressive market and assume the same buyer behavior applies now. But when rates are in the mid-6% range, buyers often slow down, ask more questions, and expect the house to justify the payment. A home with deferred maintenance, stale photos, unclear pricing, or no concession strategy can sit even if the headline price looks reasonable. If you're selling, the goal is not to panic or slash price blindly. The goal is to understand which lever solves the buyer's real objection. Sometimes that is a price correction. Sometimes it is a seller credit that helps cash-to-close. Sometimes it is fixing obvious inspection issues before listing so the buyer does not use them to renegotiate later. Cody's article on builder competition and seller strategy is relevant because nearby new construction incentives can reset what buyers expect from resale homes. My local read is straightforward: payment-sensitive buyers still buy good homes, but they are less forgiving. They notice if the house backs to a busy road, if the commute to New Braunfels or San Antonio is longer than expected, if the roof looks tired, or if the seller is priced like it's still a frenzy market. In this rate environment, pricing is not just about value. It is about removing friction before the buyer's lender, inspector, and spreadsheet give them a reason to walk.

title: Best Time to Sell a House in Cibolo: 2026 Guide
excerpt: Best time to sell a house in Cibolo is usually mid-April through May, but price, prep, and builder competition matter more than the calendar.

faqItems.q: 1) What is the best month to sell a house in Cibolo?
faqItems.a: April and May are usually the strongest months to sell a house in Cibolo because buyer activity tends to build before summer. For 2026, Realtor.com identified April 12-18 as the best national listing week, but your exact timing should depend on local comps, condition, and competing inventory.

faqItems.q: 2) Is spring always the best time to list in Cibolo?
faqItems.a: Spring often gives Cibolo sellers the best mix of buyer demand and market activity, but it is not automatic. A home that is overpriced or poorly prepared can still sit during spring, especially when buyers have resale and new-construction options.

faqItems.q: 3) Should I wait until April to sell if I need to move sooner?
faqItems.a: Not necessarily. If your move has a fixed timeline, selling sooner may be better than waiting for a seasonal advantage. A strong off-season plan usually depends on sharper pricing, strong presentation, and a clear negotiation strategy.

faqItems.q: 4) How early should I prepare my Cibolo home before listing?
faqItems.a: Most sellers should start 4 to 6 weeks before the target list date. That gives time for pricing, repairs, cleaning, photos, disclosure paperwork, and a plan for how to respond to early buyer feedback.

faqItems.q: 5) Does new construction affect when I should sell in Cibolo?
faqItems.a: Yes. Cibolo resale sellers often compete with nearby new construction, especially when builders offer incentives or quick-move-in homes. Your timing and price should account for those choices because buyers compare monthly payment, condition, location, and concessions together.

opening_question: When is the best time to sell a house in Cibolo in 2026?
quick_answer: The best time to sell a house in Cibolo in 2026 is usually the spring window, especially mid-April through May, because buyer activity tends to rise before summer schedules scatter attention. Realtor.com named April 12-18 the best national listing week for 2026, with historical conditions tied to stronger prices, more listing views, and faster market pace. For Cibolo sellers, that timing matters, but the bigger win is preparing early enough to price against resale competition, new construction incentives, and the specific buyer pool for your neighborhood. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does mid-April through May usually work best in Cibolo?
content_sections.p: Cibolo's strongest selling window usually opens before many homeowners feel ready. By the time school-year calendars, PCS orders, summer move plans, and builder promotions are already shaping buyer decisions, a seller who has not prepared yet is playing catch-up. That is why the useful answer is not just "spring." It is list when demand is building, but start the pricing and prep work 4 to 6 weeks earlier. Realtor.com's 2026 seasonality analysis identified the week of April 12-18 as the best national week to list, based on a mix of price, buyer demand, seller competition, market pace, and price-reduction risk. Their research says listings during that week have historically reached prices 1.3% above the average week and drawn 16.7% more views per listing than a typical week. That does not mean every Cibolo house should hit the market on one exact date, but it does show why the early spring window is worth planning around. For Cibolo, I think of the practical window as mid-April through May, with March as the prep and positioning month. If the home is clean, priced correctly, and competing well against nearby new construction, late March can work too. If the home needs repairs, paint, landscaping, decluttering, or a strategy for higher property-tax or HOA objections, waiting until the "perfect week" without doing the work first can cost more than the calendar helps. The part sellers sometimes miss is that Cibolo is not isolated from the rest of the northeast San Antonio corridor. Buyers compare Cibolo against Schertz, New Braunfels, Seguin, Converse, Universal City, and sometimes far north San Antonio. A spring listing needs to answer that comparison quickly. If your home is priced like it has no competition, buyers will use the extra spring inventory to keep moving.

content_sections.h: What makes Cibolo timing different from New Braunfels or Schertz?
content_sections.p: Cibolo has its own rhythm because it sits in a growth corridor with strong access to I-35, FM 1103, Randolph Air Force Base, Schertz, and the San Antonio-New Braunfels metro. The City of Cibolo says its estimated population reached 37,061 in 2023, up from 19,580 after the corrected 2010 count. That growth is a real market factor because it creates steady relocation attention, but it also creates more subdivision-by-subdivision comparison. A seller in an established Cibolo neighborhood is not only competing with the house down the street. They may also be competing with a builder offering rate buydowns, closing-cost help, appliance packages, or quick-move-in inventory. Cody's prior post on Bindseil Farms new construction in Cibolo is a good example of why the local new-home pipeline matters even for resale sellers. If a buyer can get a fresh build with incentives nearby, your pricing, condition, and showing experience have to make sense immediately. What I see with Cibolo sellers is that the first weekend on market often tells the truth. If you list in April and get showings but no serious feedback, the issue may be price-to-condition, not timing. If you list in April and buyers ask about concessions before writing, the market is telling you they see alternatives. That does not mean panic. It means your strategy needs to be built before launch, not after two quiet weeks. This is where a comp-backed home value review becomes more useful than a generic Zestimate or a national best-week article. Your best date depends on the homes buyers will compare against yours at that moment. In Cibolo, that can change quickly when a builder releases inventory, when commute-sensitive buyers start touring, or when rates shift enough to change monthly payment pressure.

content_sections.h: How do 2026 Texas market conditions affect Cibolo sellers?
content_sections.p: The 2026 Texas market is giving sellers a more nuanced message than the last few years. Texas REALTORS reported that statewide Q1 2026 home sales were up 0.7% year over year, while the statewide median price slipped 0.8%. They also reported average days on market at 80 days, which was 6 days longer than the same quarter in 2025. That is not a crash story. It is a more selective buyer story. The Texas Real Estate Research Center's May 2026 housing insight adds more context. In March, San Antonio sales rose 10.5% year over year, but San Antonio new listings jumped 39% from February to March and active inventory was up 10% year over year. That is the Cibolo seller's real spring reality: buyer activity can improve at the same time competition improves. That is why the best time to sell a house in Cibolo is not automatically the best time to overprice one. Spring can bring more eyeballs, but it can also expose weak positioning faster. Buyers have more data, more alerts, more builder options, and more patience than they had during the hottest pandemic-era market. If a home is priced ahead of the comps, buyers do not always negotiate first. Many just save the listing and wait for the price reduction. Cody's post on builder competition for local sellers applies directly here, even though the geography is broader than Cibolo. New construction incentives reset buyer expectations. A resale seller can still win, especially with location, lot, upgrades, mature landscaping, or lower monthly carrying costs, but those advantages have to be translated into the price and marketing plan. I would rather see a Cibolo seller launch at a defendable price in April than chase an extra number into May and spend June explaining stale days on market. The market does not reward optimism by itself. It rewards the best prepared listing in the buyer's search set.

content_sections.h: Should you wait for spring if you need to sell sooner?
content_sections.p: Not always. If your move is tied to a job change, PCS timeline, estate situation, divorce, new construction closing, or a home-sale contingency, waiting for spring can create more risk than reward. The right question is whether the expected spring lift is worth the extra carrying costs, preparation delay, and uncertainty in rates or competing inventory. A well-priced January or February listing can work when inventory is thinner and motivated buyers are active. A late summer or fall listing can work when the seller has the right price and the home solves a specific need. Seasonality gives you a tailwind, but it does not replace strategy. If you need to sell before April, the plan changes: sharper pricing, cleaner launch photos, stronger showing readiness, and faster feedback review. The mistake is treating the calendar like a guarantee. Realtor.com itself notes that local markets vary and that sellers in the South and West can face softer conditions because inventory is more abundant. That matters for Cibolo because the broader San Antonio-New Braunfels corridor has more choices than many inventory-starved markets. If you wait for spring but enter with an inflated price, the season will not protect you. This is also why net proceeds matter as much as sale price. A spring listing might produce a higher contract price, but if you spend months carrying payments, paying for repairs twice, or offering concessions after missing the first wave of buyers, your net can look different. Before choosing a date, run both the value range and the proceeds math through a seller net sheet so the timing decision is tied to dollars, not just a headline.

content_sections.h: What should Cibolo sellers do before choosing a list date?
content_sections.p:
Start with the buyer comparison, not the calendar. Pull active, pending, and recently sold comps in your exact search set. Then look at builder inventory nearby, because that is often where Cibolo resale sellers get surprised. If a new-home community is offering incentives in your buyer's price band, your listing has to show why a resale buyer should still choose you.

Next, decide what condition issues are worth fixing before launch. Paint, flooring touch-ups, landscaping, lighting, and deep cleaning are not glamorous, but they change how buyers interpret price. Bigger repairs need a different conversation. Sometimes doing the repair improves confidence. Sometimes pricing with disclosure and documentation is cleaner. It depends on the issue and the buyer pool.

Then choose a launch window with enough runway. If you want the mid-April to May window, March is not too early to start. That gives time for pricing, prep, photos, documents, seller disclosure, showing plan, and a negotiation strategy. Seller closing costs are also worth reviewing before you set expectations around net proceeds, because timing is only one part of the final number.

Finally, make a feedback plan before showings begin. Decide what you will watch in the first 7 to 10 days: saves, showings, second showings, buyer objections, agent comments, and comparable price changes. A good listing plan includes the first move and the adjustment plan. That way, if the market speaks, you are not making an emotional decision under pressure.

title: Relocating to Garden Ridge From Out of State in 2026
excerpt: Relocating to Garden Ridge from out of state works best with a 90-day plan that coordinates lender timing, tours, Texas paperwork, and moving logistics.

faqItems.q: 1) Is 90 days enough time to relocate to Garden Ridge from another state?
faqItems.a: For many resale buyers, 90 days is a workable planning window if financing, travel, and moving logistics start early. Add more time if you need to sell a home first, coordinate a cross-country move, build new construction, or wait for a specific work or school calendar date.

faqItems.q: 2) Where is Garden Ridge, Texas?
faqItems.a: Garden Ridge is in Comal County, and the City of Garden Ridge describes it as about 12 miles south of New Braunfels. Its location puts buyers near the I-35 corridor, New Braunfels, Schertz, Cibolo, and San Antonio-area commute routes.

faqItems.q: 3) What should out-of-state buyers check before buying in Garden Ridge?
faqItems.a: Check the full monthly payment, property taxes, insurance, HOA details, commute route, water provider, drainage, roof condition, and exact jurisdiction or school district boundary as factual property details. Do not rely only on photos or broad neighborhood assumptions.

faqItems.q: 4) How soon do new Texas residents need to update vehicle and driver documents?
faqItems.a: TxDMV says new residents have 30 days from the time they move to Texas to register a vehicle. Texas DPS says eligible new residents may drive with a valid out-of-state license for up to 90 days after moving before transferring to a Texas driver license.

faqItems.q: 5) When should a new Garden Ridge homeowner think about the homestead exemption?
faqItems.a: Put the homestead exemption on your post-closing calendar right away. The Texas Comptroller says most exemption applications are filed with the county appraisal district and the general filing deadline is before May 1, with eligibility depending on ownership and principal-residence use.

opening_question: How long should you plan for relocating to Garden Ridge from out of state in 2026?
quick_answer: Most out-of-state buyers should plan on a 90-day relocation window before they want keys in hand in Garden Ridge, with extra time if they need to sell first, build new, or coordinate a long-distance mover. The City of Garden Ridge describes the community as being in Comal County and about 12 miles south of New Braunfels, so the plan should account for both local Hill Country housing details and San Antonio-area commute patterns. After arrival, Texas gives new residents up to 90 days to transfer an eligible driver license and requires vehicle registration steps through TxDMV. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What should happen 90 days before your Garden Ridge move?
content_sections.p: Start with the date you want to unlock the door, then work backward. If you want to be living in Garden Ridge by October 1, your serious planning should begin around July 1. That does not mean you need to write an offer on day one. It means your lender, budget, home search, school district verification, moving quotes, and contingency plan all need to be moving before the market forces your hand. Garden Ridge is not the same search as central New Braunfels, Schertz, or Cibolo. The city describes itself as a Comal County community about 12 miles south of New Braunfels, and that location is exactly why out-of-state buyers are drawn to it. You can be near the I-35 corridor, New Braunfels, San Antonio, and the Hill Country without feeling like you bought in the middle of a high-volume retail corridor. The first 30 days should be about numbers and fit. Get fully underwritten or as close as your lender allows, compare realistic monthly payments with Texas property taxes, and decide whether Garden Ridge is the right match or whether nearby areas like Schertz, Cibolo, Bulverde, or New Braunfels should stay in the mix. If affordability is still the open question, use a mortgage calculator as a starting point, then have a lender confirm the real payment with insurance, taxes, and any HOA details. This is where I see relocators make the first expensive mistake. They compare a Garden Ridge list price to their current state's list price, but they do not compare the full monthly cost. Texas has no state income tax, but property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, utilities, and commute patterns can change the real budget. Before we tour, I want my clients to understand the full number, not just the number on Zillow.

content_sections.h: When should you tour, offer, inspect, and close from another state?
content_sections.p: For a resale purchase, the middle of the timeline is usually the most intense. A realistic out-of-state plan is to narrow the search remotely first, then schedule a focused tour window once your lender letter, cash-to-close estimate, and must-have list are ready. In Garden Ridge, that means looking closely at lot size, property condition, water provider, HOA structure, commute route, and whether the home sits inside the exact jurisdiction or school district boundary you expect. Once you find the right property, Texas contract timing matters. The option period is usually the buyer's main due-diligence window, and it is when inspections, repair conversations, and termination rights need to be handled with discipline. If you're still learning Texas paperwork, my guide to the Texas option period is worth reviewing before you write an offer, because the timeline moves quickly after acceptance. A normal financed resale closing often lands around 30 days after contract, but out-of-state buyers should not build the whole move on a best-case assumption. Appraisal timing, insurance quotes, repair negotiations, title work, wire logistics, and travel schedules can all add pressure. If you are also selling a home in another state, your plan should include backup lodging, leaseback options, and a clear answer for what happens if one closing shifts. The local piece most relocating buyers miss is that Garden Ridge feels close to everything on a map, but daily life is still car-oriented. You should test the commute you will actually drive, at the time of day you will actually drive it. I would rather have you learn on a Tuesday morning before you buy than discover after closing that your workday route feels different from a Saturday showing.

content_sections.h: What Texas paperwork should you plan after closing?
content_sections.p: Your real estate closing is not the end of the relocation timeline. It is the handoff into Texas resident setup. TxDMV says new residents have 30 days from the time they move here to register a vehicle in Texas, and the Texas DPS guide says eligible new residents can drive with a valid out-of-state license for up to 90 days after moving to Texas before transferring to a Texas license. That order matters because DPS says to ensure your vehicles are registered before applying for the Texas driver license. For a Garden Ridge move, build time for insurance updates, inspection or registration requirements that apply to your vehicle, the county tax office, and a DPS appointment. Do not wait until the last week if you need a Texas license address for banking, homestead documents, school records, or other move-in tasks. Property taxes deserve their own calendar reminder. The Texas Comptroller explains that property tax is locally assessed and that most exemptions require an application with the appraisal district. The general exemption filing deadline is before May 1, and the school district residence homestead exemption is $140,000 under the current Comptroller guidance. For a Garden Ridge home, you will typically be dealing with Comal County appraisal processes, though every property should be verified by legal description and county record. This is why I like building a post-closing checklist before the moving truck arrives. When buyers wait until after closing to ask about vehicle registration, license timing, utilities, tax exemptions, and appraisal district paperwork, the first month in the new house feels messy. A good relocation plan should make the first 30 days in Texas calmer, not just get the contract closed.

content_sections.h: How should you compare Garden Ridge with nearby Hill Country options?
content_sections.p: Garden Ridge tends to appeal to buyers who want a quieter residential setting, larger-lot feel in many pockets, and access to both New Braunfels and San Antonio. But it should not be chosen just because it sounds more peaceful than the places around it. You still need to compare actual home age, remodel level, drainage, trees, roof condition, insurance profile, commute, and resale appeal. If you are coming from another state, keep a short list of alternatives alive until the numbers prove themselves. New Braunfels may give you more direct access to river, downtown, Gruene, and new-construction options. Schertz and Cibolo may make sense for some buyers who need a different commute pattern toward Randolph or northeast San Antonio. Bulverde and north Comal can create a different Hill Country feel. The right answer is not a generic best area. It is the area that matches your budget, routines, tolerance for maintenance, and timing. Cody's broader New Braunfels relocation guide is a useful starting point if you are still comparing areas, and the Garden Ridge from California move plan goes deeper for California sellers bringing equity into Texas. If you are downsizing, the Garden Ridge retirement move guide may fit your situation better than a general buyer checklist. The only Cody would say this part: don't fall in love with the word Hill Country before you inspect the driveway, drainage, roof, and tax bill. I have seen buyers get emotionally attached to trees, space, and a quiet street, then realize the monthly number or maintenance plan is not the lifestyle they pictured. Garden Ridge can be a strong fit, but the best move is the one where the romance and the math both survive inspection.

title: Comal County Housing Inventory 2026: NB Market Read
excerpt: Comal County housing inventory in 2026 is giving buyers more room and sellers less margin for pricing mistakes across New Braunfels.

faqItems.q: 1) Is Comal County a buyer's market in 2026?
faqItems.a: Comal County is more buyer-friendly in 2026 than it was during the tightest inventory years, but conditions still vary by price point and property type. Perplexity-confirmed April snippets showed about 7.3 months of single-family inventory, which points to more balance and more buyer choice. Well-priced homes can still attract strong attention.

faqItems.q: 2) How many active listings are in Comal County in 2026?
faqItems.a: The Stage 2 research brief showed early-2026 inventory running around 2,000 to 2,400 active listings. A Perplexity-confirmed April 2026 snippet showed 2,086 active single-family listings, up about 14.8% year over year. The exact number changes month to month, so buyers and sellers should verify current active competition before making a decision.

faqItems.q: 3) Why are days on market important for New Braunfels sellers?
faqItems.a: Days on market show how quickly buyers are responding to price, condition, and competition. Trading Economics reported that Comal County median days on market reached 102 days in February 2026, a sharp change from the 27-day low in April 2022. Longer market time means sellers need to price and prepare carefully before launch.

faqItems.q: 4) Can buyers negotiate more in Comal County in 2026?
faqItems.a: Buyers often have more room to negotiate when inventory is higher and homes sit longer, but the strategy depends on the individual property. A stale listing with condition concerns may support a stronger ask for price, repairs, or concessions. A well-priced home in good condition may still require a clean, realistic offer.

faqItems.q: 5) What should sellers do before listing in a higher-inventory market?
faqItems.a: Sellers should compare their home against current active listings, not only closed comps. They should also address obvious condition objections, review nearby builder incentives, and choose a price that makes sense against what buyers can tour right now. A local pricing strategy matters more when buyers have more choices.

opening_question: What do Comal County housing inventory levels in 2026 mean for New Braunfels buyers and sellers?
quick_answer: Comal County housing inventory levels in 2026 point to a more balanced, choice-heavy market than New Braunfels saw during the tightest years. Perplexity-confirmed local snippets show April 2026 single-family inventory near 7.3 months, with about 2,086 active listings and average days on market around 106 days. Buyers have more room to compare, negotiate, and slow down, while sellers need sharper pricing and cleaner prep before launch. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does higher Comal County inventory change the 2026 market?
content_sections.p: Inventory is the number that tells you how much room buyers and sellers really have. In early 2026, Comal County moved away from the low-supply pressure that defined the fastest pandemic-era market. The research brief shows total listings running around 2,000 to 2,400 homes early in the year, and Perplexity surfaced April data showing 2,086 active single-family listings, up about 14.8% year over year. That does not mean homes stopped selling. It means buyers have more alternatives when a listing feels overpriced, poorly prepared, or too expensive after taxes, insurance, HOA dues, or builder competition are factored in. The second signal is time. Trading Economics, using Federal Reserve housing inventory data, noted that Comal County median days on market reached a historical high of 102 days in February 2026, compared with a low of 27 days in April 2022. Another local market snippet pulled through Perplexity showed April average days on market around 106 days. Those numbers matter because time changes behavior. A buyer who sees a home sit for three months asks different questions than a buyer fighting through the first weekend of showings. For sellers, the shift is not just about patience. It is about launch accuracy. A New Braunfels seller cannot price like inventory is still scarce and then expect buyers to ignore a similar resale down the road, a builder with closing-cost help, or a newer home with a lower repair burden. If you are selling, the first two weeks still matter, but they matter for a different reason now: they show whether your pricing strategy is aligned with the real buyer pool, not just with what you hoped the spring market would do. For buyers, higher inventory creates opportunity, but it does not remove the need for discipline. The best-fit home still depends on payment, condition, commute, property taxes, and the specific submarket. A buyer comparing Veramendi, Mission Hills Ranch, older central New Braunfels, or a north Comal acreage property is not comparing the same product. That is why a broad county inventory number should start the conversation, not end it. For a wider pricing context, see Cody's recent Comal County home price and days-on-market update.

content_sections.h: What should New Braunfels sellers do when inventory rises?
content_sections.p: Sellers need to treat 2026 like a market that rewards precision. The old approach of testing a high price and waiting for the market to catch up is riskier when buyers can scroll through more choices. A stale listing does not just lose attention. It invites sharper negotiations, longer inspection conversations, and buyer assumptions that something must be wrong even when the home is solid. Pricing has to account for competition, not just comps. A comp tells you what sold. Inventory tells you what your buyer can choose instead today. That is the part sellers miss when they only look backward. If a comparable home closed at $470,000 three months ago, but current active listings are sitting longer and builders nearby are advertising incentives, your real pricing lane may be narrower than the closed-sale number suggests. Condition matters more when buyers have choices. I see this in New Braunfels all the time: buyers will forgive a few cosmetic issues when they have no leverage, but they get much pickier when there are five alternatives in the same price band. The misconception I hear from sellers is, "A buyer can just update that later." In 2026, many buyers are already stretched by payment, taxes, and insurance. They may not want to inherit a project unless the price clearly reflects it. Negotiation starts before the offer. Your photos, prep, list price, showing access, and disclosure package all shape whether the buyer feels confident or cautious. In a higher-inventory market, a seller who prepares well can still stand out. A seller who launches with weak photos, vague condition answers, or a price above the active competition may end up negotiating from a defensive position. If you are trying to decide whether to adjust price, repair, or hold, Cody's guide to builder competition in Comal County explains why resale sellers need to watch both MLS comps and new-construction pressure.

content_sections.h: How can buyers use 2026 inventory without overplaying their hand?
content_sections.p: Buyers should use higher inventory to compare better, not to assume every seller is desperate. A market with 7.3 months of inventory gives buyers more room than a two-month market, but it is still uneven by price point, property type, and location. A well-priced home in a desirable condition band can still move faster than the county average. A home with a price, condition, or payment problem can sit. The smartest buyer move is to separate negotiable homes from competitive homes. Look at days on market, price reductions, seller disclosure quality, nearby new construction, and how the home compares to current active listings. A property at 90-plus days may create room for seller concessions, repairs, or price movement. A newer listing priced right may require a cleaner offer, even in a market with more supply. This is where payment math matters. A lower price is helpful, but a concession that buys down rate, covers closing costs, or offsets repairs may be more useful depending on your financing. If affordability is your main constraint, start with the New Braunfels mortgage calculator before you fall in love with a list price. Then compare homes by monthly cost, not just by headline price. Buyers also need to respect inspection and option-period strategy. More inventory can give you more room to ask, but the request still needs to be tied to real findings and market context. In Texas, your option period gives you time to evaluate condition and negotiate from facts. Cody's Texas inspection requests guide for New Braunfels buyers is a useful companion if you are trying to understand where a reasonable ask ends and a deal-killer begins.

content_sections.h: What local inventory patterns matter most around New Braunfels?
content_sections.p:
The county number is useful, but New Braunfels real estate is not one clean spreadsheet. Comal County includes city neighborhoods, master-planned communities, river-area homes, Hill Country acreage, Canyon Lake properties, and newer subdivisions competing with builder inventory. Two homes can share a county, a price range, and a bedroom count while attracting completely different buyers.

New construction is one of the biggest inventory wild cards. In parts of New Braunfels, Cibolo, Schertz, and north Comal, builders can influence resale pricing even when the resale home is not in the same subdivision. If a builder offers rate incentives, closing-cost help, or quick-move-in discounts, a resale seller nearby has to explain why their home is still the better value. Sometimes the answer is lot size, mature landscaping, location, or lower monthly ownership costs. Sometimes the answer is a price correction.

Property taxes and HOA costs also shape inventory pressure. A buyer comparing two similarly priced homes may choose the one with a cleaner monthly payment, even if the list prices look close. This is especially important around MUDs, PIDs, newer communities, and homes with higher assessed values. Monthly cost can change the real affordability picture even when the list price looks reasonable.

My local read is this: inventory is giving serious buyers more power, but it is exposing sellers who relied on old assumptions. The homes that struggle are usually not just "bad homes." They are homes where price, condition, payment, and buyer expectations are not lined up. The homes that still get attention usually make the buyer's decision easier. They show well, disclose clearly, and make sense against the active competition the buyer can tour this week.

content_sections.h: What should you do next if you plan to move in 2026?
content_sections.p: If you are selling in the next 30 to 180 days, do not start with a Zestimate, a neighbor's sale, or a hopeful number. Start with an active-competition review. That means looking at what sold, what failed to sell, what is pending, what builders are offering, and where your home fits today. In a higher-inventory market, the right question is not "What could we maybe get?" It is "What price and preparation plan gives us the strongest position with the buyers who are actually shopping now?" If you are buying, use the inventory shift to build a better shortlist. Tour enough homes to understand tradeoffs, but do not let more choices turn into paralysis. Decide where you are flexible and where you are not. Payment, commute, property condition, tax load, HOA rules, and timing should guide the search before paint color or staging does. For both sides, the market is more strategic than scary. Higher inventory gives buyers options and forces sellers to be more honest with the numbers. That is not bad news. It is a better market for people who prepare. The only real mistake is using a 2021 playbook in a 2026 market.

title: Texas VLB Home Loan 2026: New Braunfels VA Guide
excerpt: Texas VLB home loan benefits in 2026 can help eligible New Braunfels veterans compare VA, FHA, or conventional financing with a VLB participating lender.

faqItems.q: 1) What is the Texas VLB home loan amount in 2026?
faqItems.a: The Texas General Land Office announced that the Veterans Land Board increased the VLB home loan amount to $832,750 for 2026. Treat that as a program ceiling, not an automatic purchase budget. Your actual buying power depends on lender approval, income, debts, credit, property taxes, insurance, and the home you choose.

faqItems.q: 2) Can I combine a Texas VLB home loan with a VA loan?
faqItems.a: The Texas General Land Office says eligible Texas Veterans and Military Members can apply for VA, FHA, or conventional financing using the Veterans Housing Assistance Program and a VLB participating lender. If you plan to use a VA-backed purchase loan, ask the lender early how they handle VLB files, eligibility documentation, interest-rate discounts, and closing timelines.

faqItems.q: 3) Does the VLB program require the home to be my primary residence?
faqItems.a: Yes. The VLB home-loan requirements say the home must be the Veteran or Military Member's primary residence in Texas. The VLB also states the borrower must occupy the home within 60 days after closing and the home must remain the primary residence for at least three years.

faqItems.q: 4) What types of homes can qualify for a VLB home loan?
faqItems.a: The VLB lists eligible home types including single-family attached or detached homes, townhomes, and condominiums. Duplexes or other multi-family units have additional age requirements, and new construction must meet applicable building standards. Your lender still needs to confirm the specific property fits the loan and program requirements.

faqItems.q: 5) Is the VLB home loan enough to start shopping in New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Not by itself. Before shopping, you should confirm eligibility, talk with a VLB participating lender, and build a full monthly payment estimate with property taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and closing-cost assumptions. Then match the search to commute, occupancy timing, property condition, and offer strategy.

opening_question: How does the Texas VLB home loan work for New Braunfels VA buyers in 2026?
quick_answer: The Texas Veterans Land Board home loan program can help eligible Texas Veterans and Military Members buy a primary residence in Texas through a VLB participating lender, often paired with VA, FHA, or conventional financing. For 2026, the VLB announced a home loan amount increase to $832,750, and the state says Veterans with a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or greater may qualify for a discounted interest rate. For New Braunfels and JBSA-area buyers, the practical value is not just the headline limit. It is knowing how the VLB layer, VA benefit, lender approval, property requirements, and PCS timing all fit together. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What changed with the Texas VLB home loan amount in 2026?
content_sections.p: The clean headline is that the Texas Veterans Land Board announced an increase in the VLB home loan amount to $832,750 for eligible Texas Veterans and Military Members. That matters in the New Braunfels area because price bands can move quickly between entry-level resale homes, newer builder inventory, and Hill Country homes with more land, views, or commute advantages toward San Antonio and JBSA. The important part is that the VLB program is not a shortcut around underwriting. The state describes the Veterans Housing Assistance Program as a way for eligible Veterans and Military Members to use VA, FHA, or conventional financing through a VLB participating lender. That means you still need a lender to review credit, income, debt, assets, occupancy, and the property itself. The VLB benefit can be powerful, but it needs to be built into the loan plan early rather than mentioned after you already found a house. I would treat the $832,750 figure as a planning ceiling, not a target purchase price. In real client conversations, the better question is usually: what monthly payment works after property taxes, insurance, HOA dues, possible MUD or PID assessments, and the VA funding fee if it applies? A buyer can technically look at a higher number and still decide the smarter move is a lower price point in Schertz, Cibolo, Seguin, or New Braunfels because the payment gives them breathing room. This is also where the Texas Hill Country market can surprise PCS buyers. New Braunfels straddles Comal and Guadalupe counties, and the same list price can feel different once taxes, commute, builder incentives, and neighborhood costs are included. Before you anchor to a price ceiling, confirm the actual loan structure with a lender who handles VLB and VA files.

content_sections.h: Can you use the VLB program with a VA loan?
content_sections.p: Yes, the state says eligible Texas Veterans and Military Members can apply for VA, FHA, or conventional financing using the Veterans Housing Assistance Program and a VLB participating lender. That is why this topic matters for VA buyers. The VLB program is not replacing the VA loan. For many buyers, it is part of the financing conversation alongside the VA benefit. The VA's own purchase-loan guidance says a VA-backed purchase loan often offers no down payment as long as the sales price is not higher than the home's appraised value, no private mortgage insurance, and the ability to use the benefit again. Those are meaningful advantages, especially when a military household is moving into the San Antonio to New Braunfels corridor with relocation costs, temporary housing, storage, and command reporting dates all happening at once. The catch is that every layer has rules. VA approval, VLB eligibility, lender overlays, appraisal standards, contract terms, and seller negotiations all have to line up. If you are planning around seller concessions, closing costs, or a funding fee, Cody's prior guide to VA funding fee rates in Texas is worth reading before you compare offers. If you expect to ask the seller to help with costs, the VA seller credits rule in New Braunfels can affect how the contract is written. Here is the local piece I see people miss: a VA buyer can be strong on paper and still lose time if the property choice does not match the loan path. Older Hill Country homes, rural acreage, new construction timelines, condos, and properties with condition issues can all create different questions. I do not want a veteran buyer to find the right house and then discover late that the lender, VLB requirements, appraisal concerns, or seller expectations were never aligned.

content_sections.h: Which New Braunfels homes can fit the VLB requirements?
content_sections.p: The VLB home-loan page says the home must be the Veteran or Military Member's primary residence in Texas. It also lists eligible property types such as a single-family attached or detached home, townhome, or condominium. Duplexes or other multi-family units must have been built at least five years before loan closing, and new construction has to meet applicable local building standards. That property language matters because New Braunfels buyers often compare very different housing choices in one weekend. You might see a resale near Gruene, a builder home off the IH-35 growth corridor, a townhome closer to shopping, and a Hill Country property that feels like a different world even though the drive time is not that far. The VLB program may be available across several property types, but the property still has to pass the lender's and program's checks. Occupancy is another planning point. The VLB says the home must remain the borrower's primary residence for at least three years, and the borrower must occupy the home within 60 days after loan closing. That can matter for active-duty buyers, retirement moves, deployment timing, and families trying to coordinate school calendars, lease endings, and household goods delivery. The goal is not to memorize every rule. The goal is to sequence the move so your contract, closing date, and occupancy plan make sense. For JBSA-area buyers, New Braunfels is not one simple commute decision. Randolph, Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, and Camp Bullis can create very different daily realities. content_sections.h: What should a veteran buyer do before shopping with VLB benefits?
content_sections.p: Start with the lender, not the listing. A strong preapproval should reflect the actual program you plan to use, not a generic estimate that gets rebuilt after you are under contract. Run the payment with Texas costs included. New Braunfels buyers need to look beyond principal and interest. Property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, possible special assessments, and closing costs can change the comfort level. The VLB home loan amount increase helps with buying power, but your real decision should be based on the monthly number and the cash needed to close. Match the property search to the loan. If you are using VA and VLB benefits, your search should favor homes that fit the financing path. That does not mean avoiding older homes, new construction, townhomes, or rural properties. It means asking the right questions early: condition, appraisal risk, condo approval, builder timeline, occupancy, floodplain, septic, well, HOA, MUD, PID, and whether seller concessions are realistic in that specific segment. Plan the offer before the showing rush starts. This is where I get direct with military buyers: the house you want is only half the job. The other half is making the offer clean enough that the seller understands the VA/VLB path and does not panic over terms they do not understand. I walk clients through this before we write, because a well-explained offer can prevent a good buyer from being misread as complicated. title: Texas Seller Disclosure Form 2026: New Braunfels Guide
excerpt: Texas seller disclosure form rules in 2026 affect New Braunfels sellers before pricing, inspections, and buyer negotiations begin.

faqItems.q: 1) Is a Texas seller disclosure form required in 2026?
faqItems.a: For most previously occupied one-unit residential properties in Texas, yes. Texas Property Code Section 5.008 requires a seller to give the buyer a written disclosure notice unless a statutory exception applies. Sellers should confirm the current form and timing with their REALTOR or attorney before listing.

faqItems.q: 2) What is the difference between TREC OP-H and TREC No. 55-0 or 55-1?
faqItems.a: OP-H has historically been associated with the TREC Seller's Disclosure Notice, while TREC's 2026 updates refer to Standard Contract Form TREC No. 55-0 and draft/revised form numbering such as 55-1. Because form numbers and mandatory-use dates can change, sellers should use the current version posted or required for their transaction date.

faqItems.q: 3) Does the seller disclosure replace a buyer inspection?
faqItems.a: No. The disclosure is based on the seller's knowledge of the property's condition as of the date signed. It is not a warranty and it is not a substitute for inspections, repair negotiations, or buyer due diligence during the option period.

faqItems.q: 4) What New Braunfels issues should sellers think about before disclosure?
faqItems.a: Common local issues include prior water intrusion, floodplain questions, roof age, HVAC history, septic systems, wells, private roads, easements, HOA or MUD details, and insurance claim history. Not every property has these issues, but sellers should gather documents early so the form is accurate and consistent with the listing strategy.

faqItems.q: 5) Can a disclosure issue lower my New Braunfels sale price?
faqItems.a: It can, depending on the issue, documentation, buyer demand, competing inventory, and how the home is priced. A known issue does not automatically sink a sale, but vague or late disclosure can weaken buyer confidence. The better approach is to price, document, and negotiate with the disclosure in mind from the start.

opening_question: What do New Braunfels sellers need to know about the Texas seller disclosure form in 2026?
quick_answer: Most Texas sellers of a previously occupied one-unit residential property must give buyers a written Seller's Disclosure Notice under Texas Property Code Section 5.008. In 2026, TREC's Seller's Disclosure Notice update became effective May 28, 2026, and related revised forms move toward mandatory use July 1, 2026, so New Braunfels sellers should verify the current form before listing. The form is not a warranty, but it can shape buyer confidence, inspection negotiations, and whether a contract stays together. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does the Texas seller disclosure form matter before you list?
content_sections.p: The Texas seller disclosure form is one of the first documents a serious buyer studies after they fall in love with a home. It tells the buyer what the seller knows about the property's condition as of the date signed. That includes systems, known defects, prior flooding questions, insurance-related issues, repairs, and other property facts that can affect a buyer's risk tolerance. For a New Braunfels seller, this is not paperwork to rush through the night before going live. The disclosure influences how buyers read the listing price. A clean, complete, consistent disclosure can support confidence. A vague or sloppy disclosure can make buyers wonder what else might be missing, even when the home itself is solid. Texas Property Code Section 5.008 says a seller of residential real property comprising not more than one dwelling unit located in Texas shall give the purchaser a written notice prescribed by the statute or a substantially similar notice with the required items. The notice itself also makes clear that it is a disclosure of the seller's knowledge, not a substitute for inspections and not a warranty. That difference matters. You are not promising the house is perfect. You are disclosing what you know so the buyer can make an informed decision. I see sellers get tripped up when they treat disclosure as separate from pricing. It is not. If the roof is older, the HVAC has needed service, there was prior water intrusion, or a septic item needs context, those facts can affect both buyer expectations and the negotiation plan. The smarter move is to line up the disclosure, pricing strategy, and likely inspection objections before the listing hits the market. That is the same logic behind a comp-backed home value review, because condition and confidence both show up in what buyers are willing to pay.

content_sections.h: What changed with TREC Seller's Disclosure Notice updates in 2026?
content_sections.p:
TREC's 2026 Seller's Disclosure Notice update is more than a form-number detail. TREC's rule page for Standard Contract Form TREC No. 55-0 says the update followed direction from the Sunset Advisory Commission and adds questions tied to insurance, private road maintenance, aboveground storage tanks over 500 gallons that have stored petroleum products or other chemicals, and conservation easements. Those are not abstract issues in the Hill Country. They can matter on acreage, rural-edge properties, and homes outside the tight city-core pattern.

The 2026 transition also creates a practical timing issue. The brief for this post identified that some revised forms became available for voluntary use once posted, with mandatory use beginning July 1, 2026 for the remaining revised forms. If you are listing around that transition, you want your file checked against the current form package, not last year's downloaded PDF sitting in a folder.

This is where sellers should avoid guessing. The seller disclosure form has legal consequences, and Cody is not your attorney. But from a listing strategy standpoint, your REALTOR should help you slow down, identify what deserves a supporting document, and make sure your transaction file uses current forms. If something is unclear, that is when you ask the right professional before a buyer turns uncertainty into a repair demand, price reduction, or termination.

The part I keep seeing in New Braunfels is that buyers do not read disclosures like lawyers. They read them like people trying to decide whether they trust the house. A private road note, a prior leak, a septic item, or a floodplain question may not scare off the right buyer if it is explained cleanly. But if it appears late, conflicts with listing remarks, or sounds incomplete, buyers start filling in the blanks with worst-case assumptions. That is exactly what a good pre-listing review is meant to prevent.

content_sections.h: Which New Braunfels property issues deserve extra attention?
content_sections.p: New Braunfels sits in a market where property condition questions can change block by block. Some homes are in older central neighborhoods with mature systems and prior repairs. Some are in newer master-planned areas where builder warranties, MUD taxes, drainage, and HOA details matter. Some are outside city limits, where septic, wells, propane, private roads, drainage, easements, and outbuildings become part of the buyer's decision. Flood disclosure deserves special care in this part of Texas. The brief notes enhanced flood disclosure requirements were added after Hurricane Harvey in 2019, and New Braunfels sellers have real local reasons to pay attention. Guadalupe River, Comal River, Dry Comal Creek, Cibolo Creek, low-water crossings, and Hill Country drainage patterns can all make a buyer ask sharper questions. That does not mean every property has flood risk. It means sellers should verify, disclose what they know, and avoid casual answers when documentation is available. Septic and well details also belong in the conversation for Hill Country listings. A home can look move-in ready in photos, but if the septic system has not been serviced, the drain field location is unclear, or a buyer cannot understand how the water source works, that can slow the deal. I would rather surface those items before showings than have them surprise everyone during option period. If your property has septic, this Texas Hill Country septic disclosure guide is a useful companion topic. Insurance questions may also feel different in 2026 because the updated TREC notice specifically includes coverage-related information. In practice, buyers are already paying more attention to roof age, prior claims, hail history, and insurability. A seller who can pair clear disclosure with helpful context gives the buyer less room to assume the worst. That is also why pricing should be built around the full condition story, not just the prettiest active comps.

content_sections.h: How can disclosure strategy protect your price and negotiation leverage?
content_sections.p: A strong seller disclosure strategy does not mean over-explaining every scratch in the house. It means being accurate, current, and ready. If the buyer's inspector calls out an item that is already disclosed and priced into the strategy, the seller is in a stronger position than if the issue appears to be new information. That changes the tone of the negotiation. This matters because New Braunfels buyers have more ways to compare homes than they used to. Resale sellers may be competing against builder inventory, rate buydowns, repair credits, and homes that have already taken price reductions. If your disclosure raises questions and your price leaves no room for those questions, the buyer may move on. If your pricing and disclosure tell a coherent story, the home can still compete even when it is not perfect. I walk sellers through this before we list because the option period is not the time to build the strategy from scratch. We look at likely buyer objections, recent comparable sales, competing homes, condition, documentation, and the most likely inspection pressure points. If you want a broader view of seller costs and net numbers, this seller closing costs guide for New Braunfels pairs well with a disclosure review. Disclosure also helps decide what to fix before listing. Some items are worth correcting because they create buyer friction greater than the repair cost. Other items are better disclosed, documented, and handled through pricing or negotiation. There is no universal answer. The right answer depends on your home's condition, price point, neighborhood, timeline, and buyer pool. That is why disclosure should sit beside your seller net sheet, not in a separate folder no one studies until the last minute.

content_sections.h: What should sellers do before signing the disclosure notice?
content_sections.p: Start by gathering documents before you open the form. Look for roof invoices, HVAC service records, foundation reports, plumbing repair invoices, insurance claim paperwork, septic records, HOA documents, survey documents, warranty information, and any permits or receipts for major work. You may not need every file in the disclosure itself, but having them close by helps you answer carefully instead of relying on memory. Next, read every question slowly and answer from your actual knowledge. If you do not know an answer, do not guess. If the form gives an unknown option and that is the honest answer, use it. The point is not to sound perfect. The point is to be accurate and consistent with what you know. A buyer will still have inspections, and the disclosure is not a replacement for that process. Then line up the disclosure with the listing strategy. If the form mentions a repair, the marketing remarks, showing conversations, pricing notes, and negotiation plan should not tell a different story. That is where avoidable friction starts. The same applies if you are deciding whether to sell as-is or make repairs first. This New Braunfels as-is versus fix-it guide can help frame that decision. Finally, ask for help before you publish the listing, not after the first buyer objects. Cody can help you compare the disclosure against the likely buyer questions for your neighborhood and price point, then build a practical pricing and negotiation plan around it. For many sellers, that early conversation is what keeps the deal from becoming reactive later.

title: Contingency Offers Texas: New Braunfels 2026 Guide
excerpt: Contingency offers Texas buyers write in 2026 can still win in New Braunfels when the dates, financing, appraisal, and backup plan are clear.

faqItems.q: 1) What is a contingency offer in Texas real estate?
faqItems.a: A contingency offer is an offer that depends on a specific condition being satisfied, such as financing approval, appraisal terms, inspection decisions, or the sale of the buyer's current home. In Texas, the exact rights and deadlines depend on the contract and any addenda used. Buyers should review the language with their agent and lender before signing.

faqItems.q: 2) Can I buy a New Braunfels home before selling my current home?
faqItems.a: Yes, but the right path depends on your cash position, lender approval, and whether you need proceeds from the sale to close. Some buyers use a sale-of-property contingency, while others explore bridge financing, leasebacks, or timing the closings closely. The seller will usually want proof that your current-home sale is realistic.

faqItems.q: 3) Does a home-sale contingency make my offer weaker?
faqItems.a: It can, but it does not automatically make the offer weak. A home-sale contingency is stronger when your current home is already listed, priced correctly, under contract, or near closing. Sellers usually care less about the label and more about how likely the buyer is to close on time.

faqItems.q: 4) What contingencies should Texas buyers watch most closely?
faqItems.a: Texas buyers should pay close attention to financing approval, appraisal language, inspection and option-period deadlines, sale-of-property language, earnest money, and closing date. Each one changes the buyer's risk and the seller's confidence in the offer. The safest strategy is to decide these terms before emotions take over during negotiation.

faqItems.q: 5) How do I make a contingent offer more competitive?
faqItems.a: Make the offer easier for the seller to trust. Have your lender fully involved, document the status of your current-home sale, use realistic dates, and be clear about which terms you can safely strengthen. A local agent can help package the offer so the seller sees a plan, not just a list of conditions.

opening_question: Can contingency offers still work for Texas buyers in New Braunfels in 2026?
quick_answer: Yes, contingency offers can still work for Texas buyers in New Braunfels in 2026, but sellers judge them by certainty, timing, and how much risk the buyer is asking them to carry. TREC lists the Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer as Form ID 10-6, and its own description says it is used when buyers cannot buy the new property unless their existing property is sold and closed. In practice, your offer gets stronger when your current home is already listed, under contract, or close to closing, and when your financing, option period, appraisal language, and closing timeline are clean. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What makes a contingency offer different in Texas?
content_sections.p: A contingency offer is not one single thing. In Texas, it usually means the buyer is asking for a specific condition to be satisfied before the purchase fully moves forward. That condition might involve financing approval, inspection negotiations during the option period, appraisal protection, or the sale of the buyer's current home. Each one changes the seller's risk in a different way. The clearest example is the TREC Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer. TREC describes that form as being used when buyers will be unable to buy the new property unless their existing property is sold and closed. That is a very different risk profile from a buyer who only needs a normal lender approval or inspection window. A seller in New Braunfels is not just asking, "Is the price good?" They are asking, "How many things have to go right before this buyer can close?" This is where buyers sometimes get tripped up. They hear "contingent offer" and think it automatically sounds weak. It does not have to. A clean contingent offer with a strong current-home contract, reasonable dates, solid lender communication, and clear earnest money can be more attractive than a vague non-contingent offer from a buyer who has not finished the lending work. If you are still learning the broader offer mechanics, my guide to Texas option period basics is a good companion because the option period often becomes the first real decision point after acceptance. In New Braunfels, this matters because the market is not one uniform thing. A resale home near Gruene may get a different seller response than a builder-competing resale on the edge of town. A well-priced house under $400K may still draw quick attention, while a move-up home with more days on market may give a contingent buyer room to negotiate. The contract language matters, but the local leverage comes from the property, price point, condition, and seller motivation.

content_sections.h: Which contingencies affect your negotiating strength most?
content_sections.p: Sale-of-property contingency. This is usually the biggest one because it makes the seller depend on another transaction they do not control. If your current home is not listed yet, the seller is likely to see that as a major uncertainty. If it is listed with strong showing activity, that helps. If it is already under contract with buyer financing moving along, that helps more. If it has cleared inspection and appraisal issues, your position gets stronger again. Financing contingency. TREC's Third Party Financing Addendum is used when third-party financing will provide all or part of the purchase price. That is normal for many buyers, so the concern is not the existence of financing. The concern is whether the lender file is real. A vague prequalification letter is not the same as a fully reviewed approval path with income, assets, credit, and loan type already discussed. If monthly payment is the pressure point, run the numbers early with the New Braunfels mortgage calculator before you get emotionally attached to a home. Appraisal protection. TREC's contracts page lists the Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal as one of the available contract addenda. Appraisal language becomes especially important when a buyer is stretching, using a low down payment, or competing near a price point where recent comparable sales are thin. Sellers want to know whether a low appraisal kills the deal, triggers renegotiation, or still leaves the buyer able to close. Inspection and option period decisions. In Texas, the option period gives the buyer an unrestricted right to terminate within the agreed time if the option fee is paid on time under the contract terms. That does not mean sellers ignore it. A long option period, low option fee, and vague repair expectations can make an offer feel tentative. A focused option period and a buyer who understands what inspections are really for can make the same offer feel much more serious. I wrote more on this in Texas inspection request strategy, because inspection language is often where a deal either steadies or starts wobbling.

content_sections.h: How do New Braunfels sellers read contingent offers in 2026?
content_sections.p:
Most sellers do not reject contingencies just because the word appears in the offer. They reject uncertainty. That distinction matters. If the offer price is strong but the buyer's home is not listed, the seller may wonder whether they are taking their property off the market for a maybe. If the buyer's current home is already pending with a realistic closing date, the conversation changes.

What I see in New Braunfels is that sellers usually care about the chain behind the chain. It is not only your purchase of their home. It is your buyer's lender, your buyer's inspection, your buyer's appraisal, your title timeline, and whether your closing proceeds are truly what you need for the next purchase. That is the part relocating buyers and move-up buyers often underestimate. They focus on the house they want, while the seller focuses on every link that could break before funding.

Local context can cut both ways. If a seller is competing with new construction incentives nearby, a serious contingent buyer may still be worth working with, especially if the buyer understands closing costs and is not asking the seller to solve every payment issue. If the home is in a pocket with limited inventory and strong demand, the seller may ask for tighter dates, additional earnest money after waiver, or backup-contract protection. A buyer who understands Texas earnest money rules can make those conversations with a lot more confidence.

This is also where I push buyers to be honest with themselves before we write. If you need your current home to sell, we do not hide from that. We package it. We show the seller what has already been done, what still has to happen, how the timeline works, and why the offer is still worth taking. A contingency presented clearly is easier for a seller to trust than a clean-looking offer that falls apart once hard questions start.

content_sections.h: How can a buyer make a contingent offer stronger?
content_sections.p:
Start by tightening the current-home side of the story. If your existing home must sell first, get your pricing strategy, prep, listing timeline, and expected net proceeds handled before you go shopping seriously. The seller of your next home will care whether your current home is priced to move, whether it has a signed contract, and whether that contract has obvious weak points. If you are not sure what selling would produce, run a seller net sheet before you write a purchase offer that depends on those proceeds.

Next, make the financing clean. Your lender should understand the contingency, the source of funds, the timing of your sale proceeds, and whether you need bridge financing, temporary occupancy, or a same-day closing structure. This is not the place for guesswork. If the lender has not mapped the sequence, the seller's agent will usually feel that gap.

Then decide where you are willing to be flexible. Some buyers can shorten the option period. Some can offer stronger earnest money. Some can give the seller a leaseback. Some can write a cleaner appraisal structure because their cash position is stronger. Others should not do those things because it would put them in a bad spot. Good negotiation is not about giving everything away. It is about knowing which terms matter most to this seller and which ones you can safely improve.

Finally, connect the contingency to a real buyer game plan. Your offer should tell a coherent story: why this home, why this price, why this timeline, and why the seller should believe you can close. That is exactly the kind of question I walk clients through before we ever send the contract. If we cannot explain the offer clearly to the seller's side, we probably have not built it clearly enough for you either.
