title: Disabled Veteran Tax Exemption Texas 2026 Application
excerpt: Disabled veteran tax exemption Texas applicants should file through the appraisal district, match the right form to VA rating, and plan early.

faqItems.q: 1) What form do I use for the Texas disabled veteran property tax exemption?
faqItems.a: Many disabled veterans use Form 50-135 for the Tax Code Section 11.22 disabled veteran exemption. A 100% disabled veteran residence homestead exemption is tied to the residence homestead application, Form 50-114. Check the current Comptroller form and your county appraisal district instructions before filing.

faqItems.q: 2) What is the deadline to apply for the disabled veteran exemption in Texas?
faqItems.a: The standard exemption filing deadline is April 30 for the tax year requested. The Texas Comptroller says disabled veterans applying under Tax Code Section 11.22 may late-file up to five years after the delinquency date for taxes on the property. File early when possible so your appraisal district has time to process the application.

faqItems.q: 3) Do I file with the VA, my lender, or the county appraisal district?
faqItems.a: You file the property tax exemption application with the county appraisal district where the property is located. The VA award letter supports the application, but the VA does not process the local Texas property tax exemption. Your lender should know about the exemption for payment estimates, but the appraisal district handles approval.

faqItems.q: 4) Can the disabled veteran exemption apply to any property I own?
faqItems.a: The Texas Comptroller says the Tax Code Section 11.22 disabled veteran exemption can apply to any one property owned by the qualifying disabled veteran. The 100% disabled veteran residence homestead exemption is different because it applies to the qualifying residence homestead. That distinction is why matching the right form to your situation matters.

faqItems.q: 5) How does this affect buying a home near New Braunfels or JBSA?
faqItems.a: The exemption can change the tax portion of your ownership cost, but it should be reviewed with the full payment picture. New Braunfels-area buyers should compare county appraisal districts, tax units, HOA dues, insurance, lender estimates, and closing costs before choosing a home. A local VA + PCS plan helps keep those numbers organized before closing.

opening_question: How do you apply for the disabled veteran property tax exemption in Texas in 2026?
quick_answer: To apply for a disabled veteran property tax exemption in Texas in 2026, file with the county appraisal district where the property is located, not with the mortgage company or the VA. Most disabled veterans use Form 50-135 for the Tax Code Section 11.22 exemption, while a 100% disabled veteran residence homestead exemption is handled through the residence homestead application, Form 50-114. The standard filing deadline is April 30, and Comal Appraisal District says disabled veteran exemption applicants can late-file no later than five years after the delinquency date when eligible. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Which disabled veteran exemption form should Texas buyers use in 2026?
content_sections.p: The first move is matching your benefit to the right exemption. Texas does not have one single disabled veteran exemption path for every situation. The Comptroller explains that Tax Code Section 11.22 is the disabled veteran exemption for a veteran of the U.S. armed services who is classified as disabled by the VA or the applicable branch of service, is a Texas resident, and owns qualifying property. That exemption can apply to any one property the disabled veteran owns, which is different from the disabled person exemption that applies only to a residence homestead. For many veterans with a VA disability rating below 100%, the application to know is Form 50-135, Disabled Veteran's or Survivor's Exemption Application. That is the form tied to the Section 11.22 disabled veteran exemption. The exemption amount is based on the disability rating, so a current VA award letter matters. If you are relocating to New Braunfels, Schertz, Cibolo, Seguin, or another JBSA-connected corridor, this should be part of your purchase planning before you assume a monthly payment is final. A 100% disabled veteran residence homestead exemption is a different lane. The Comptroller says Tax Code Section 11.131 exempts the total appraised value of the residence homestead for Texas veterans awarded 100% compensation from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs due to a 100% disability rating or individual unemployability. That one is tied to the residence homestead, so the property has to be your qualifying homestead. If you want the broader context before choosing a form, my prior guide on disabled veteran tax exemption Texas steps is a useful companion. Here is the part I walk military clients through carefully: the exemption can change the carrying cost conversation, but it does not replace lender qualification, closing-cost planning, HOA review, insurance quotes, or flood-zone checks. A house that looks comfortable after a tax exemption may still have a high monthly payment if insurance, MUD taxes, HOA dues, or interest rate assumptions are off. Before you lock onto a price point, verify the actual exemption treatment with the appraisal district and your lender.

content_sections.h: Where do Comal and Guadalupe County veterans file the application?
content_sections.p: You file with the appraisal district for the county where the property sits. That matters in New Braunfels because the city crosses county lines. A home west of I-35, near many established New Braunfels and Gruene-area addresses, is often in Comal County. Some eastern New Braunfels addresses around the FM 1101 and Solms side can be in Guadalupe County. The address, legal description, and appraisal district account are what control the filing path, not the city name on the mailing address. For Comal County, Comal Appraisal District says applicants must complete the application and attach a current dated letter from the Veterans Administration showing the disability percentage awarded. The district also points taxpayers to its forms page for the Homestead Exemption, including the homestead for 100% disabled veteran exemptions, and the Disabled Veteran's Exemption for disabled veterans with a 10% to 90% rating. Comal's page lists filing methods by mail, email in PDF format, or drop-off at the New Braunfels office, so a buyer does not have to guess where the paperwork goes. For Guadalupe County, Guadalupe Appraisal District lists an online application tool for homestead, disabled veteran, and surviving spouse exemptions, with printable forms still available. That is especially relevant for buyers looking at Schertz, Cibolo, Seguin, Marion, or eastern New Braunfels. If you are comparing homes across county lines, do not assume the same filing portal, same account lookup process, or same processing pace applies. What I see in the New Braunfels market is that relocating buyers often treat the county line like a map detail. It is not. It can affect who appraises the property, where you file the exemption, what taxing units appear on the bill, and how quickly you can confirm your estimated taxes. I do not want a veteran household finding that out after closing when the first escrow analysis shows up. If you are still sorting out where to buy, start with the New Braunfels relocation guide and build the county filing question into your short list.

content_sections.h: What deadlines and documents should veterans prepare before closing?
content_sections.p: The standard Texas exemption deadline is April 30 for the tax year requested. The Comptroller says disabled veterans applying under Tax Code Section 11.22 may late-file up to five years after the delinquency date for taxes on the property. Comal Appraisal District states the same late-filing window for disabled veterans on its exemptions page. That late-filing option is helpful, but it is not a reason to drift. File early when you can, because tax estimates, escrow setup, and personal budgeting are cleaner when the appraisal district has what it needs. The documents usually start with a completed application, a current VA disability award letter showing the disability percentage, and identity or residence documentation required by the form and appraisal district. For a residence homestead exemption, appraisal districts commonly compare the property address to the address on a Texas driver's license or state-issued ID. If your PCS timeline means your ID, closing date, move-in date, and homestead status do not line up neatly, ask the appraisal district what it will accept before you submit a half-ready package. This is also where buyers need to separate tax exemption strategy from loan strategy. Your lender may qualify you using one tax estimate, the seller's current tax bill may reflect a different exemption, and your future bill may change after ownership and appraisal updates. The exemption can help, but it is not the only number in the payment. If you are still building your buying budget, talk with a VA-experienced lender before you count on any single estimate. I tell clients to make a simple file before they shop hard: VA award letter, projected duty or retirement timeline, preferred counties, lender estimate, insurance quotes, and exemption questions. That turns the exemption conversation from a vague promise into a checklist. It also helps when we compare a resale in New Braunfels with new construction in Schertz or Cibolo, because the monthly cost picture can change more than the list price suggests. For related financing context, my Texas VLB home loan guide explains another veteran-specific tool that may belong in the same planning conversation.

content_sections.h: How should a disabled veteran use the exemption when choosing a New Braunfels-area home?
content_sections.p: Use the exemption as part of a complete homebuying plan, not as the whole plan. A 100% disabled veteran residence homestead exemption can be powerful because the Comptroller describes the exemption as the total appraised value of the qualifying residence homestead. But your payment may still include principal, interest, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, possible MUD or PID assessments, and other costs tied to the specific property. The right question is not just, "What will the exemption save me?" It is, "What will this exact home cost me to own month after month?" In Comal and Guadalupe County, two homes at the same purchase price can carry different tax expectations because of taxing units, city limits, school district boundaries as property features, special districts, and new construction assessment timing. That is why I slow this conversation down with VA and PCS buyers. A house near the county line may look similar online, but the tax bill, filing district, commute pattern, and builder concession picture can all be different. If you are planning a JBSA-area move, combine the exemption application with your VA loan timeline. Review your Certificate of Eligibility, lender approval, funding fee treatment, disability award letter, and appraisal district filing plan together. My recent post on VA loan new construction in Texas goes deeper on the builder side, where incentives and tax estimates can create confusion if nobody is translating the numbers. The strongest move is to choose the home with clear eyes. I want you to know the likely payment, filing steps, documents, timing risk, and county process before you are emotionally attached to the house. Then the exemption becomes part of a smart VA + PCS roadmap instead of a surprise after closing. If you want a local read before you pick a target area, Cody Posey Real Estate can compare county filing paths, payment assumptions, and practical next steps for your New Braunfels-area move.

title: Crossvine Cibolo PID Payment Check for 2026 Buyers
excerpt: Crossvine Cibolo PID costs can change a 2026 buyer's payment. Learn what to verify before comparing this neighborhood to nearby options.

faqItems.q: 1) What is a PID assessment in Crossvine Cibolo?
faqItems.a: A PID assessment is a Public Improvement District charge tied to improvements funded for properties inside the district. It is separate from the normal city, county, school district, and other property tax rates. Buyers should ask for the current notice or assessment schedule for the exact home before writing an offer.

faqItems.q: 2) Does a PID assessment count in my mortgage payment?
faqItems.a: Lenders usually treat known recurring assessments as part of the housing-cost picture when they qualify you. That means the PID can affect the monthly payment you are comfortable with, even if the list price looks manageable. Ask your lender to include the assessment in the estimate from the beginning.

faqItems.q: 3) Is Crossvine more expensive than nearby Cibolo neighborhoods?
faqItems.a: It depends on the exact home, price, tax stack, assessment amount, HOA dues, insurance, and any repairs or incentives involved. A Crossvine home can still be the right fit, but you need to compare it against real nearby homes using the full monthly payment. Do not compare only list prices.

faqItems.q: 4) Can a Crossvine PID assessment be paid off at closing?
faqItems.a: Some PID obligations may have payoff information available, but buyers should not assume that without written confirmation. Ask the seller, builder, title company, or district administrator for the current payoff details if they exist. Your purchase decision should work even if the assessment remains part of the recurring cost.

faqItems.q: 5) What should I verify during the option period?
faqItems.a: Use the option period to confirm the PID notice, tax estimate, HOA documents, insurance quote, title commitment, and lender payment calculation. This is also the right time to compare one or two nearby alternatives. If the payment or documents do not match your comfort level, you want to know that before the option period expires.

opening_question: How should 2026 buyers compare Crossvine Cibolo homes with the PID assessment included?
quick_answer: Crossvine Cibolo buyers should compare homes by the full monthly payment, not just the list price, because a Public Improvement District assessment is layered on top of the normal tax bill. Cibolo's posted combined property tax rate as of October 1, 2025 is $1.9299 per $100 of assessed value before any separate PID assessment, HOA dues, insurance, or lender-specific escrow assumptions. The right move is to get the assessment notice, have the lender run the exact address, and compare that payment against one or two nearby non-PID options before the option period ends. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does Crossvine's PID matter when the list price looks right?
content_sections.p: A Crossvine home can look affordable on the search page and still land differently once the tax, assessment, insurance, and HOA numbers are in the lender's worksheet. That is the main reason I want buyers to slow down before they treat two Cibolo homes at the same price as equal. The payment is where the difference shows up. A Public Improvement District, usually shortened to PID, is not the same thing as a normal city or county tax rate. Texas Local Government Code Chapter 372 allows a city or county to create a district to fund public improvements, then recover those costs through assessments charged to the properties that benefit from the improvements. In buyer terms, that means the neighborhood's infrastructure story can become part of your recurring housing cost. Cibolo already has a tax stack buyers need to understand. The city tax page lists the total property tax rate at $1.9299 per $100 as of October 1, 2025, with pieces for the City of Cibolo, Guadalupe County, Schertz-Cibolo-Universal City ISD, and lateral road. A PID assessment is a separate layer to verify on the exact property. If you are comparing Cibolo, Schertz, and New Braunfels corridor homes, start with Cody's broader Hill Country area comparison, then narrow the numbers address by address. Here is the part I see buyers miss: the list price is negotiable, but an existing assessment attached to a property usually is not something you can talk away in the offer. You can ask the seller, builder, title company, and lender to explain it. You can sometimes ask whether there is a payoff option. But if it remains attached after closing, your affordability decision has to include it from the start.

content_sections.h: How do you run a real monthly payment check in Crossvine?
content_sections.p: Start with the exact address or lot, not the model name, subdivision name, or a rough price range. Your lender needs the real property details to estimate escrow correctly, and your title company can help identify recorded assessment information during the contract process. If the home is new construction, ask the builder for the current PID disclosure and any assessment schedule before you spend emotional energy on finishes, incentives, or upgrade packages. The cleanest payment check has four pieces: principal and interest from your lender, taxes based on the current jurisdiction stack, insurance based on current quotes, and special assessments or HOA dues tied to the address. If a lender quotes the payment without the PID assessment, the number can be too light for a real decision. That is why I like side-by-side lender scenarios: one for the Crossvine home with the known PID assumption and one for a nearby non-PID option at a similar price. This is also where rate sensitivity matters. When interest rates are already stretching the budget, an extra recurring assessment can change the loan amount that feels comfortable. Cody has a separate guide on the interest rate impact New Braunfels buyers face in 2026, and the same payment logic applies in Cibolo. A lower list price is not automatically the lower-stress buy if the all-in monthly number is higher than expected. Use the Texas option period as your verification window. During that time, you can ask for the assessment notice, confirm the tax estimate, review HOA documents, compare insurance quotes, and make sure your lender is underwriting the payment the same way you are. This is not just paperwork. It is the difference between choosing Crossvine on purpose and discovering after contract that the monthly number is tighter than you thought.

content_sections.h: When can Crossvine still make sense for a payment-conscious buyer?
content_sections.p: A PID does not automatically make a neighborhood a bad fit. That kind of blanket thinking is how buyers miss homes that may still line up with their needs, commute, layout, age of construction, and maintenance expectations. The better question is whether the home's total monthly cost earns its place against the alternatives you can actually buy. Crossvine can still make sense when the home gives you enough value in the categories that matter to you: newer construction, floor plan, community amenities, location near the I-35 and FM 1103 corridor, or a price point that still works after the full assessment stack is included. It can also make sense if nearby homes without a PID need major repairs, have a less workable layout, or carry insurance and maintenance costs that close the gap. The point is not to avoid the PID. The point is to measure it honestly. What I tell buyers in this part of Cibolo is pretty direct: do not compare Crossvine to a vague idea of a cheaper neighborhood. Compare it to two or three real addresses you would actually buy this month. If the Crossvine payment is higher but the home reduces other costs or solves location needs, you may decide the tradeoff is worth it. If the payment is higher and the home does not beat the alternatives, that is useful information too. For buyers looking at new construction and newer resale options around Cibolo, it also helps to understand how builder pricing and resale pricing interact. Cody's guide to new construction vs resale in Cibolo is a good companion to this payment conversation because incentives can make the front-end price feel attractive while taxes, assessments, and long-term costs still need a separate review.

content_sections.h: What documents should buyers ask for before writing an offer?
content_sections.p: Ask for the PID notice or assessment disclosure. Texas Property Code rules require notice tied to improvement district obligations, and the practical buyer takeaway is simple: do not rely on a verbal summary when a written notice should exist. You want the current annual amount, whether the assessment is billed through the tax office or another administrator, and whether any payoff option exists. Ask for the latest tax estimate by exact address. Cibolo's posted tax table is a helpful starting point, but the real number comes from the property's assessed value, exemptions, district lines, and any special assessment attached to that parcel. If you are relocating from another Texas market or from out of state, do not assume the tax pattern works like your current city. Cibolo, Schertz, New Braunfels, and unincorporated Hill Country addresses can have very different stacks. Ask the lender to underwrite the full recurring cost. A payment estimate that leaves out the assessment is not a decision tool. Have the lender include principal, interest, property taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and the PID assumption, then ask what purchase price still fits your target payment. If you need help sequencing the process before touring, Cody's home buying process guide lays out the steps buyers should have organized before an offer gets serious. Ask how the PID may affect resale conversations later. Future buyers will ask the same questions you are asking now. That does not mean the home will be hard to sell, and there are no guarantees either way. It means the next buyer will also care about the monthly payment. If you buy in Crossvine, keep your assessment documents organized so a future listing can explain the numbers clearly instead of letting uncertainty become an objection.

faqItems.q: 1) Is Garden Ridge a good place to retire near New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Garden Ridge can be a strong retirement fit for buyers who want a smaller Comal County community, larger-lot feel, and access toward New Braunfels and San Antonio. The key is affordability and daily convenience. Review taxes, utilities, maintenance, and drive patterns before deciding it fits your retirement plan.

faqItems.q: 2) Are Garden Ridge homes expensive compared with nearby areas?
faqItems.a: Many Garden Ridge homes price above entry-level New Braunfels or Schertz options because lot size, location, and property type can push values higher. One market snapshot listed a median home value of $859,195. Your exact budget should be based on active listings, property taxes, insurance, condition, and the total monthly cost.

faqItems.q: 3) What property tax questions should retired buyers ask in Garden Ridge?
faqItems.a: Ask for the current tax bill, assessed value, exemptions, tax jurisdictions, and whether the seller has exemptions that may not transfer to you. Texas property taxes can be a major retirement budget item. You should also ask the appraisal district or a tax professional about homestead and age-based exemptions that may apply to your situation.

faqItems.q: 4) What should I inspect closely before buying in Garden Ridge?
faqItems.a: Inspect the roof, foundation, drainage, trees, irrigation, utilities, septic or well systems if present, and any improvements that affect long-term maintenance. For retirement moves, also study stairs, bathroom layout, driveway slope, garage access, and how easy the home will be to live in over time.

faqItems.q: 5) Should I compare Garden Ridge with New Braunfels before buying?
faqItems.a: Yes. Garden Ridge, New Braunfels, Bulverde, Schertz, Cibolo, and Canyon Lake can all solve different retirement goals. Compare monthly cost, drive time, property size, amenities, maintenance, and resale considerations before choosing one area.

opening_question: Is moving to Garden Ridge after retirement a smart Hill Country move?

content_sections.h: What makes Garden Ridge different from a typical New Braunfels retirement search?
content_sections.p: Garden Ridge is not the same kind of search as buying a lock-and-leave home near downtown New Braunfels or choosing a newer subdivision along the IH-35 corridor. It sits in Comal County, has a smaller city feel, and tends to attract buyers who are comparing lot size, privacy, mature trees, and access back toward San Antonio. That can be a strong fit after retirement, but it also means you need to study the full ownership picture instead of treating it like a simple Hill Country lifestyle upgrade. The city points residents to Comal ISD as the local school district, which matters as a property feature even if schools are not your personal driver. For retired buyers, the more relevant questions are usually property type, road access, HOA rules if any, utility setup, floodplain questions, septic or well considerations in surrounding pockets, and how often you expect to drive toward New Braunfels, San Antonio, Schertz, or Cibolo. If you're comparing communities across the region, Cody's Texas Hill Country retirement housing options guide is a useful companion to this Garden Ridge cost check. Here is the part I see buyers miss: Garden Ridge can feel like a peaceful Hill Country move when you tour on a weekday morning, but your real life happens on grocery runs, doctor visits, airport drives, grandkid visits, volunteer commitments, and dinner plans. I want clients to test those routes before they write an offer. A beautiful lot is still a daily decision, and retirement makes convenience more important, not less.

content_sections.h: How should retirees think about Garden Ridge home prices and property taxes?
content_sections.p: Start with the monthly number, not the list price. Ownwell's Garden Ridge tax trend page listed a $859,195 median home value and a $6,636 median annual property tax bill. That does not mean every buyer will pay those numbers, and tax-assessed value can differ from market value, but it does tell you something important: Garden Ridge is often a premium-property conversation, not just a downsize conversation. Texas has no state income tax, but property taxes are a major part of the housing budget. Retired buyers should look at the current tax bill, the tax-assessed value, the exemptions already on the property, the city and county rates, and what may change after purchase. If you're relocating from another state, do not compare only mortgage payments. Compare total monthly housing cost after taxes, insurance, HOA dues, utilities, maintenance, and any improvements you expect in the first two years. This is where a buyer plan matters. A home that looks comfortable at the contract price can feel different after you factor in roof age, tree maintenance, irrigation limits, longer driveway upkeep, or the cost of making a house easier to live in long term. You can test payment ranges with a lender or calculator, but the smarter move is to pair the payment with a property-specific cost review before you choose a neighborhood. If you are selling another property before buying in Garden Ridge, also map your net proceeds before you shop. Some retirees think they are downsizing because the next home has fewer bedrooms, but in Garden Ridge the lot, location, and condition can make the purchase price feel more like a lifestyle trade than a budget reduction. Cody's Austin to Hill Country cost check covers that same trap for buyers leaving higher-cost markets.

content_sections.h: What lifestyle tradeoffs should you compare before choosing Garden Ridge?
content_sections.p: Garden Ridge works best when the property itself is the point. Buyers are often looking for more breathing room, mature landscaping, a less subdivision-heavy feel, and a location that keeps San Antonio access realistic. Paul Davis Park, listed by the city at 20685 Grass Creek, is one local amenity to know, but the bigger question is how your week actually works. A retired buyer who wants restaurant variety, medical access, church, errands, and airport routes close by may evaluate the same home differently than someone who wants maximum lot privacy. Water and landscaping deserve attention too. In this part of Comal County, outdoor space is part of the appeal, but it is also part of the maintenance budget. Ask how irrigation is handled, what watering restrictions may apply, what trees need care, and whether the current landscape is practical for the way you want to live. A pretty yard can become an expensive weekend project if it was designed for a different season of life. The local-only thing I tell clients is this: don't buy Garden Ridge for the idea of the Hill Country. Buy it because the actual address solves your daily life. Some properties feel tucked away but are still practical. Others feel tucked away because every errand becomes a plan. I like to put the map, the tax bill, and the inspection concerns on the same page before we talk about whether the home feels right. Also compare Garden Ridge with nearby alternatives. New Braunfels may put you closer to river, restaurant, and medical routines. Bulverde may widen the Hill Country search. Schertz or Cibolo may make sense if access toward Randolph or northeast San Antonio matters. Canyon Lake can offer a different lifestyle entirely, especially if water, view, or acreage questions are driving the move. For buyers weighing more land, Cody's Hill Country acreage buying checklist is worth reviewing before you assume bigger is better.

content_sections.h: What should your Garden Ridge retirement buying plan include?
content_sections.p: Your plan should start with a budget range that includes taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, and improvement reserves. Then it should narrow the search by property style: one-story living, manageable yard size, driveway grade, garage setup, storage, guest space, and whether the floor plan still works if mobility needs change later. Those details do not sound as exciting as the view from the back porch, but they often determine whether the home still fits five years from now. Next, compare timing. If you need to sell before buying, you may need a contingency strategy, bridge option, temporary housing plan, or tighter listing timeline. If you are paying cash, you still need to protect yourself with inspection, title, survey, and insurance review. If you are financing, verify whether retirement income, Social Security, investment distributions, or pension income will be documented the way your lender needs. A lender can answer the approval side, while Cody can help you compare how different properties behave in the local market. Finally, decide what you will not compromise on. For many retirement moves, the real non-negotiables are not granite counters or fresh paint. They are drive time, monthly cost, floor plan comfort, tax exposure, and the ability to maintain the property without turning retirement into a second job. Cody's New Braunfels relocation guide can help you compare the broader area before you commit to one city. The strongest Garden Ridge purchases happen when the buyer slows down just enough to separate emotion from fit. You can still love the home. You just need the numbers, route, condition, and long-term livability to agree with that feeling.

faqItems.a: Yes, many public data sources show a slower pace than the fastest years of the market. Zillow reported homes going pending in around 61 days, Realtor.com showed a median time on market around 103 days, and Redfin's average days on market snapshot was higher. The exact number varies by data source, but the pattern is clear: buyers have more time to compare.

faqItems.q: 3) Does a higher median sale price mean sellers can price aggressively?
faqItems.a: Not necessarily. A stable or higher median sale price does not erase buyer resistance, builder competition, condition issues, or payment pressure. Sellers still need a comp-backed list price and a plan for how to respond if traffic or feedback is weaker than expected.

faqItems.q: 4) Is Comal County a buyer's market or seller's market in 2026?
faqItems.a: It depends on the price band and property type. The market is more balanced than the fastest pandemic-era conditions, but well-priced homes can still draw serious attention. Buyers should compare value carefully, and sellers should price with current competition, not old assumptions.

faqItems.q: 5) How should I use Comal County market data before making a move?
faqItems.a: Use county-wide data to understand the big picture, then get specific. Compare active listings, pending activity, recent sales, taxes, condition, and competing builder inventory in your exact segment. That is the difference between reading the market and making a good decision inside it.

opening_question: What does the Comal County median sale price mean for New Braunfels buyers and sellers in 2026?
quick_answer: The Comal County median sale price is running in the mid-$400Ks in 2026, with public snapshots ranging from about $437,027 in Zillow home value data to $464,000 in Redfin's March closed-sale snapshot. The more important signal is pace: Zillow shows homes going pending in about 61 days, while Realtor.com shows a median market time around 103 days and Redfin's average days on market is longer. For buyers, that means more room to compare homes carefully. For sellers, it means the first price still matters, because stale listings get negotiated harder. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does the Comal County median sale price look stronger than the market feels?
content_sections.p: The short answer is that median sale price and market speed are telling two different stories. A mid-$400Ks median can make the market sound strong on the surface, but longer days on market tell you buyers are taking more time, comparing more homes, and pushing back when a property feels overpriced. That is the tension shaping New Braunfels and nearby Comal County decisions in 2026. Redfin's Comal County snapshot showed a median sale price near $464,000 for March 2026, while Zillow's home value page showed an average home value around $437,027 and homes going pending in about 61 days. Realtor.com showed a lower median listing price around $357,000 with a median time on market around 103 days. Those numbers are not identical because each source measures a different slice of the market: closed sales, estimated values, active listings, and listing timelines do not always line up. That is why I do not coach clients to treat one headline number as the market. I use it as a starting point, then narrow the view to the specific property type, price band, neighborhood, condition, and competition. A home near downtown New Braunfels, a newer build along the IH-35 corridor, a larger Hill Country lot, and a property near Canyon Lake can all sit inside the same county-wide report while behaving very differently. For a seller, the practical read is this: your home can be in a county where prices look stable and still need a sharper launch strategy. For a buyer, it means the county-wide median should help you understand the budget range, but it should not decide what a fair offer looks like. If you are trying to connect price, tax load, payment, and timing, compare that number against homes that actually match your search.

content_sections.h: What should New Braunfels sellers do with longer days on market?
content_sections.p: Longer market time does not mean sellers are out of options. It means the market is less forgiving of wish pricing. When a home starts too high, buyers often wait, save it, compare it to new builder inventory, and come back later with a lower number. That is a different seller experience than the fast-moving market many people still remember from a few years ago. The part I see sellers miss in New Braunfels is builder competition. A resale home may have better location, mature landscaping, upgraded finishes, or a larger lot, but the buyer is still comparing it against builder incentives, rate buydowns, closing cost help, and brand-new finishes. If your list price ignores that comparison, the market will make the adjustment for you. I would rather price and position the home with that pressure in mind before the listing gets stale. This is where median sale price can be useful, but only after it is filtered. If the county median is in the mid-$400Ks, that does not automatically make a $475K listing competitive. You still have to ask: what else can a buyer get at that payment, what condition objections will show up during showings, how many similar homes are active, and how much seller concession pressure is already showing in the price band? A good pre-listing plan should include a value range, likely appraisal conversation, buyer objection list, showing-readiness plan, and negotiation strategy. If seller math is part of the decision, run the high-level number before you choose a list price, then tighten it with neighborhood-level comps. I covered this same pricing pressure in Builder Competition: Sell in Comal County in 2026, and it is still one of the biggest reasons two similar listings can get very different results.

content_sections.h: How should buyers read the 2026 Comal County market?
content_sections.p: Buyers should not hear "longer days on market" and assume every seller is desperate. Some listings are still priced well, prepared well, and positioned well. Others are sitting because the seller is anchored to last year's expectation, the condition does not match the asking price, or the home is competing directly with new construction incentives. The opportunity is in knowing which situation you are looking at. A home that has been listed for 70, 90, or 120 days deserves a closer read, not an automatic low offer. You want to know whether there have been price reductions, whether the seller already adjusted once, what the inspection risk looks like, whether taxes or HOA costs change the payment, and whether the property is in a floodplain, MUD, PID, or other cost structure that needs extra attention. In Comal County, those details can change the real monthly cost more than the list price alone suggests. I tell buyers relocating from Austin or San Antonio that New Braunfels is not one market. The IH-35 side, Gruene, Veramendi, Vintage Oaks, River Chase, Canyon Lake edges, and rural Comal County all have different inventory and buyer expectations. The mistake is assuming a county median tells you whether a specific house is a deal. It tells you the broad temperature. The comp set tells you whether to move, negotiate, or wait. If you are buying in the next 30 to 180 days, pair the county-wide data with a tighter buying plan and compare active listings against recent sales. For offer strategy, this related guide on competitive offers in New Braunfels explains how to stay credible without overpaying in a slower market.

content_sections.h: What is the real market read for Comal County right now?
content_sections.p: The real read is balance with friction. Prices have not collapsed in the public data, but buyers have more time and more choices than they had during the fastest part of the market. That means sellers need to earn attention with condition, presentation, and price. Buyers need to use the extra time wisely instead of assuming every listing has the same negotiation room. For sellers, the first two weeks still matter because they tell you whether the market agrees with the price. If showings are light, saves are low, or feedback keeps pointing to price, waiting usually does not make the home feel fresher. You need a plan before the listing launches, including when you would adjust, what concessions you would consider, and where your true walk-away number sits after closing costs and payoff. For buyers, the slower pace should create more discipline, not less. You can compare value, verify taxes, ask better inspection questions, and avoid rushing into a property that does not fit. But if a home is priced right in a tight submarket, the correct response may still be a clean, serious offer. Days on market gives context. It does not replace judgment. The only Cody would say this moment is simple: in New Braunfels, the buyer's objection is often not the house. It is the payment after taxes, insurance, HOA, MUD or PID, and any builder alternative down the road. If a seller can answer that comparison before the buyer asks it, the listing is stronger. If a buyer understands it before writing the offer, the negotiation is cleaner. That is the work behind a useful market read, and it is why the county median should lead to a local plan, not a quick conclusion. For broader context, see the recent Comal County housing inventory update.

title: River vs Lake Property: Hill Country 2026 Buyer Guide
excerpt: River vs lake property in the Texas Hill Country comes down to water use, access, flood risk, carrying cost, and resale expectations in 2026.

faqItems.q: 1) Is river property or lake property better in the Texas Hill Country?
faqItems.a: Neither is automatically better. River property usually fits buyers who want moving water, shade, kayaking, tubing, and a more natural setting. Lake property usually fits buyers who want boating, open views, marinas, and a more predictable weekend-water routine. The better choice depends on how you will use the property and what risk, maintenance, and cost you are willing to carry.

faqItems.q: 2) What should I check before buying riverfront property near New Braunfels?
faqItems.a: Verify whether the property has direct frontage, shared access, or nearby public access. Review floodplain status, insurance quotes, drainage, prior water intrusion disclosures, bank stability, septic placement, and road access during heavy rain. These details should be reviewed during the Texas option period before your earnest money is fully at risk.

faqItems.q: 3) Does Canyon Lake water level affect real estate value?
faqItems.a: Yes, water level can affect buyer perception, usability, photos, dock access, and resale expectations. A high-water snapshot can help a listing look strong, but buyers should also study drought conditions and longer-term usability. The durable value is not just whether the lake looks full today. It is whether the property still works when conditions change.

faqItems.q: 4) Are river and lake homes harder to insure in the Hill Country?
faqItems.a: They can be, depending on the property. Flood zone status, elevation, prior claims, proximity to water, construction details, and lender requirements can all affect insurance. Buyers should get insurance quotes early instead of waiting until late in the contract. A local agent can help flag which questions to ask, but the quote should come from an insurance professional.

faqItems.q: 5) Can I use a Hill Country river or lake home as a short-term rental?
faqItems.a: Possibly, but do not assume it will be allowed or profitable. Check city rules, county context, HOA restrictions, deed restrictions, parking limits, occupancy rules, lender requirements, and insurance before building rental income into your offer. A property can be attractive for personal use and still be a poor fit for short-term rental plans.

opening_question: Should you buy river property or lake property in the Texas Hill Country in 2026?
quick_answer: River property usually fits buyers who want shade, moving water, tubing access, kayaking, and a more natural Hill Country setting. Lake property usually fits buyers who want boating, open-water views, marinas, dock potential, and a more predictable weekend-water routine. The 2026 buyer question is not just which view looks better. It is how the property handles access, floodplain, water-level swings, insurance, septic, HOA rules, and resale demand. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What is the real difference between river and lake property?
content_sections.p: The biggest difference is how you will actually use the water. River property in the New Braunfels and Hill Country area is usually about movement: current, shade trees, limestone banks, swimming holes, tubing, fishing, kayaking, and a setting that can feel tucked into the land. Lake property is usually about open water: boating, longer views, marinas, neighborhood access points, dock questions, and a more classic lake-weekend pattern. That sounds simple until you start comparing real listings. A riverfront home on the Guadalupe River near New Braunfels, Sattler, or Canyon Lake can be very different from a home that is only river-adjacent or has community river access. A Canyon Lake property can be true waterfront, lake-view, lake-access, or simply near the lake. Those labels matter because the price, financing conversation, insurance review, and resale story can change fast. For buyers moving in the next 30 to 180 days, I would not start with the prettiest photo. I would start with the use case. If your weekends revolve around a boat, trailer storage, ramps, and open-water time, lake property deserves a hard look. If you picture morning coffee under cypress trees, walking down to moving water, and being close to the river culture around Gruene or the Guadalupe corridor, river property may fit better. The part relocating buyers from Austin or out of state often miss is that "near water" is not the same as usable water. I have seen buyers fall for a gorgeous listing photo, then realize the slope is steep, the access is awkward, the floodplain needs a deeper insurance review, or the water feature is seasonal in a way they did not understand. That is why I like to compare lifestyle, access, and risk before we compare finishes. For a wider area comparison, Cody's guide to moving to the Texas Hill Country from Austin is a helpful next layer.

content_sections.h: How should buyers compare access, flood risk, and water levels?
content_sections.p: Access is the first filter. With river property, confirm whether the deed includes direct frontage, whether access is shared, whether there are easements, and whether the bank is realistically usable. With lake property, confirm whether the home is waterfront, lake-view, lake-access, or just close to the lake. Then ask practical questions: where is the nearest ramp, what does the HOA allow, what are the parking rules, and how far is the actual usable water from the house? Flood risk is the second filter, especially along the Guadalupe River, Comal River, Cibolo Creek, and low-water crossings throughout the Hill Country. A property can look calm on a normal day and still require serious review during the option period. Buyers should check FEMA flood maps, elevation certificates when available, drainage, prior water intrusion disclosures, insurance quotes, and local road access during heavy rain. This is not about fear. It is about knowing what you are buying before your option period clock runs out. Lake-level behavior is different from river behavior. Canyon Lake is a managed reservoir with public recreation, water-supply, and flood-risk-management roles. In July 2026, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said Canyon Lake was holding water to reduce downstream flood risk and expected the reservoir to reach its conservation pool for the first time in more than four and a half years. Water Data for Texas showed Canyon Lake near 98% full on July 19, 2026, after being much lower earlier that month. That one stat is useful, but it should not be the whole decision. A buyer should underwrite a lake property by normal-year usability, not one high-water snapshot. Ask what the view looked like during drought, how long the walk to water became, whether the dock was usable, and how a future buyer might react if levels are lower when you sell. Cody's Canyon Lake water-level guide goes deeper on that exact issue, and the Hill Country flood-zone questions buyers should ask are worth reviewing before you write an offer.

content_sections.h: Which property type usually carries more hidden cost?
content_sections.p:
Neither river nor lake property is automatically more expensive to own. The carrying cost depends on the exact home, location, improvements, insurance requirements, HOA structure, utility setup, and how the property is used. A river property may require more attention to flood insurance, bank stability, erosion, septic placement, access steps, retaining walls, and drainage. A lake property may bring dock, boat storage, ramp access, HOA, marina, shoreline, and water-level usability questions.

Insurance deserves early attention. Do not wait until a week before closing to learn that a property needs flood coverage, has a higher premium than expected, or requires more documentation. The same goes for septic and well questions in unincorporated Hill Country areas. Many buyers love the extra space and scenery outside city limits, but the due diligence is different from buying a subdivision home in New Braunfels. If the property is outside a city utility footprint, verify water source, septic records, maintenance history, and inspection options before the option period expires.

Short-term rental assumptions also need to be handled carefully. Some buyers look at river and lake property and immediately think about offsetting costs with rentals. That may or may not work depending on city rules, county context, deed restrictions, HOA rules, lender requirements, insurance, parking, occupancy limits, and property management. Do not build your offer price around rental income unless you have verified the rules and numbers with the right professionals.

What I tell clients is direct: the water view gets your attention, but the paperwork tells you whether the property fits. You want the survey, seller disclosure, floodplain review, insurance quote, utility details, HOA documents, septic records, and access rights in front of you early. A pretty property can still be a bad fit if the total monthly cost, restrictions, or future resale story do not match your plan.

content_sections.h: Which choice is stronger for resale in the Hill Country?
content_sections.p: Resale strength depends on buyer depth. Lake property can attract buyers who want boating, views, water recreation, and a recognizable Canyon Lake lifestyle. River property can attract buyers who want Hill Country character, moving water, trees, and proximity to places like Gruene, New Braunfels, Sattler, and the Guadalupe corridor. Both can have strong appeal, but both can narrow the buyer pool if access is awkward, cost is high, restrictions are tight, or risk feels hard to understand. A clean resale story matters. A buyer should be able to understand what the property offers in one or two sentences: true river frontage with usable bank access, lake-view home with neighborhood ramp access, Canyon Lake waterfront with dock questions to verify, or Hill Country home near the river without direct access. If the listing language needs a paragraph of qualifiers, the next buyer may hesitate too. This is where local positioning matters. A river home with excellent access but older finishes may beat a more polished home with poor access. A lake-view home with strong outdoor living and clear HOA rules may beat a property that technically sits closer to the water but has confusing restrictions. A lower-maintenance home near Canyon Lake may be a better fit than a dramatic waterfront lot if you do not want ongoing outdoor maintenance. For buyers comparing Hill Country areas, I like to map three lanes: how you want to use the water, what risk and maintenance you are willing to carry, and what a future buyer will understand quickly. That exercise turns a lifestyle dream into a real estate decision. If you are still choosing between New Braunfels, Canyon Lake, Bulverde, Spring Branch, or nearby Hill Country pockets, start with the broader Hill Country area comparison before you lock onto one water feature.

title: PCS to Cibolo From California: VA Loan Timeline Guide
excerpt: PCS to Cibolo from California with a VA loan usually works best when you build the timeline around orders, lender prep, appraisal, and commute reality.

faqItems.q: 1) Can I use a VA loan when I PCS from California to Cibolo?
faqItems.a: Yes, eligible service members and Veterans can use a VA loan for a primary residence in Cibolo if the buyer, property, and loan file meet VA and lender requirements. You should confirm your Certificate of Eligibility, occupancy timing, income documentation, and entitlement with your lender before making offers.

faqItems.q: 2) How long should I plan for a VA closing in Cibolo?
faqItems.a: A practical planning range is often 30 to 45 days from contract to closing when the buyer file is clean and the property does not create appraisal or repair issues. Faster closings can happen, but PCS buyers should avoid building the whole move around a best-case calendar.

faqItems.q: 3) Do VA loans require a down payment in Texas?
faqItems.a: Many VA buyers can buy with no down payment, depending on eligibility, entitlement, lender approval, and property fit. No down payment does not mean no cash needed, because closing costs, inspections, option fee, earnest money, insurance, and prepaid items still have to be planned.

faqItems.q: 4) What can slow down a VA loan during a PCS move?
faqItems.a: Common delays include missing income documents, unclear PCS orders, appraisal scheduling, repairs tied to VA minimum property requirements, insurance timing, title issues, or payment estimates that were not fully reviewed upfront. A coordinated lender and agent plan reduces surprises.

faqItems.q: 5) Is Cibolo a good fit for a JBSA PCS buyer?
faqItems.a: Cibolo can be a practical fit for some JBSA buyers because of its northeast San Antonio location, access to Schertz and Randolph-area routes, and mix of resale and newer homes. The right answer depends on your assigned installation, commute pattern, payment target, tax picture, and preferred property type.

opening_question: How long does a PCS move from California to Cibolo take with a VA loan?
quick_answer: A PCS move from California to Cibolo with a VA loan usually needs a practical 30 to 45 days from contract to closing once your file is clean, with extra planning time before you write an offer. The fastest timelines happen when your PCS orders, Certificate of Eligibility, lender pre-approval, BAH picture, and document file are ready before the right home appears. Cibolo is especially relevant for JBSA-Randolph and northeast San Antonio access, so your housing timeline should also account for commute testing, appraisal timing, and any VA minimum property requirement questions. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: What should you do before you start house hunting in Cibolo?
content_sections.p:
Before you look seriously at homes in Cibolo, get your PCS order picture, Certificate of Eligibility, lender pre-approval, and cash-to-close estimate lined up. VA loans can be a strong fit for military buyers, but the timeline gets tight when the buyer starts shopping before the lender has reviewed income, service status, entitlement, debts, and projected payment comfort. That matters even more when you're moving from California because your current housing costs, move-out timing, travel dates, and household goods schedule can all collide with the Texas contract calendar.

The VA explains that the funding fee can usually be financed or paid in cash, and that some Veterans are exempt, including certain Veterans receiving service-connected disability compensation. That one detail can change your cash-to-close and monthly payment estimate, so you want the lender to verify it early instead of treating it like a closing-week surprise. If you're comparing buying power before you arrive, use a mortgage calculator as a rough planning tool, then have a VA-experienced lender tighten the estimate.

Cibolo buyers also need to match the loan plan to the local market, not just to the pre-approval letter. Some homes are resale, some are newer construction, and some areas include PID, MUD, HOA, or tax-rate details that change the monthly number. If you are comparing Cibolo, Schertz, New Braunfels, and nearby Guadalupe County options, a relocation plan is the better starting point than a generic home search because the move is really a timeline problem first.

What I see with PCS buyers is that the house is rarely the only pressure point. The real pressure comes from trying to solve orders, lender paperwork, inspection timing, appraisal timing, shipment dates, temporary lodging, and base commute assumptions all at the same time. I walk clients through the timing first, then the homes, because the right house at the wrong contract pace can still create a mess.

content_sections.h: How does the VA loan timeline usually move after contract?
content_sections.p: Once you're under contract, the timeline typically runs through earnest money and option period delivery, inspection, repair negotiations if needed, lender underwriting, title work, VA appraisal, final approval, closing disclosure, and signing. In Texas, the title company handles the closing process, and the option period gives the buyer a negotiated window to inspect and decide whether to move forward. For a PCS buyer, that option period is where you need the most discipline because you may be reviewing inspection results from another state. A realistic contract-to-close target is often 30 to 45 days when the file is clean and the property does not create appraisal or condition issues. Some loans can close faster, but I do not like building a PCS plan around best-case timing. Your safer plan is to assume underwriting will ask for updated documents, the appraiser may need a few days, and any repair item tied to VA minimum property requirements can add friction. The VA loan does not mean the home has to be perfect. It does mean the property has to meet VA standards for safety, soundness, and sanitation, and the appraisal process matters. If you're already comparing property types, review VA loan inspection requirements in Texas so you understand the difference between a general home inspection and the VA appraisal. Those are related, but they are not the same thing. Seller-side expectations matter too. Some listing agents understand VA financing well, and some still carry outdated assumptions. That is where offer structure can help. Clean timelines, clear lender communication, realistic repair expectations, and a strong local agent-to-agent conversation can keep a VA offer from being treated like a question mark.

content_sections.h: What makes Cibolo different for a California PCS buyer?
content_sections.p: Cibolo is not just a cheaper substitute for San Antonio or New Braunfels. It sits in a practical northeast-corridor lane near Schertz, Randolph, IH-35, FM 1103, and the broader JBSA orbit. That can make it attractive for military households who want suburban inventory, newer homes, and access to both San Antonio and New Braunfels without committing to a more rural Hill Country commute. The part buyers relocating from California often miss is that a map can make everything look closer than it feels at 7:15 in the morning. Cibolo, Schertz, Garden Ridge, New Braunfels, and northeast San Antonio all look manageable online, but the daily pattern changes depending on which gate, which shift, which highway, and which side of town your life actually uses. I do not call one area better than another. I help you compare the actual tradeoffs: commute routes, property taxes, house age, new-construction incentives, resale competition, HOA or PID costs, and how the payment feels after Texas insurance and taxes are included. For Cibolo specifically, new construction and master-planned communities can create a different decision than an older resale. A builder may offer incentives, but the monthly cost can still move if taxes, assessments, HOA dues, rate buydowns, and closing-cost credits are not compared correctly. If Crossvine or nearby new-construction options are on your list, the Crossvine Cibolo PID payment guide is worth reading before you decide that the lowest advertised payment is the cleanest option. Fair housing rules matter in this conversation, so the right comparison is never about who lives where or which area is supposedly "best." The useful comparison is property-based and lifestyle-based: home age, lot size, commute path, tax picture, nearby services, construction type, and what the home needs before it can close with VA financing.

content_sections.h: How should you sequence the move from California to closing day?
content_sections.p: The cleanest sequence starts before you travel. First, gather orders if available, LES, W-2s, bank statements, debt information, COE access, VA disability documentation if relevant, and any current housing obligation details. Then talk with a VA-experienced lender and get a pre-approval that reflects your actual move, not a generic online estimate. Cody Posey Real Estate can also connect you with lender options that understand VA and PCS timing, without turning that into a one-size-fits-all recommendation. Next, narrow the geography before you narrow the house. Decide whether the daily pattern points you toward Cibolo, Schertz, New Braunfels, or another northeast San Antonio option. You can browse homes online, but your best shortlist should be filtered by payment, commute, property condition, tax profile, and contract risk. For VA buyers, that means the prettiest listing photo is not enough. Once the home is selected, move quickly but not carelessly. Your offer should account for option period length, inspection availability, appraisal timing, closing date, seller expectations, and whether any concessions are being requested. VA rules allow sellers to pay certain costs, and the VA notes that some seller concessions are capped at 4% of the loan amount, though not every seller-paid cost falls inside that cap. That is why your offer should be built with the lender and agent talking before it goes out. The final week should not be when you discover a missing document, unresolved condition issue, or payment mismatch. By then, you want title, lender, insurance, final walk-through, utilities, and travel timing coordinated. If you're comparing this topic to a broader JBSA move, the VA loan Schertz PCS guide gives a helpful nearby-market frame.

title: Guadalupe County Homestead Deadline: 2026 Buyer Guide
excerpt: Guadalupe County homestead exemption deadline guidance for 2026 buyers: file with the appraisal district before May 1 after you own and occupy the home.

faqItems.q: 1) What is the Guadalupe County homestead exemption deadline for 2026?
faqItems.a: The general Texas homestead exemption deadline is before May 1 for the tax year, so Guadalupe County buyers should treat April 30, 2026, as the practical filing deadline. File with the Guadalupe Appraisal District after you own and occupy the home as your principal residence.

faqItems.q: 2) Do I file my homestead exemption with the Guadalupe County tax office?
faqItems.a: No. Texas Comptroller guidance says property tax exemption applications are filed with the appraisal district in the county where the property is located. For a Guadalupe County property, that means the Guadalupe Appraisal District, while the tax office handles tax collection.

faqItems.q: 3) Can my lender or title company file the homestead exemption for me?
faqItems.a: You should not assume that. Your title company handles closing documents, and your lender may manage escrow, but the homestead exemption application is filed with the appraisal district. Ask the district directly if you have a documentation or timing question.

faqItems.q: 4) What documentation does Guadalupe Appraisal District require?
faqItems.a: Guadalupe Appraisal District materials say the law requires a copy of your driver's license or state-issued personal identification certificate with the homestead exemption application. Check the current application instructions before filing so the address and documentation are correct.

faqItems.q: 5) How much can the Texas homestead exemption save me?
faqItems.a: The amount depends on your appraised value, tax rates, and which exemptions apply to your property. The Texas Comptroller gives an example where a $300,000 home with a $140,000 school district exemption is taxed for school purposes as if it were worth $160,000. Use that as a mechanism example, not a guaranteed savings estimate.

opening_question: What is the Guadalupe County homestead exemption deadline for 2026 homebuyers?
quick_answer: The Guadalupe County homestead exemption deadline for 2026 is before May 1, with local materials commonly treating April 30 as the practical filing date. You file with the Guadalupe Appraisal District, not the tax office, and Texas Comptroller guidance says exemption applications are filed with the appraisal district in the county where the property is located. The homestead exemption can reduce the taxable value used for property taxes, including a school-tax example where a $300,000 home with a $140,000 exemption is taxed for school purposes as if it were worth $160,000. For expert updates, contact Cody Posey Real Estate.

content_sections.h: Why does the Guadalupe County homestead exemption deadline matter before you buy?
content_sections.p: The homestead exemption is one of those Texas details buyers hear about late, usually after closing, when the mailbox starts filling with appraisal district notices, lender escrow statements, and property tax estimates. If you're buying in Guadalupe County, including the New Braunfels side near FM 1101, Solms, Seguin, Cibolo, Marion, or Schertz, you want the deadline on your calendar before you are under contract. The general deadline is before May 1 for the tax year, and the clean practical target is April 30. That does not mean every buyer can file the moment they start shopping. A residence homestead exemption is tied to ownership and occupancy. The key planning point is this: you buy the house, make it your principal residence, then file with the appraisal district using the required documentation. That is different from your lender's escrow setup, different from your title company closing statement, and different from the county tax office that eventually receives tax payments. I see this confuse New Braunfels buyers all the time because the city crosses county lines. Two homes can be ten minutes apart, both feel like New Braunfels, and still route through different appraisal districts. If the property is in Guadalupe County, you're dealing with Guadalupe Appraisal District. If it's in Comal County, that's a different district. This is one reason I want buyers checking the county, taxing entities, and exemption path as part of the offer strategy, not after the keys are handed over. The exemption is not a magic discount on the purchase price. It affects taxable value, which then flows into your property tax bill and your lender's escrow analysis. If you're still comparing monthly payment scenarios, use the New Braunfels mortgage calculator as a planning tool, then verify the tax estimate with your lender, appraisal district information, and the actual property record before making a final offer decision.

content_sections.h: Where do Guadalupe County buyers file the homestead exemption?
content_sections.p:
File with the appraisal district in the county where the property is located. For Guadalupe County homes, that means the Guadalupe Appraisal District. The Texas Comptroller's property tax exemption guidance is clear that exemption applications go to the county appraisal district, not to the tax office, the title company, the city, or your mortgage servicer.

This distinction matters because Texas property tax work is split between different offices. The appraisal district handles appraised values and exemptions. Taxing units set rates. Tax offices collect tax payments. Your mortgage servicer may collect escrow and pay the bill on your behalf, but that does not mean your servicer files the homestead exemption for you. Buyers who assume someone else handled it can miss the filing window or lose months of tax planning clarity.

Guadalupe Appraisal District guidance also notes that the homestead exemption application requires a copy of your Texas driver's license or state-issued personal identification certificate as documentation. The practical buyer takeaway is simple: after closing, make sure your ID address and exemption application details line up with the property. If something about your timing, occupancy, or documentation is unusual, ask the appraisal district directly before the deadline instead of guessing.

This belongs in the same bucket as closing cost and escrow planning. Your cash to close is one number, your monthly payment is another, and your property tax escrow can shift after exemptions, appraisal changes, or tax-rate updates. If you need the broader cost picture before you write an offer, build a buyer plan around the full monthly number, not just principal and interest.

content_sections.h: How can the exemption affect a 2026 buyer's payment plan?
content_sections.p: The exemption can reduce the taxable value used by certain taxing entities, which can lower the tax amount compared with having no exemption. The Texas Comptroller gives a simple school-tax example: if a home is appraised at $300,000 and qualifies for a $140,000 school district exemption, school taxes are calculated as if the home were worth $160,000 for that purpose. That example is helpful because it shows the mechanism, not because it guarantees your exact savings. Your result depends on your property's appraised value, the exemptions you qualify for, the taxing units attached to that property, and tax rates adopted for the year. Local option exemptions can also come into play, and the Comptroller notes that a local option exemption cannot be less than $5,000. Texas Tax Code Section 11.13 also includes a $3,000 residence homestead exemption for counties that collect farm-to-market or flood control taxes. The part buyers miss is timing. If you're buying in 2026, the home may have the seller's current exemption history, a prior appraised value, a new purchase price, and a future escrow adjustment all in the same conversation. That is why I don't like buyers shopping off a single online payment estimate. In Guadalupe County, especially around fast-growing New Braunfels and Cibolo corridors, property tax assumptions can change the comfort level of a payment faster than a small price negotiation can. For a practical comparison, I usually walk buyers through three numbers before we chase houses: today's estimated payment, the payment if taxes reset closer to the purchase price, and the payment after the homestead exemption is filed and reflected. That keeps you from being surprised later, because a strong offer is not just about winning. It's about winning a house you can still comfortably own.

content_sections.h: What should New Braunfels buyers do after closing in Guadalupe County?
content_sections.p: After closing, confirm the county and appraisal district for the property, then file the exemption application with the Guadalupe Appraisal District if the home qualifies as your principal residence. Keep the before-May-1 deadline in mind, and treat April 30 as the date you do not want to miss. Save proof of submission, because clean records help if you need to follow up later. Do not rely on closing alone to finish this. Title companies handle a lot, but the homestead exemption is still your filing. Lenders care about escrow, but they do not replace the appraisal district. The tax office collects payments, but it is not where the exemption application starts. If there is one practical sentence to remember, it is this: appraisal district for exemptions, tax office for tax bills. This is also the right moment to check your total housing file. Make sure your lender's escrow estimate, homeowners insurance, HOA dues if applicable, municipal utility district or public improvement district payments if applicable, and property tax assumptions still match the home you actually bought. That matters in parts of Guadalupe County where one subdivision may have a different tax stack than the next one down the road. If you're still in the shopping stage, the better move is to build this into your buyer game plan now. A lot of people want to start with bedroom count and finishes. I want you to know the county line, tax setup, commute pattern, floodplain questions where relevant, and exemption path before we get emotionally attached to the wrong payment. The New Braunfels buyer guide is a good starting point, and this deeper Texas homestead exemption guide for New Braunfels buyers can help you connect the tax detail with the rest of the contract timeline.
